Null attributes are passed as undefined, because the view props are optional rather than nullable. The document stores references, never values. Each data node and token carries its binding definition, so a pasted node or a page opened months later can still be re-resolved, and gckToken.text is always "". renderHTML writes …, so editor.getHTML(), server-side generateHTML and the stored JSON contain no numbers that could go stale or leak another viewer's rows. The cost is that editor.getText() and

gck/packages/target-tiptap/src/to-native.ts (new) toNative no longer calls resolveToken: the Tiptap output is identical whatever the bindings' current values are, so a refresh never changes the document (and never creates an undo step or a collaboration update); only the node views re-render. Every block becomes exactly one top-level node, which is what lets applyPatch treat "block" and "top-level node" as the same thing. gckBlockId is written unconditionally: in an editor without GckBlockIds, ProseMirror's NodeType.create keeps only the attributes a node type declares, so the extra key is dropped on the way in instead of failing the schema check.

Transform and edit intents ("turn this page into a dashboard", "rewrite the second section shorter") start from the host's content (5.1). fromHost reads the whole document, or the current selection when there is one (editor.state.doc.cut(from, to).toJSON()), and builds a partial Artifact: for transform its blocks become submit's selection; for edit the host merges it over the artifact it applied earlier (keeping id, bindings and provenance) and passes that as baseArtifact. Ids come from gckBlockId, so the base artifact's block ids are the ones in the document, including blocks the user edited by hand since the apply. Plain digits found in host text are kept, but the engine's edit prompt tells the model they are user-authored and the validator reports them as I5 warnings instead of errors for edit intents. gck/packages/target-tiptap/src/from-host.ts (new) Because the definitions travel in the nodes, fromHost returns a partial Artifact whose bindings are complete and refreshable even for a document that was saved, closed and edited by hand since the apply. The edit run's engine re-resolves every binding the result references, so an edited page never mixes fresh and old numbers. The import is lossy by design for anything the IR does not model (code blocks, native tables, host nodes such as mentions). The client shows which nodes were not imported, and a replace apply only replaces the range that was imported, so unmodeled content outside it is never deleted.

An edit run ends with a final artifact and the controller's ArtifactDiff against the base. patchEditor turns that into one ProseMirror transaction: it indexes the top-level nodes of the current document by gckBlockId, replaces each changed block's node with the new one from native (toNative of the final artifact), deletes removed blocks, and inserts added blocks next to their nearest neighbor that is already in the document. Section headings are not blocks and do not appear in the diff, so patchEditor reconciles them from the artifact itself: a changed section title replaces its H2, a new section with a title inserts one, and an H2 whose section is gone is deleted only when the first block under it is also being removed (so headings that belong to other content in the document are never touched). gck/packages/target-tiptap/src/patch.ts (new) Three properties of the code are deliberate. Nothing is dispatched until every position is computed, and all steps share one Transaction, so the history records the whole edit as one undo step, the same rule as 8.5. A changed block that is no longer in the document (the user deleted it after the apply) fails the whole patch with patch_anchor_missing instead of silently skipping it; the apply bar then offers replace. Removed blocks that are already gone are ignored, since the end state is the one the user asked for. editor.view.dispatch also works before the editor is mounted: Tiptap 3 returns a stub view with a dispatch that applies the transaction to the editor state, which is what the test below relies on. Gotcha: ids are copied by paste and lost by editors without the extension Copying a paragraph and pasting it elsewhere copies its gckBlockId. index keeps the first node with a given id and reports the rest as patch_duplicate_id, so a patch can change the wrong copy if the user moved the original. fromHost runs stampGckBlockIds before every edit run, which gives each later duplicate a fresh id, so the base artifact and the document agree again. Splitting a node with Enter does not duplicate the id, because the attribute is declared with keepOnSplit: false. Gotcha: patch does not move blocks The diff lists added, removed and changed ids, not moves. If an edit run only reorders two blocks, neither is in the diff and the document keeps its order. Gotcha: Handlebars formatNumber is not d3 The plugin's formatNumber helper is number.toLocaleString(locale) (apache/superset: superset-frontend/plugins/plugin-chart-handlebars/src/components/Handlebars/HandlebarsViewer.tsx:121-130), so SMART_NUMBER, ,.3s and other d3 specs cannot be reproduced: $591k in the other targets is $591,190 in the dashboard sentence. The adapter keeps the binding's prefix, suffix and currency symbol as literal

Superset's own editor does not save layouts through position_json. It puts the layout into json_metadata.positions and PUTs that (apache/superset: superset-frontend/src/dashboard/components/Header/index.tsx:465). On the backend, DashboardDAO.set_dash_metadata (apache/superset: superset/daos/dashboard.py:820) reads positions, rebuilds the dashboard's chart membership (dashboard.slices) from the CHART nodes, writes uuid into every chart node, and stores the result as position_json (dashboard.py:920). Create runs the same function when json_metadata is present (apache/superset: superset/commands/dashboard/create.py:67). The adapter therefore always sends the layout inside json_metadata.positions, and also as position_json. DashboardPostSchema (apache/superset: superset/dashboards/schemas.py:460) accepts dashboard_title (up to 500 characters), slug, description, editors, viewers, position_json (validated only as JSON, validate_json, schemas.py:115), css, theme_id, json_metadata (validated against DashboardJSONMetadataSchema, which includes positions, schemas.py:201 and :222), published, certified_by, certification_details, is_managed_externally, external_url and uuid. The endpoint is POST /api/v1/dashboard/ (apache/superset: superset/dashboards/api.py:1029), answering 201 with id, result and uuid (api.py:1085). Updates go to PUT /api/v1/dashboard/<pk> (api.py:1097, schema DashboardPutSchema, schemas.py:535). gck/packages/target-superset-dashboard/src/apply.ts (new) The undo for an existing dashboard is "PUT the previous layout back", which is the blueprint's rule for this host (keep the previous position_json for revert). For a new dashboard, undo is deletion, which the UI offers as an explicit action rather than an automatic one. The adapter, createSupersetDashboardTarget({ tabs, chartNames, chartParams, allowChartCreation?, dashboardId? }), returns a TargetAdapter<DashboardNative> whose toNative is toPositions and whose apply is applyDashboard; its promptHints ask for headline numbers in metric blocks and for qualitative prose around them, because only metric-only sentences can become live text. chartParams are the parsed params of the catalog's charts, which the host reads together with their names. Once applied, the generated tab needs no kit code to stay live; Superset's frontend does the refreshing, as the viewer, for every CHART on it, including the derived and Handlebars charts: Trigger Superset behavior Kit involvement dashboard open every chart queries with the viewer's identity, so RBAC and row level security apply per viewer none native filter change charts in the filter's scope re-query the generated tab is in scope when the filter's scope.rootPath covers it (below) dashboard "Refresh" every chart re-queries none auto refresh (interval) json_metadata.refresh_frequency (apache/superset: superset/dashboards/schemas.py:215), read by the frontend at superset-frontend/src/dashboard/actions/hydrate.ts:411 toPositions writes it from artifact.refresh.intervalSec, never below 60 s, and never overwrites a value the dashboard already has a viewer without access to a chart's dataset Superset's own error for that chart none: the generated tab holds no copied numbers that could leak Embeds need no special handling here: an embed block is a CHART of its saved chart, rendered natively whatever its viz type (maps, deck.gl, Sankey), which is the one target where every Superset visualization is fully live. Native filter scope is decided by layout, not by the cached chart lists. On master, chartsInScope and tabsInScope in native_filter_configuration are documented as denormalized caches that the client recomputes from each filter's scope and the layout on every load (apache/superset: superset/dashboards/filter_scope.py:17-35); a chart is in scope when one of its layout parents is in scope.rootPath and it is not in scope.excluded (get_chart_ids_in_scope, filter_scope.py:71). A filter scoped to the whole dashboard (rootPath: ["ROOT_ID"]) therefore covers the new tab's charts without any change to json_metadata, because every node's parents starts at ROOT_ID. A filter scoped to specific tabs does not, and applyDashboard reports it as filter_scope_review instead of guessing. This file is on master only; on 6.1 the same client-side recomputation is assumed but not verified here, so the integration test opens the dashboard and checks which filters apply. When the artifact was generated on this same dashboard, its saved-chart bindings carry the captured filter context (filter_context.mode: "captured"), but on the dashboard itself the live native filters win: the

The text target is the simplest and the most reused: the dashboard target uses it for MARKDOWN components, and the Superset host uses it for alert and report narratives and for the "text" surfaces described in Host integrations. It has four output profiles. Text is live or a snapshot depending on where it is shown, and the target is explicit about which: Where the text lives Data How rendered by the kit: previews, the and web components live: same binding store and refresh controller as a Tiptap page (on open, Refresh, interval of at least 60 s through a refresh-interval attribute, filter change) render re-runs whenever the store changes exported: a Markdown file, plain text, HTML, an email body, a Superset Markdown component snapshot, stamped "Data as of" render(..., { dataAsOf: "footer" }), the default scheduled report or alert narrative re-resolved per send, as the schedule's executor the schedule calls the engine's render endpoint, which resolves the definitions and renders with this target (Live Superset data); a schedule that cannot re-render must not carry tokens, and the validator for the alert and report surfaces rejects them with tokens_not_live Profile Used for Headings Data blocks Escaping markdown Superset Markdown components, chat # levels chart and table as a Markdown table from the snapshot, metric as bold value Markdown punctuation escaped in plain segments plain SMS, notifications, title fields none (uppercased line) Label: value lines none html Superset Markdown components when HTML is wanted h2 to h4 full HTML escaping, then sanitizing email report description (email body)

A user has the Sales dashboard (id 37) open, filtered to EMEA through its "Region" native filter, and types into the Tiptap page panel next to it: Write a QBR summary for EMEA from the Sales dashboard: headline numbers, the revenue trend, and where revenue came from. The run carries target: tiptap-doc, data.allowedChartIds: [411, 412, 413, 414], data.allowedDatasetIds: [12] (the sales dataset behind the dashboard) and, as data.scope, the dashboard's filter state with a permalink key. The catalog (Step 6.1) turns them into five candidates, each resolved once as the user so its mapping could be derived from real result columns: Key Source Kind Derived mapping b_m12_revenue saved metric revenue of dataset 12, last quarter, compared with one year earlier metric {metric: "revenue", previous_column: "revenue__1 year ago"} b_c411 chart 411, big_number (orders by month with trendline) metric {metric: "count", x: "order_date", compare: "previous_period"} b_c412 chart 412, big_number_total (average deal size) metric {metric: "AVG(deal_size)"} b_c413 chart 413, echarts_timeseries_bar (revenue by month) chart {x: "order_date", series: ["SUM(revenue)"], series_labels: {...}, sort: "x_asc"} b_c414 chart 414, table (top countries) table {columns: ["country", "revenue", "revenue_share"], max_rows: 10} Every binding carries the captured filter context (Region = EMEA, permalink Xk2pQ9), so a later refresh asks for the same EMEA scope the text was written about. Snapshot values are illustrative; meta is shown on the first binding only. The Artifact (full JSON) Four properties make this artifact refreshable rather than a record of one moment. Every number in prose is a token with text: "", so there is nothing to go stale in the prose itself and I5 passes. Every binding has a populated mapping and the captured EMEA filter context, so any resolver (the engine, Part VIII's refresh service, a host's refresh controller) can re-run it as whoever is viewing. "Sep 2026" is a token (argmax:Revenue) because it is data: the best month changes when the data does, and as plain text it would pass I5 through the calendar allowlist but be frozen. And generatedAgainst records which snapshot the prose was written against, so a later refresh that changes the numbers can tell the reader the sentences may be outdated (Live Superset data). The table binding shows why per-column formats exist:

Adapters are pure, so their tests need no LLM and no running host. Golden files. Each target keeps fixtures/artifacts/*.json (shared across targets, including the worked example and edge cases: empty sections, forbidden bindings, unknown block types, maximum limits) and golden/<target>/*.json|md|html. The test serializes, pretty-prints with sorted keys, and compares. Updating a golden file is an explicit command, so a change in output always shows up in review. gck/packages/target-superset-dashboard/test/golden.test.ts (new) Structural checks against the host's own rules. Golden files prove stability, not validity. The dashboard tests also walk every generated layout with a port of Superset's nesting table (isValidChild.ts:58) and assert that every row's widths sum to at most 12; the Tiptap tests build a real editor schema from [StarterKit, ...gckNodes] with getSchema from @tiptap/core and call schema.nodeFromJSON(doc).check() on every output; the text tests run the email profile through an nh3-equivalent sanitizer with Superset's allowlist and assert the output is unchanged by sanitizing. Round-trip tests. For the Tiptap target the core property is fromHost(toNative(a)) equals a, ids included (they travel in gckBlockId), except for the lossy cases listed in 8.1 and the section fields the document does not hold (layoutHint): gck/packages/target-tiptap/test/roundtrip.test.ts (new) Token segments compare exactly, text included, because both sides hold ""; binding definitions come back through collectBindings and are compared with the fixture's bindings minus runtime state. Marks on token segments (the bold revenue token) survive because inline puts them on the gckToken node and rich reads them back. Patch tests. patchEditor runs against a real editor. Tiptap 3 can create an editor without an element (element: null), so the test needs no mounting; it checks the document after the patch, that content the artifact does not own survives, and that one undo restores the original: gck/packages/target-tiptap/test/patch.test.ts (new) The section title change ("Plan" to "Plan B") is not in the diff; the first test also proves that patchEditor reconciles headings from the artifact. The text target's equivalent test is a single assertion in its own package: textTarget.applyPatch hands apply the Markdown of the final artifact with mode replace, and returns that result

Reads: servers/fastapi/utils/sse.py, servers/fastapi/models/sse_response.py, servers/fastapi/api/v1/ppt/endpoints/presentation.py, servers/fastapi/api/v1/auth/principal.py, servers/fastapi/api/main.py, servers/nextjs/app/(presentation-generator)/outline/hooks/useOutlineStreaming.ts, servers/nextjs/app/(presentation-generator)/services/api/chat.ts, servers/nextjs/app/(presentation-generator)/services/api/header.ts · Builds on: Artifact Spec and targets · Time: ~60 min This chapter specifies the wire contract between the browser and the GCK Engine and builds both ends of it: the run lifecycle and endpoints, every stream event with a JSON example, ordering and idempotency, block-level JSON Patch plus text.delta, outline review, the error model, resume with Last-Event-ID from a server-side event log, heartbeats, auth and CORS. You get the full TypeScript for @gck/protocol events and the @gck/client transport, an AG-UI mapping, and a FastAPI sketch of the event log that generalizes Presenton's SSE helpers. A run resolves each data binding once, but no GCK output may keep the numbers of that moment. The data side of the protocol (protocol 1.1, additive to gck.artifact/1) therefore has two halves: inside a run, binding.resolved carries each binding's live Superset snapshot, status and error (Step 3); after the run, the refresh protocol (/v1/data/catalog, /v1/data/resolve, /v1/render, Step 16) re-resolves the stored binding definitions as the viewing user on open, on demand, on an interval, when artifact parameters change and when host filters change, and headless for schedules. The data model itself (binding sources, snapshots, parameters, refresh policies, per-target behavior and viz coverage) is in Live Superset data. Files under gck/ and gck_engine/ are new code for Part IX; files under servers/ are Presenton at snapshot 571461f. Superset citations of the form apache/superset: path:line refer to the Superset master clone used for Part IX.

docs.t: Step 1: What the protocol must fix in Presenton's streams
docs.x: Streaming (SSE) covers Presenton's streams; four of their properties block reuse. The stream is the generation. A dropped outline or Standard stream restarts all LLM calls (the hooks reset their buffers before retrying, servers/nextjs/app/(presentation-generator)/outline/hooks/useOutlineStreaming.ts:82-100); a Smart stream re-runs the generator, which replays checkpointed slides and continues (servers/fastapi/api/v1/ppt/endpoints/presentation.py:1941-1993). Frames carry no id. SSEResponse.to_string() writes only event: and data: lines (servers/fastapi/models/sse_response.py:10-11), so the browser has nothing to send back as Last-Event-ID. The browser uses EventSource, which can only GET without custom headers (useOutlineStreaming.ts:105-109). Auth therefore rides on the session cookie, which resolve_request_principal checks before any Bearer API key (servers/fastapi/api/v1/auth/principal.py:22-57). Errors are a string plus optional metadata. Smart streams add source, status_code, error_type, retryable, completed_slides and total_slides (presentation.py:2246-2267); outline and Standard streams send only detail. A component mounted inside Superset, a Tiptap page or a third-party site needs the opposite on every point: generation that survives the connection, numbered events, header-based auth with no cookie, and machine-readable errors.

docs.t: Step 2: The run lifecycle and endpoints
docs.x: A run is one request to turn a prompt plus host context into an Artifact (the IR from Artifact Spec and targets). The engine executes the run as a background task; HTTP connections only observe it. Paths below are relative to the engine base URL {engine}, the engineUrl given to GckClient. It never contains /v1 (the client appends /v1/runs... itself): a standalone engine is https://gck.example.com, an engine behind a same-origin ingress is for example /gck-engine, and an engine mounted inside Presenton is /api/gck (Extracting the engine from Presenton). The URLs in RunCreated are absolute paths that include that mount prefix; the client does not rely on them. Method and path Request Success response Idempotency POST /v1/runs RunRequest JSON, headers Authorization, optional Idempotency-Key 201 {runId, streamUrl, inputUrl, cancelUrl, createdAt}; with Accept: text/event-stream instead 200 and the event stream, run id in header GCK-Run-Id same key within 24 h returns the same run (200) GET /v1/runs/{runId}/events headers Authorization, optional Last-Event-ID 200 text/event-stream safe to repeat GET /v1/runs/{runId} none 200 RunSummary (state, lastEventId, artifactVersion, pending input, error) safe GET /v1/runs/{runId}/artifact none 200 {version, lastEventId, artifact, bindingState}; bindingState is the latest binding.resolved payload per binding (protocol 1.1) safe POST /v1/runs/{runId}/input {inputId, kind, decision, outline?} 202 {accepted: true} same inputId and same body returns 202 again; a different body returns 409 input_already_resolved POST /v1/runs/{runId}/cancel {reason?} 202 {state} always 202; a terminal run reports its final state Bindings are re-resolved outside any run through three more endpoints, GET /v1/data/catalog, POST /v1/data/resolve and POST /v1/render; they share this chapter's auth, SSE framing and error model and are specified in Step 16. The request body is the one fixed in the blueprint, with the protocol 1.1 data fields filled in for a run started on a filtered Superset dashboard: POST /v1/runs (request body) data field Since Meaning provider 1.0 Data provider id, "superset". allowedChartIds 1.0 Saved charts the viewer can see (from the catalog); the planner may bind only these. allowedDatasetIds 1.1 Datasets the planner may use for superset_dataset and superset_metric sources. scope 1.1 HostDataScope: the host's filter state at

docs.t: Step 3: The event envelope and every event type
docs.x: Each SSE frame carries one event: id: is the sequence number, event: repeats the type for curl and devtools, and data: is one line of compact JSON: One frame on the wire Envelope fields: v (protocol major, 1), id (gapless from 1), runId, ts (ISO 8601), type, data, and an optional progress {phase, message?, completed?, total?} that replaces Presenton's free-text status frames. The client trusts the JSON type, not the event: line. type data When run.started {runId, target: {id, manifestVersion}} first event of every run plan.proposed {outline: OutlineItem[], planVersion, final} after planning; again with final: true after review run.awaiting_input {kind: "outline_review", inputId, expiresAt} only when options.reviewOutline artifact.patch {baseVersion, version, ops: JsonPatchOp[]} primary content channel text.delta {blockId, path, delta, format, baseVersion} optional, inside one block binding.resolved BindingUpdate: {bindingId, status, snapshot?, snapshotAt?, error?, changed?, reason?} (Step 16.4) per data binding, from the final plan on, in section order run.warning {code, message, blockId?} non-fatal problems run.completed {artifactVersion, usage} terminal, success run.failed {code, message, retryable, retryAfterMs?, details?, completedSections?, totalSections?} terminal, failure or cancel Examples of each payload (envelope fields other than type omitted): Event payloads completedSections and totalSections are the generalization of Smart mode's completed_slides and total_slides error metadata (presentation.py:2258-2267).

binding.resolved carries exactly the BindingUpdate that the refresh protocol sends (Step 16), so one reducer in the browser serves runs and refreshes. Its snapshot has one normative shape per binding kind, in snake_case, the same JSON that Part VIII stores in slide_data_bindings (Story 1): Binding kind snapshot Example metric MetricSnapshot {value, previous?, previous_label?, meta?} {"value":1840000,"previous":1610000,"previous_label":"Sep 2026"} chart ChartSnapshot {categories, series: [{name, key?, values}], meta?} {"categories":["Germany","France"],"series":[{"name":"Pipeline","key":"pipeline","values":[412000,388000]}]} table TableSnapshot {columns, labels?, coltypes?, rows, meta?} with raw cell values {"columns":["country","revenue"],"labels":["Country","Revenue"],"coltypes":["string","number"],"rows":[["Germany",412000]]} embed none: a live Superset chart, never a snapshot meta is what lets a view be honest about the data: query_ts is the "data as of" stamp, truncated and rowcount say whether the row cap cut the result, resolved_by is the viewer key of whoever's row-level security view this is, scope_hash identifies the effective filters, time_range feeds the period token, and applied_filters / rejected_filters show which captured dashboard filters reached the query. Field-by-field definitions are in Live Superset data. status snapshot error Meaning ok present absent Fresh result for this viewer and scope. stale absent absent A transient failure (reason holds the retryable code, for example timeout); the client keeps the snapshot it has and shows it as stale with Retry, or the unavailable panel with Retry when it has none. error absent {code, message, retryable} No usable data; the view shows "Data unavailable" and, when retryable, a Retry action. forbidden absent, always {code, message, retryable: false} The viewer may not read this data; nothing is shown, never another user's snapshot. pending is the status a binding is stamped with before its first resolution; the engine never sends it. binding.resolved for the failure statuses How the engine produces these events during a run: Start at the final plan. As soon as plan.proposed with final: true names the bindings, the engine resolves them as the run's principal (the data token comes from a token exchange, Step 10) and appends binding.resolved in section order, so the first section's numbers arrive

Three counters keep the client consistent, each with one job. Counter Scope Rule on the client Event id per run, gapless from 1 Drop any event with id <= lastEventId (a replay duplicate). If id > lastEventId + 1, a frame was lost: abort and reconnect with Last-Event-ID: lastEventId. Artifact version per run, increments by exactly 1 per artifact.patch Apply only when baseVersion === store.version. If version <= store.version, skip (already applied). Otherwise call GET /v1/runs/{id}/artifact and replace the store. planVersion per run The newest plan.proposed wins; final: true locks the outline. text.delta, binding.resolved and run.warning never change the artifact version. A text.delta whose baseVersion is older than its block's last replace is discarded. Binding runtime state (snapshot, snapshotAt, status, error) lives in an overlay beside the artifact, because the browser's data provider (@gck/data-superset) also resolves bindings after the run (Step 16) and must not fork the engine's version line. For the same reason GET /v1/runs/{id}/artifact returns the overlay as bindingState next to the artifact, and a resync keeps it (store.reset(artifact, version, { keepBindings: true })); at gck.applied the run controller copies the definitions and the overlay into the host's BindingStore, whose refresh controller takes over (React SDK and UI kit). Several binding.resolved events for one binding are applied last-writer-wins by event id. On the request side, POST /v1/runs honors an Idempotency-Key header (the client generates a UUID per user submission), so a retried POST after a network timeout cannot start two paid runs. POST /input is keyed by the engine-issued inputId. POST /cancel is idempotent by definition. Gotcha Presenton's Standard slide chunks concatenate without commas into invalid JSON, so the client parses each chunk alone (servers/nextjs/app/(presentation-generator)/presentation/hooks/usePresentationStreaming.ts:454-510). In GCK every artifact.patch is complete JSON; the only partial JSON is a format: "json" text.delta for one block.

docs.t: Step 5: JSON Patch at block granularity, plus text.delta
docs.x: artifact.patch uses RFC 6902 JSON Patch (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6902) over JSON Pointers (RFC 6901, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6901). The engine follows four rules that keep patches cheap to apply and easy to render: The first patch is a root replace ("path": "", the whole document in RFC 6901) that installs the skeleton at version 1, except in an edit run, which starts from the base (below). The same op doubles as the resync snapshot after log compaction (Step 9). Blocks are the unit of change. Ops target /sections/-, /sections/{i}/blocks/-, /sections/{i}/blocks/{j}, /bindings/{id} or top-level fields such as /title, never anything deeper than a block. Renderers key by block id, not by index. Only add, replace and remove are emitted. move and copy complicate index bookkeeping in a streaming renderer; test is reserved for client-side edit patches. A patch is atomic. RFC 6902 requires that a patch with a failing op is not applied at all; the client applier in React SDK and UI kit copies on write and commits only after the last op. A typical section arrives as three patches: Three artifact.patch payloads for one section An edit run has no skeleton to install: the stream starts from the base artifact in context.document, which is version 0 on both sides. The engine sends no root replace; its first artifact.patch has baseVersion: 0 and changes the base in place, block by block, and run.completed carries the final version. Untouched blocks are never re-sent, changed blocks are replaced under their existing id, removed blocks are removed and new blocks get new ids, so the client can diff the final artifact against the base by block id (the run controller exposes that diff as run.diff). For the edit request above: The edit run's stream (payloads only) An edit run re-resolves every binding the resulting artifact references, not only the one behind the new metric block, so an edited page never mixes fresh numbers with numbers from the original run. changed compares the new snapshot hash with the binding's generatedAgainst: b_c412 moved since the page was generated, so the engine re-stamps it (the artifact.patch at version 3) because the rewritten text now describes the new value; b_c413 did not move and keeps its stamp. A client therefore resets its store to the base at version 0 before it reads the stream (createRunController and runToCompletion

When options.reviewOutline is true, the engine pauses after planning for the user to confirm the outline: the checkpoint Presenton implements as a whole page (User journey), here a pause inside one run. The engine emits plan.proposed (final: false) then run.awaiting_input with an inputId and an expiresAt (default 30 minutes). The stream stays open and sends heartbeats. The client may disconnect; the run stays parked. The client posts the decision: POST /v1/runs/{runId}/input decision is approve (no outline), edit (full replacement list: reorder, delete, rename and add are all expressed by the list) or cancel. New sections have sectionId: null; the engine assigns ids. The engine validates: at most limits.maxSections from the manifest, titles of at most 200 characters, and bindings a subset of what the planner offered (no chart ids outside allowedChartIds, no dataset ids outside allowedDatasetIds). Failures return 422 and leave the run waiting. On success the engine emits plan.proposed with planVersion: 2, final: true (normalized, all ids assigned), then artifact.patch events. If expiresAt passes, the run ends with run.failed {code: "input_expired", retryable: false}.

Every error, whether returned as an HTTP response body or as run.failed, has the same shape: Error body code HTTP retryable Meaning and client action invalid_request 400 / 422 false Validation failed; show message. unauthorized 401 false No or bad token. token_expired 401 true Refresh the token once, retry. forbidden 403 false Not allowed for this target, host or run. not_found 404 false Unknown run, or someone else's. conflict / input_already_resolved 409 false Stale input or duplicate decision. rate_limited 429 true Wait retryAfterMs (also sent as Retry-After). quota_exceeded 429 false Tenant budget spent. context_too_large 413 / stream false Ask the user to narrow context. model_output_invalid stream true The model failed schema validation after the engine's own retries. model_unavailable 502 / 503 / stream true Provider down or timed out. data_forbidden stream false The target requires data and every requested binding is forbidden for the user. One forbidden binding among others is a binding.resolved with status: "forbidden", not a run error. data_unavailable stream true Protocol 1.0 only. A 1.1 engine never sends it: a failing data provider becomes per-binding stale or error. data_token_expired 401 / stream true The engine could not exchange the caller's engine token for a data token (protocol 1.1). Call the token provider with forceRefresh: true and retry once. input_expired stream false Outline review timed out. cancelled stream false Cancel endpoint or engine shutdown. internal 500 / stream true Anything else. For unclassified exceptions, retryable follows Presenton's Smart rule: true for 408, 429 and 500 or more (presentation.py:2257-2264). A retryable run.failed means "a new run with the same request may succeed"; the run itself is terminal. Transport problems (dropped connection, heartbeat timeout, proxy 502 on GET /events) never produce run.failed; the client reconnects (Step 9). Data problems are a second, smaller error model that lives per binding, in binding.resolved.data.error ({code, message, retryable}) or, for transient failures, in binding.resolved.data.reason, in runs and refreshes alike. The codes, grouped by the status they produce: Binding error.code status Retryable Client action forbidden, chart_forbidden, datasource_forbidden forbidden no Show nothing, never Retry. chart_not_found, datasource_not_found, no_query_context,

docs.t: Step 8: Why fetch-based SSE, not EventSource
docs.x:
The WHATWG HTML standard defines EventSource with one option, withCredentials; there is no way to set the method or request headers (https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/server-sent-events.html). That is why Presenton's stream routes are GETs keyed by an id in the path (useOutlineStreaming.ts:105-109, usePresentationStreaming.ts:300). For GCK the limits are blocking: Need EventSource fetch + ReadableStream Authorization: Bearer header not possible; cookie only yes POST with a JSON body (one-shot mode) no yes Read the JSON body of a 401 or 429 no; any non-200 fails the connection and only fires error yes Control reconnect timing and give up browser-controlled; the spec reconnects after network errors fully client-controlled Last-Event-ID on reconnect automatic, but only for its own reconnects the client sets it explicitly on every reconnect it makes; after a page reload the run is found again by its id Cancel with AbortSignal close() only yes Detect a silent dead connection no heartbeat watchdog Presenton already has a fetch-based reader for chat: it POSTs with an AbortSignal (servers/nextjs/app/(presentation-generator)/services/api/chat.ts:104-116), reads response.body with a TextDecoder and splits frames on "

" (chat.ts:294-308; quoted in Story 4). @gck/client keeps that structure and fixes three things for a general transport: it splits lines on CR, LF and CRLF as the SSE grammar requires (the chat reader looks for "

" before it strips  inside processSseFrame, chat.ts:136, so a CRLF-framed stream would never split), it honors id: and retry: fields (ignored by the chat reader, chat.ts:141-149), and it treats comment lines as heartbeats. Gotcha Presenton's getHeader() sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin, Access-Control-Allow-Methods and Access-Control-Allow-Headers as request headers (servers/nextjs/app/(presentation-generator)/services/api/header.ts:1-9). Those are response headers; on a request they do nothing except force a CORS preflight and require the server to allow them. It works today only because FastAPI allows every header (servers/fastapi/api/main.py:94-100). Do not copy getHeader() into the kit.

The SSE standard says that a non-empty last event id is sent in a Last-Event-ID header on reconnection, and that an id containing U+0000 is ignored. GCK uses the same header for its own reconnects, set by the client: The client remembers lastEventId, the highest event id it has processed (not just received). On reconnect it sends GET /v1/runs/{id}/events with Last-Event-ID: 41. The engine reads events with seq > 41 from the event log, sends them, then tails new events live. If the log was compacted past 41, the engine first sends a synthetic root-replace artifact.patch with baseVersion: 0, which the client treats as "reset the store" (isSnapshotPatch, Step 11). Compaction keeps the latest binding.resolved row per binding, and the engine replays those rows right after the synthetic patch, so a resumed client gets its data overlay back and not only the text. Gotcha The event log holds the run principal's data, so it is readable only by that principal (load_run_for_principal_or_404, Step 13), and 24 hours after the run completes the engine rewrites every binding.resolved payload to {bindingId, status, snapshot_hash}. A replay after that window restores the text and the binding statuses but no numbers; the client's refresh controller fetches fresh ones as the viewer. Never serve a run's log to a different user to "share" a result: share the artifact, whose bindings each viewer resolves as themselves. A page reload can resume too: with a resumeKey, @gck/react keeps the active run's {runId} in sessionStorage and, after the reload, replays that run's log from the first event into a fresh store (React SDK and UI kit). This generalizes what Presenton does for Smart mode. There, slides are checkpointed to the database before they are emitted: servers/fastapi/api/v1/ppt/endpoints/presentation.py (excerpt) (presentation.py:2075-2078.) On reconnect, stream_smart_presentation replays every saved slide as a slide_html frame and resumes from the next slide (presentation.py:1941-1993). GCK keeps the rule (persist before you emit) and changes two things: it persists events, not domain rows, so any target can replay; and generation is a background task, so a reconnect only replays and tails. In Presenton the generation task is cancelled when the stream generator exits early (presentation.py:2189-2192); in GCK only POST /cancel cancels.

The log is the buffer. The run task appends and notifies; each subscriber reads the log at its own pace, by sequence number, in pages of 200. A slow browser costs a cursor and a database read, never a growing in-memory queue. At the source, the engine coalesces text.delta per block into at most one event per 50 ms, and marks those rows ephemeral so they are pruned once the block's final replace is committed. On the client, the store notifies React at most once per animation frame, so a burst of replayed events renders once.

No Presenton SSE endpoint sends keepalives; the bundled nginx relies on 30-minute read timeouts (nginx.conf:45-69). That fails behind a load balancer with a 60-second idle timeout, which is where an embedded component lives. The WHATWG standard suggests a comment line about every 15 seconds. The engine writes : hb every 15 seconds of silence, and the client aborts and reconnects after 45 seconds without any bytes (three missed heartbeats). The engine also sends Cache-Control: no-cache, no-transform and X-Accel-Buffering: no so nginx-style proxies do not buffer the stream.

The kit never holds a long-lived secret. The host passes a token provider callback: The client calls it before every request, including every reconnect, so a token that expired during a long review pause is replaced transparently. Hosts cache the token until shortly before expiry. Tokens are short-lived (5 minutes) and audience-scoped to the engine, minted by the host's own backend (Host integrations). On 401 token_expired the client calls the provider once with forceRefresh: true and retries once. Requests use credentials: "omit": no cookie, so no third-party-cookie blocking and no CSRF surface. The engine token is not a data token, and the browser never holds one. When a run or a refresh needs Superset data, the engine exchanges the caller's engine token for a short-lived data token at a new Story 8 endpoint, POST /api/v1/ai_slides/token-exchange (RFC 8693 shape, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8693: grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange, the engine token as subject_token, scope=ai_slides:refresh, client authentication by private_key_jwt). Superset verifies the subject token, resolves the user and returns a 15-minute Bearer token with audience analytics-data. The engine caches it per (sub, scope) until 30 seconds before expiry and never logs it or writes it into an event. Every query then runs inside Superset as that user, under override_user (apache/superset: superset/utils/core.py:1633), and goes through Superset's chart data command (apache/superset: superset/commands/chart/data/get_data_command.py:36), so the user's permissions and row-level security apply. If the exchange fails because the subject token expired, the engine answers data_token_expired and the client refreshes its engine token once. Hosts without a Superset session or a shared identity provider get no data token at all; their bindings resolve to error with no_data_identity. The identity bridges per host are in Live Superset data. When the engine is cross-origin, every GCK request is preflighted (an Authorization header and Last-Event-ID are not CORS-safelisted). The engine's CORS policy should be: Header Value Access-Control-Allow-Origin the exact host origin from an allowlist, never * for authenticated routes Access-Control-Allow-Methods GET, POST, OPTIONS Access-Control-Allow-Headers Authorization, Content-Type, Accept, Last-Event-ID, Idempotency-Key,

The protocol package is types plus JSON Schemas with zero runtime dependencies. This file covers runs and events; Artifact, DataBinding and TargetId come from src/artifact.ts and TargetManifest from src/target.ts, both specified in Artifact Spec and targets; the protocol 1.1 data types (BindingUpdate, HostDataScope, ParamValue and the refresh events) come from src/data.ts (Step 16.4 and Live Superset data). The package index re-exports every file (export * from "./artifact", "./target", "./data", "./run"), so run.ts does not re-export Artifact itself. Protocol 1.1 is a minor, additive bump: PROTOCOL_VERSION (the major in v and in the GCK-Protocol header) stays 1, and a 1.0 client that meets the new optional fields or event types ignores them. HostContext in target.ts is an alias of RunContext below: one JSON object, the run request's context, under two names. gck/packages/protocol/src/run.ts (new) isGckEvent is a structural guard only; full validation uses JSON Schemas shared with the engine's Pydantic models (Frontend engineering and quality). Gotcha An unknown type from a newer engine must be ignored, not treated as an error: every switch over events ends in a default branch that drops it. Breaking changes bump v; the engine rejects a client whose GCK-Protocol header is too old with invalid_request and details.minProtocol.
gck/packages/client/src/sse.ts (new)
gck/packages/client/src/errors.ts (new)

gck/packages/client/src/client.ts (new) Two design notes. The generator suspends at yield until the consumer asks for the next value, so lastEventId moves past an event only after the consumer has processed it; if a reducer throws, the event is replayed after reconnect instead of skipped. And failures resets after every successful event, so only consecutive failures count toward maxAttempts. TextDecoderStream does the job of decoder.decode(value, { stream: true }) in Presenton's chat reader (chat.ts:299). Gotcha fetch rejects with a TypeError for network failures and CORS rejections alike, so a misconfigured engine CORS policy looks like a flaky network and burns every retry. When onTransport shows only connect/disconnect pairs and no event was ever received, show "Cannot reach the AI engine (check CORS and network)" instead of retrying silently.

docs.t: Step 13: Engine side, the event log in FastAPI
docs.x: This sketch shows how the engine (Extracting the engine from Presenton) persists and serves events with Presenton's building blocks: SQLModel and async_session_maker, StreamingResponse, the error boundary of safe_sse_stream (servers/fastapi/utils/sse.py:10-38), the SSEResponse.to_string() frame format plus an id: line, and smart_error_metadata's retryable rule. gck_engine/runs/event_log.py (new) The router ties it together. POST /v1/runs (omitted) validates the body, resolves the Idempotency-Key and starts run_guard as a task stored in RUN_TASKS, so POST /cancel can reach it; the stream endpoint never starts or stops generation. gck_engine/runs/router.py (new, excerpt) FastAPI's Header maps last_event_id to the last-event-id header. The compaction branch (Step 9.1) belongs at the top of stream_run_events: if after is below the run's compacted floor, yield one synthetic root-replace frame built from GET /artifact data, with the sequence number of the last compacted event. Gotcha safe_sse_stream converts any late exception into an error frame (servers/fastapi/utils/sse.py:24-38). That is right when the stream is the generation, and wrong here: a database blip while reading the log would tell the client the run failed while the run task is still producing. In GCK the stream wrapper only logs and closes; run.failed comes exclusively from run_guard, which owns the run. Gotcha asyncio.Condition and RUN_TASKS live in one process. With several workers, a subscriber on worker B only sees appends from worker A at the next 15-second poll, and POST /cancel on B cannot reach a task on A. In production, use Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY or Redis pub/sub keyed by run id, and make cancel a row flag the run task checks between LLM calls; stream_generate_events already polls a stop condition every 0.1 s (servers/fastapi/utils/llm_utils.py:458-518, interval CLIENT_DISCONNECT_POLL_SECONDS at :27) and is the natural place for it.

AG-UI (https://docs.ag-ui.com/concepts/events) is an open event protocol between agent backends and UIs. Its type values are names such as RUN_STARTED and STATE_DELTA (https://docs.ag-ui.com/sdk/js/core/events), and its state deltas are RFC 6902 JSON Patch, so GCK maps closely: GCK event AG-UI event Mapping notes run.started RUN_STARTED threadId = host session or run id, runId = runId. progress.phase change STEP_STARTED / STEP_FINISHED stepName = planning, generating, resolving_data. plan.proposed STATE_DELTA on /plan Or CUSTOM {name: "gck.plan.proposed"} for clients that do not keep plan state. run.awaiting_input RUN_FINISHED with outcome: {type: "interrupt", interrupts: [...]} Interrupt draft (https://docs.ag-ui.com/concepts/interrupts): interrupt id, reason, optional responseSchema, expiresAt. The answer arrives as RunAgentInput.resume (interruptId, status, payload); the adapter turns it into POST /input. first artifact.patch (root replace) STATE_SNAPSHOT snapshot = {artifact}. artifact.patch STATE_DELTA delta = ops with paths prefixed by /artifact. Version fields go in metadata. text.delta CUSTOM {name: "gck.text.delta"} Not TEXT_MESSAGE_CONTENT: generic AG-UI chat clients would print the page as a chat reply. binding.resolved STATE_DELTA on /bindingState/{id} Refresh streams (Step 16) are not runs and are not mapped. run.warning CUSTOM {name: "gck.warning"} run.completed RUN_FINISHED result = {artifactVersion, usage}. run.failed RUN_ERROR message, code; retryable has no AG-UI field and goes in metadata. heartbeat comment none Transport concern. Recommendation: keep GCK's own protocol and ship an AG-UI adapter, not a dependency. GCK needs artifact versions with baseVersion checks, a retryable flag, ephemeral in-block deltas and a binding overlay, none of which AG-UI models directly; interrupts are still a draft in AG-UI, while outline review is GCK's core interaction; and @gck/protocol has a zero-dependency rule. The adapter, toAgUi(event, threadId) in gck/packages/protocol/src/ag-ui.ts (new), is a pure generator that implements the table row by row with structural types (no @ag-ui/core import) and drops unknown event types, so AG-UI clients such as a chat sidebar can observe GCK runs. Gotcha The outcome field on RUN_FINISHED comes from AG-UI's interrupt draft; the JS SDK's RunFinishedEvent documents only threadId, runId, result and usage. An AG-UI

A run ends, but its numbers must not. Every target (slides, tiptap-doc, superset-dashboard, text) shows Superset data fetched as the person viewing it, and re-fetches it after generation: when the page opens, when the viewer presses Refresh, on an interval, when the tab becomes visible again after the data went stale, when an artifact parameter or a host filter changes, before an export, and on a schedule for headless outputs. The refresh protocol is the wire contract for all of that. It is new code, it reuses this chapter's auth, SSE framing, heartbeats, CORS and error body, and it carries the same binding.resolved payload as a run, so one reducer in the browser serves both. Which binding refreshes when (refresh policies and per-target defaults), the Superset side of every query and the viz coverage are in Live Superset data; this step specifies the endpoints, events and types. The superset-dashboard target is the one exception on the wire: its data blocks are native Superset charts, which query Superset on open, on native filter change and on the dashboard's own refresh (refresh_frequency, read at apache/superset: superset-frontend/src/dashboard/actions/hydrate.ts:411), so nothing in the kit calls this protocol for them.

Method and path Request Success response Called by GET /v1/data/catalog?dashboardId=&q=&datasetIds=&cursor= headers Authorization 200 DataCatalog: the charts and datasets the caller can read (Story 8 catalog plus dataset metadata), each with refreshable and a reason, plus the caller's viewerKey the run controller before POST /v1/runs (it fills allowedChartIds and allowedDatasetIds) POST /v1/data/resolve ResolveRequest (16.4); Accept: text/event-stream or application/json SSE stream of refresh events (16.2), or 200 {refreshId, results, summary} the browser's refresh controller through @gck/data-superset; server callers and tests use the JSON form POST /v1/render RenderRequest: {artifact, target: "text", profile, params?, scope?} 200 {output, dataAsOf, warnings} headless callers only: schedules, alerts, reports (16.5) All three take the engine token from Step 10 and never a data token: the engine exchanges the caller's engine token for a short-lived data token at Story 8's token-exchange endpoint (Step 10), so every row is read inside Superset as the caller, under that user's permissions and row-level security. ResolveRequest.bindings holds definitions only: the engine ignores any snapshot, snapshotAt, status or error sent with them, so a client cannot inject numbers and a persisted artifact never needs to carry any. Every request names its trigger. The engine uses it for force, telemetry and the throttles in 16.6; the refresh controller in React SDK and UI kit picks the bindings. trigger Sent when Bindings in the request force on_open the controller starts on a saved page, deck or preview every binding the view uses, priority = the ones in the viewport false manual the viewer presses Refresh, or Retry on one binding all, or the retried id true, throttled (16.6) interval the controller clock fires (intervalSec of at least 60, plus or minus 10 percent, paused while the tab is hidden) bindings whose policy has interval false on_visible the tab becomes visible again bindings older than staleAfterSec (default 3600) false on_filter_change an artifact parameter or the host's filter state changed (16.3) the dependents of that parameter, or the follow_host bindings of that dashboard false before_export the host exports a file (PPTX, PDF, HTML, email) the bindings the export renders false on_schedule a headless caller re-renders for a scheduled send (16.5) every

A refresh stream uses the run stream's frame format with one change in the envelope: refreshId replaces runId. id counts from 1 within the refresh, the engine writes the : hb heartbeat comment every 15 seconds of silence (a Story 8 batch can take up to its 30-second timeout), and the response carries the same Cache-Control: no-cache, no-transform and X-Accel-Buffering: no headers. There is no resume: refresh events are not written to the event log, Last-Event-ID is ignored, and a dropped refresh stream is simply re-requested, because a refresh is cheap to restart and the engine's 60-second per-viewer cache answers the repeat. One refresh frame on the wire type data When refresh.started {refreshId, total, viewerKey, trigger} first event; viewerKey is the viewer's opaque key, compared with meta.resolved_by by the redact policy binding.loading {bindingId} before the engine sends a binding's item to Superset (not for engine cache hits) binding.resolved BindingUpdate {bindingId, status, snapshot?, snapshotAt?, error?, changed?, reason?} once per binding, priority ids first, then artifact order refresh.completed {ok, stale, errors, forbidden, durationMs} terminal, the request finished (whatever each binding's status) refresh.failed GckErrorBody (Step 7) terminal, the whole request failed: rate_limited, data_token_expired, unauthorized A full on_open refresh of the edit example's two bindings, one of which Superset answered too slowly (payloads only): POST /v1/data/resolve, trigger on_open (event payloads) b_c412 came back changed: true against its generatedAgainst stamp, so a view can offer "Text was written against data as of ... Regenerate?", which starts an edit run (Step 5). b_c413 is stale: Story 8 timed out, so the update carries no snapshot and the client keeps the snapshot it already holds, badged as stale with a Retry action; the next trigger (Retry, interval or tab return) resolves it again. The JSON form of the same request returns the updates keyed by binding id: POST /v1/data/resolve with Accept: application/json (response, snapshot elided) Gotcha isGckEvent (Step 11) requires a runId, so it rejects every refresh frame. That is deliberate: a refresh event fed into a run's artifact store by mistake would be dropped, not applied against the run's version line. Refresh events go to the BindingStore, whose apply accepts both a refresh event and a run's

Artifact parameters (Artifact.parameters, for example p_region) are inputs the viewer can change; their current values live in view state (host state or a URL parameter such as ?gck_p_region=APAC), never in the artifact. A binding depends on a parameter through params: [{param, as, column?, op?}]. When a value changes, the refresh controller waits 400 ms for more changes, aborts any in-flight request for the dependent bindings, and sends one request with only those bindings, the parameter definitions and the viewer's current values. Tokens and charts over other bindings do not move. POST /v1/data/resolve after a parameter change (request body) The engine computes one effective scope per binding from four layers, lowest first: the saved query (L0), the dashboard filter context (L1, here the captured region IN [EMEA]), artifact parameters with the viewer's values (L2, here region IN [APAC]) and the binding's pinned overrides (L3). A higher layer replaces a lower layer's filter on the same column and replaces time_range and time_grain_sqla; it does not add to it, because Superset ANDs extra filters and region IN [EMEA] AND region IN [APAC] returns no rows. A parameter with as: "time_range" or as: "time_grain" replaces the time range or grain the same way. The result carries a new meta.scope_hash, so the engine's cache, the view and a later comparison can tell the two scopes apart, and meta.applied_filters / meta.rejected_filters show which filters reached the query. Every filter still passes Story 8's column and operator allowlist inside Superset. A value of the wrong shape for its parameter, or a filter on a column the dataset does not have, ends that binding with status: "error" and param_invalid or invalid_override; it never fails the request. Pinning and parameterizing the same column on one binding is rejected when the artifact is validated (I12_PARAMS), not at refresh time. Host filter changes use the same request with scope instead of new params. A binding whose filter_context.mode is follow_host follows the viewer's live dashboard filters: the host's watchScope (dashboard Redux dataMask inside Superset, or the Embedded SDK's observeDataMask with dashboardUiConfig.emitDataMasks, apache/superset: superset-embedded-sdk/src/index.ts:44, 164-165, 613-614) reports a new HostDataScope, the controller sends {trigger: "on_filter_change", scope, bindings: <the

The binding model (BindingDefinition, BindingStatus, BindingError, the snapshots, ArtifactParameter, ParamValue, HostDataScope, RefreshPolicy) lives in src/data.ts and is specified in Artifact Spec and targets. The refresh protocol adds the request, the update and the events to the same file: gck/packages/protocol/src/data.ts (new, protocol 1.1, refresh protocol excerpt) run.ts imports BindingUpdate, HostDataScope and ParamValue from this file and data.ts imports GckErrorBody from run.ts; both are import type, which TypeScript erases, so the cycle costs nothing at runtime and the package keeps its zero-dependency rule.

A schedule, an alert or a report has no browser and no viewer session, yet its text must not repeat the numbers of the day it was generated. Headless refresh needs no model: the stored definitions are re-resolved and re-rendered by the text target. The caller is the Superset-side scheduler, which resolves the schedule's executor the way Superset's own reports do (ALERT_REPORTS_EXECUTORS, default [ExecutorType.EDITOR] on master, apache/superset: superset/config.py:2838; executor lookup get_executor, apache/superset: superset/tasks/utils.py:58), mints an engine token for that user server side with the same signer as the host's engine-token endpoint (Host integrations), and calls POST /v1/render (or POST /v1/data/resolve with trigger: "on_schedule" when it renders itself). The data is therefore the executor's data, under the executor's row-level security, never a shared service account's. POST /v1/render (response) gck_engine/data/render.py (new, sketch) The rendered text always ends with "Data as of" the oldest snapshotAt it used, and says when some values could not be refreshed; error and forbidden tokens render n/a. Exported text is still a snapshot once it leaves the engine (an email cannot re-query), which is why the scheduler re-renders per send instead of storing the first rendering.

docs.t: 16.6 Errors, limits and the Part VIII event mapping
docs.x: Request validation (invalid_request, context_too_large above 100 bindings) and engine-token auth are checked before the stream opens and answer with an HTTP error in the Step 7 body. Rate limiting and the token exchange happen inside the stream, so an SSE caller receives them as refresh.failed and a JSON caller as the HTTP status. Per-binding failures never fail the request: each binding ends ok, stale, error or forbidden with the codes of Step 7. Limit Value On breach bindings per request 100 413 context_too_large items per Story 8 call, calls in flight per request 25, 4 batching, not an error Story 8 call timeout 30 s the item ends stale with reason: "timeout" and no snapshot; the client keeps the one it holds engine result cache 60 s, keyed by (viewerKey, hash of source, effective scope and row limit), in-flight dedup on the same key served as binding.resolved without binding.loading force: true at most once per binding per viewer per 30 s downgraded to a cached read, meta.force_throttled: true per-viewer rate 60 resolve requests per minute, 600 binding resolutions per 10 minutes 429 rate_limited with retryAfterMs (as refresh.failed on a stream) data token 15 minutes, cached per (sub, scope) until 30 s before expiry data_token_expired: call getToken({ forceRefresh: true }) once, retry Gotcha: the engine cache key must start with the viewer Superset's data cache is safe across users because its key includes the user's row-level security clauses (apache/superset: superset/security/manager.py:6304). The engine's 60-second cache sits in front of Superset and knows nothing about row-level security, so its key starts with viewerKey. Without it, two viewers with different access would get each other's rows for up to a minute. Presenton decks keep Part VIII's deck-scoped refresh routes (Story 1) as a second transport of @gck/data-superset. Its events translate one to one, so the same BindingStore reducer applies them: Part VIII event Refresh protocol event refresh_started {total, viewer_key} (viewer_key is a Story 1 addition) refresh.started {total, viewerKey} binding_loading {binding_id, slide_id} binding.loading {bindingId} binding_data {binding_id, element_patch, snapshot_at, changed, meta} (plus snapshot, a Story 1 addition) binding.resolved {status: "ok", snapshot, snapshotAt, changed} binding_error {binding_id, code, message} binding.resolved {status:

GckClient owns every engine route, so it gains two methods, dataCatalog(query, signal) and resolveData(request, signal), built in Live Superset data. resolveData reuses send (token provider, credentials: "omit", one retry on token_expired) and createSseParser, but not stream()'s reconnect loop: with no resume, a dropped refresh stream ends the iterator with an error, and the refresh controller retries the whole request (three attempts, 1, 2 and 4 seconds, retryable codes only, retryAfterMs for rate_limited). The browser never calls POST /v1/render, and never calls Superset's chart data API directly: mapping rows into snapshots happens once, server side, in the shared gck_data mappers. Gotcha A scope in the request moves only bindings whose filter_context.mode is follow_host; the default, captured, deliberately ignores it so the narrative and its numbers keep describing the same filter selection. A host that sends scope on every dashboard filter change and sees nothing move is looking at captured bindings. Either generate with follow_host (and accept that the prose can drift from the numbers, which changed then reports), or expose the dimension as an artifact parameter so the change is explicit.

Reads: servers/nextjs/app/(presentation-generator)/outline/components/OutlineContent.tsx, servers/nextjs/app/(presentation-generator)/outline/components/OutlineItem.tsx, servers/nextjs/app/(presentation-generator)/components/useStableOutlineIds.ts, servers/nextjs/app/(presentation-generator)/presentation/hooks/PresentationUndoRedo.ts, servers/nextjs/app/(presentation-generator)/presentation/hooks/useAutoSave.tsx, servers/nextjs/store/slices/undoRedoSlice.ts, servers/nextjs/store/store.ts · Builds on: Run protocol and client · Time: ~65 min This chapter builds the browser half of the kit on @gck/client: the headless @gck/core (state machine, artifact store with structural-sharing JSON Patch, plugin registry, a run controller that submits generate, transform and edit intents and diffs edit results, and the headless runToCompletion helper), @gck/react (GckProvider, four run hooks, and the data views GckChartView, GckMetricView, GckTableView with GckBindingsProvider, useGckBinding and useGckToken) and the styled @gck/react/ui (PromptComposer, OutlineReview, StreamingPreview, RunStatusBar, ApplyBar). It also covers reuse from Presenton's outline page, Redux hosts, and the Next.js App Router. Generated content never freezes numbers. Every data block and token keeps a binding definition (a Superset chart, dataset or metric source), and the kit re-resolves it as the viewing user after generation: on open, on demand, on an interval, when a parameter changes and when the host's filters change. This chapter builds that browser side (protocol 1.1): the DataProvider interface, the framework-free BindingStore and RefreshController in @gck/core, the live variant of GckBindingsProvider with useLiveBindings, useGckRefresh, GckRefreshButton and GckParameterBar, and GckEmbedView, the live fallback for Superset charts the kit cannot redraw. The end-to-end data path (engine resolve endpoint, Superset refresh API, identity and caching) is in Live Superset data. Files under gck/ are new code for Part IX; files under servers/ are Presenton at snapshot 571461f.

docs.t: Step 1: The layers and the component tree
docs.x: @gck/core has no React or DOM imports, so one controller drives React, the <gck-generate> web component and plain scripts. Two stores on purpose: machine state (a few dozen changes per run) and the artifact store (every patch and delta), so RunStatusBar never re-renders per token. A third store takes over after apply: the host's binding store, which outlives the run and is kept fresh by a refresh controller (Step 4.1), so applied charts and tokens keep updating when the run store is reset.

The states are the blueprint's, with failed carrying error.retryable. SUBMIT carries the whole submission (prompt, intent, selection, base artifact, preferred apply mode), so one machine serves all three intents; an edit run additionally gets a block diff (DIFF_READY) once it is ready. That one field serves three readers: the controller builds the run request from it, ApplyBar preselects input.apply, and RunStatusBar's Retry resubmits it unchanged, so a retried transform rewrites the same selection even if the user has since clicked elsewhere. The store holds the Artifact, its version, text.delta drafts, the binding overlay and a block index. getSnapshot() returns an immutable object whose identity changes only on change, and subscribe() notifies at most once per animation frame, which is what useSyncExternalStore needs.

The applier copies on write along each op's path, so untouched sections and blocks keep their identity: memoized blocks skip re-rendering, changed blocks are detectable with ===, and a failing op leaves the original untouched (RFC 6902 atomicity). gck/packages/core/src/json-patch.ts (new) move and copy are rejected because the engine never emits them; a rejected patch becomes a conflict and a resync. test compares with JSON.stringify, which depends on key order: fine for the kit's own edit patches, not for arbitrary input.

Any framework can use the store directly: store.subscribe(() => render(selectSectionCount(store.getSnapshot()))). Two protocol 1.1 changes reach the store. binding.resolved carries an optional error ({ code, message, retryable }), plus changed and reason that the store ignores, so the overlay keeps the error code the views need for their message and Retry button (Step 14.3). And reset(..., { keepBindings: true }) is what a resync after a patch conflict uses (Step 5): the artifact is replaced, but resolved data stays, so a conflict mid-run no longer drops every chart back to a skeleton. resolveBinding keeps the previous snapshot under stale and error (the views badge it) and drops it under forbidden, so a viewer who lost access never keeps seeing the last numbers. Three levels, chosen per concern: Prompt: defaultPrompt (uncontrolled), or prompt plus onPromptChange when the host stores drafts. Outline review: the children render prop hands items, edit, move, remove, add and submit to host markup. The whole run: create the controller with createRunController and pass it as controller, so the host owns its lifetime, can start runs from a menu command and can subscribe() outside React. The intent: pass intent and getInput to PromptComposer, or call run.submit({ prompt, intent, ... }) from host UI such as a bubble menu. A Tiptap host wires the two non-generate intents like this. The selection and the base come from the target's fromHost direction (fromProseMirror); the base keeps the applied artifact's id, bindings and provenance and takes its sections from the editor, so it includes the user's edits since the last apply: app/editor/AiActions.tsx (new, host code, excerpt) By default the rewrite run applies with "replace" (over the selection) and the composer's edit run with "patch". SUBMIT records the submitted prompt in the machine, so after rewrite an uncontrolled composer shows "Make this shorter and plainer"; a host that wants to keep the user's draft uses the controlled prompt and onPromptChange instead.

A complete integration in about 40 lines (host code): app/ai/GenerateText.tsx (new, host code)

Data blocks (chart, metric, table) and inline tokens hold a bindingId, never numbers. Something has to turn the binding's snapshot into pixels wherever the block lands: the Tiptap node views of Artifact Spec and targets (GckChart, GckMetric, GckDataTable, GckToken), a host's own preview, or a read-only page. @gck/react ships that layer as one provider, a few hooks and four views, and they render only from snapshots, so a binding.resolved event redraws every chart and token without touching the host document. Since protocol 1.1 the provider can also fetch: given binding definitions and live, it creates a binding store and a refresh controller (Step 4.1), resolves every binding as the viewer on mount, and keeps them fresh by the refresh policy, so a page opened next week shows next week's numbers.

The views reuse Story 4's UI statuses (Story 4, native charts and refresh UX): the server's ok, stale, error, forbidden plus the browser-only idle and loading, with stale also recomputed from the snapshot's age (default one hour, Story 4's DEFAULT_STALE_AFTER_MS). DataBinding as seen by the view status Has snapshot View renders unknown id, or no status and no snapshot idle no skeleton pending with no request in flight (a saved definition not resolved yet) idle no skeleton pending during a run, or loading: true in a binding store loading no skeleton as above loading yes data plus "Refreshing" badge any, under sharedSnapshotPolicy: "redact", snapshot meta.resolved_by is not the current viewer idle hidden skeleton until the viewer's own refresh lands ok (or no status) and snapshotAt younger than staleAfterMs ok yes data stale, or ok older than staleAfterMs stale yes data plus "Data as of 3 hours ago" badge stale (a transient failure, reason set) stale no "Data could not be loaded" panel with Retry error error yes data plus "Couldn't refresh" badge error error no "Data could not be loaded" panel forbidden forbidden any "You don't have access to this data" panel, never the snapshot error bindings also carry error.code. The view picks its message from the code (chart_not_found shows data.chartNotFound, unsupported_viz and source_unsupported show data.unsupportedViz with an "Open in Superset" link, mapping_changed shows data.mappingChanged, no_data_identity shows data.noIdentity) and offers Retry (refresh([id], { force: true })) only when error.retryable is true or the binding is stale (the engine reports transient failures as stale with the code in reason), never for forbidden. The full code table is in Live Superset data.

The provider holds a binding source, in one of three forms: Props Source Who fetches Use it for store={run.store} a run's artifact store: the run artifact's bindings merged with the binding.resolved overlay the run previewing a run bindingStore={store} (optional controller) a host-owned BindingStore (Step 4.1), for example the one the run controller seeded at gck.applied the host's own RefreshController hosts that already drive refresh, such as Presenton through Part VIII's deck routes bindings={map} and live definitions from the host (a saved document's node attributes) the provider: it calls useLiveBindings, resolves on mount and follows the policy every saved page, deck or preview opened after generation bindings without live keeps the 1.0 behavior (a static map, nothing fetched), which is only right for fixtures and tests. The store's copy-on-write patches keep both identities when an unrelated block or binding changes, so a deck with forty charts re-renders one chart per binding.resolved, not forty. The cache is also what keeps useSyncExternalStore from looping: read must return the same object until something changed.
