GckChartView, GckMetricView and GckTableView draw a snapshot; the fourth view, GckEmbedView (Step 14.5), shows a live Superset chart the kit cannot redraw. All of them read binding.error.code for the message, offer Retry only for retryable codes, and surface snapshot.meta notes (rows cut at the row limit, missing values drawn as 0, a query rebuilt from the chart's form data). gck/packages/react/src/data-views.tsx (new) How the pieces fit: One frame, one vocabulary. DataFrame owns the state rendering of 14.1 for all three views; each view only supplies the "has data" body as a function, so the body never runs (and never casts a missing snapshot) in the skeleton, error or forbidden branches. Errors by code. The message comes from binding.error.code through ERROR_MESSAGE; Retry calls refresh([id]), which forces past the cache for that binding only, and appears only when error.retryable is true and a live controller exists (a run preview has none). "Open in Superset" appears for codes that mean "the kit cannot redraw this chart" and links to the saved chart in Explore, where Superset checks the viewer's access again. Honest notes. snapshot.meta turns into small captions: truncated (the query reached its row cap, so totals drawn from the rows are partial), nulls_coerced (Presenton's ChartSeries.values is a list of floats, so missing values were drawn as 0) and query_context_source: "rebuilt_from_form_data" (the chart was never saved with a query context; on Superset master the refresh API rebuilt one from its form data). Lazy Chart.js. loadChartJs is the same pattern as a target's loadPreview: a module-level promise around a dynamic import("chart.js/auto"), shared by every chart on the page, so an editor without charts never downloads Chart.js and a page with forty charts imports it once. chart.js/auto registers every controller, scale and plugin the mapping uses (including the filler for area and the radial scale for polarArea), and its default palette colors the series. A failed import resets the promise so the next chart retries, and the failed chart shows its numbers as a table meanwhile. Chart kinds. The eleven ChartKinds (Presenton's ChartType, servers/fastapi/templates/v2/models/elements.py:74-85) map onto six Chart.js types: horizontal_bar is a bar chart with indexAxis: "y", stacked_bar stacks both axes, horizontal_stacked_bar does both, area is a filled

Two small styled controls (new, @gck/react/ui) sit next to the document, inside the same provider. Both return null outside a live provider, so a run preview or a fixture renders without them. gck/packages/react/src/ui/data-controls.tsx (new) What happens when the viewer picks a value: ParamControl calls useGckParameters().set(id, value), which calls controller.setParams(...) and the host's onParamsChange (the host writes ?gck_p_region=EMEA into the URL or its own view state; the value never enters the artifact, so it never changes what other viewers see). The controller marks only the bindings whose params list that parameter, drops any in-flight results for them at once, and after 400 ms without another change sends one POST {engine}/v1/data/resolve with trigger: "on_filter_change" and the new values. The engine applies the value as layer L2 of the scope (it replaces a lower-layer filter on the same column instead of adding a second one, which Superset would AND into an empty result) and returns binding.resolved for those bindings only. Charts and tokens that do not depend on the parameter never move. Options from a dataset column must be loaded as the viewer, so a viewer only picks values row-level security lets them see. The kit does not call Superset itself (outside Superset the browser has no Superset session), so the host supplies loadOptions. Inside Superset it is one same-origin GET on the column-values route (superset/datasource/api.py:225-227, response { result: [...] }): Superset host: loadOptions (new, host code) The time-range presets are the values Superset's own date filter offers (superset-frontend/src/explore/components/controls/DateFilterControl/utils/constants.ts:47-63) and its parser accepts (superset/utils/date_parser.py:521-526); the grains are a subset of the ISO 8601 ids in TimeGranularity (superset-frontend/packages/superset-ui-core/src/time-format/types.ts:29-47). A host with its own design system skips the styled bar and builds controls on useGckParameters() directly. Gotcha: a parameter that follows a native filter has no control here A parameter with hostFilterId takes its value from the host's HostDataScope.dataMask, so the dashboard's native filter bar is its control. Rendering a second control for it would let the two disagree; the bar skips it, and the host passes the live scope through the provider's scope prop instead.

docs.t: 14.5 GckEmbedView: the live fallback for charts the kit cannot redraw
docs.x: Story 8's catalog marks many Superset viz types as not refreshable into a snapshot (Sankey, treemap, box plot, gauge, maps, deck.gl, mixed time series and more; the full table is in Live Superset data). The engine keeps them as bindings of kind embed with mapping: {}, and the artifact places them as an embed block ({ type: "embed", bindingId, title? }, Artifact Spec and targets). The kit never draws them and never shows a picture of them: it shows Superset's own chart, live. gck/packages/react/src/embed-view.tsx (new) Why it is live and correct: Same session, same user. The iframe loads /explore/?slice_id=<id>&standalone=1 (the slice_id and standalone URL parameters, superset-frontend/src/constants.ts:26-27, :62-63). /explore/ is served by ExploreView.root behind @has_access (superset/views/explore.py:33-48), so Superset renders the saved chart with the viewer's own session, permissions and row-level security, and queries it on every load. This is the same standalone mode Superset's "Embed code" button produces (superset-frontend/src/explore/components/EmbedCodeContent.tsx:82, an Explore permalink plus ?standalone=1), which is gated by the EMBEDDABLE_CHARTS feature flag (default True, superset/config.py:987). Refresh follows the policy. The chart refreshes itself when the iframe loads. Keying the iframe by the controller's lastRefreshedAt reloads it whenever the rest of the page refreshes (on open, Refresh data, interval), so an embedded chart is never older than the charts around it. Each reload re-runs the Superset page, which costs more than a snapshot refresh; the interval floor of 60 s applies here too. Honest fallback. Without a same-site Superset session (a page on another site, a logged-out viewer, a frame policy that refuses the host), the view is a link card with no data, and Superset decides access when the viewer follows it. The engine's binding status still applies: a viewer who may not see the chart gets the forbidden panel, not a frame. The kit uses the plain Explore page, not the Embedded SDK, on purpose. You will see how a host fills in the host adapter contract from chapters 62 to 64 (HostContext, ContextProvider, DataProvider, HostApi and its well-known capabilities), then build five hosts on it: a Superset dashboard host that generates a new tab or a new dashboard from a prompt, a Superset text host for Markdown components, SQL Lab results and alert narratives, a Tiptap extension GckGenerate with a /ai slash command, bubble actions and streaming insertion that undoes in one step, Presenton (AI Slides) as the host of the slides target, and a framework-agnostic <gck-generate> web component with an iframe fallback. The chapter ends with a mount matrix and three end-to-end sequence diagrams. Every host also keeps the generated content's data live after the run. No host stores frozen numbers or screenshots: a host persists binding definitions (which Superset chart, dataset or metric, with which filters), and the numbers are fetched again as the viewing user when the content is opened, when the user asks for a refresh, on an opt-in interval and when the host's filters change. Each step below says what triggers a refresh in that host and how the result is scoped to the viewer; where a host can only store static text (a dashboard Markdown component, an email, a PPTX file), the output carries a "Data as of" stamp and the kit offers a live alternative. The shared data path (the engine's resolve endpoint, the Superset refresh API, identity, caching and limits) is specified once in Live Superset data, and Step 7 summarizes the behavior per host. A host is anything that can (a) describe where the user is and what they selected, and (b) accept host-native content and say what happened. The kit splits those two jobs: context providers and one data provider produce the context and data parts of the run request (Run protocol and client), and the host API is what a target adapter's apply() uses to commit the result (Artifact Spec and targets). Every type in this step is defined in chapters 62 to 64; this step shows how a host fills them in and which conventions the hosts below share.

HostContext is not a second shape: it is an alias of the run request's context object, RunContext, so the two names can never drift. Only host is required; surface, locale, theme, selection and document are optional, and an index signature lets a host add its own top-level keys such as dashboardId. gck/packages/protocol/src/run.ts (excerpt, defined in Run protocol and client) gck/packages/protocol/src/target.ts (excerpt, defined in Artifact Spec and targets) The values of surface and selection are conventions shared by the hosts in this chapter, not types, so a new host can add its own without a protocol release: surface Host Meaning dashboard Superset a dashboard page, or a dashboard picked elsewhere dashboard_markdown Superset one MARKDOWN component of a dashboard sqllab Superset SQL Lab with a result set alert Superset (headless) an Alerts and Reports narrative document Tiptap a Tiptap document presentation Presenton a Presenton deck page <gck-generate> any page hosting the web component selection.kind Other fields Produced by text text, from, to a plain text selection in a host without a target fromHost (for example a <textarea> page) dashboard_component componentId a picked Superset layout node chart chartId a chart menu entry point slides slideIds selected Presenton slides These kinds are what context providers send with a generate run, as a hint about where the user is. The two other intents carry content instead, and the run controller writes it itself from submit's input (React SDK and UI kit): submit({ intent: "transform", selection }) sends context.selection as a flat list of Artifact blocks (the target's fromHost output for the user's selection) and applies with replace by default, and submit({ intent: "edit", baseArtifact }) sends context.document as the artifact applied earlier, re-read with fromHost, and applies with patch by default. The controller writes those keys after collecting context, so they win over anything a provider put there. Host-specific facts that the apply step needs later (a dashboard's changed_on, for example) go under a top-level key named after the provider that wrote them, such as context["superset.dashboard"], and travel to the engine with the rest of the context. The outcome of an apply is 62's ApplyResult, defined in @gck/protocol and re-exported by @gck/core: { ok: boolean; mode; nativeRef?; warnings: string[];

docs.t: 1.2 Context providers, the data provider and context collection
docs.x: Providers are small, independent and registered in the @gck/core registry, either through GckProvider's contextProviders and dataProviders props or at runtime with registry.registerContextProvider (React SDK and UI kit). A Superset dashboard flow registers one context provider for the dashboard, a Markdown flow adds one for the picked component, and a Tiptap host registers one for the selection and the document outline. gck/packages/core/src/registry.ts (excerpt, defined in React SDK and UI kit) Five rules follow from that contract, and every host in this chapter relies on them: Register only the providers that apply. A provider has no host or surface filter; the flow that mounts the kit decides which providers exist. The surface goes into baseContext on useGenerationRun, which the controller merges under the collected context ({ host: "web", ...baseContext, ...context }). Registration order resolves conflicts. Contributions are merged with Object.assign, so a later provider overwrites an earlier one's keys. Each provider should therefore own its keys: the dashboard provider writes dashboardId, document, filters and superset.dashboard; the Markdown picker writes selection. Chips are the user's veto. Every contribution lists chips ({ id, label, removable, keys }); PromptComposer shows them, and excluding a removable chip deletes the context keys it names before the request is sent. The dashboard host uses this to show the captured filter values before the user submits (Step 2.6). Data is separate from context. The allowed charts come from exactly one DataProvider, picked by dataProviderId, and become the request's data: { provider, allowedChartIds } plus, in protocol 1.1, the host's captured filter state as data.scope (a HostDataScope). Context providers never write data. The same data provider keeps applied content live. After gck.applied the run controller hands the applied artifact's binding definitions and their current state to a host-owned BindingStore, and a RefreshController built on the same provider's resolve takes over: it re-resolves on open, on Refresh, on an opt-in interval (60 s minimum), on tab return when the data is older than staleAfterSec, and on parameter or filter changes (React SDK and UI kit). Every resolve runs as the viewer: the browser sends definitions with its engine token, the engine exchanges that token for a short-lived data

gck/packages/core/src/adapter.ts (excerpt, defined in Artifact Spec and targets) A target asks for what it needs by name and handles absence itself (62's adapters return ok: false when a capability is missing), so one adapter works in any host that offers the capability. The names used in this chapter: Capability Type Offered by superset.http { request(path, init: { method; body? }): Promise<any> }; body is an object that the host serializes, and the host adds CSRF Superset host superset.positionLimit number, the server's SUPERSET_DASHBOARD_POSITION_DATA_LIMIT (default 65535) Superset host, optional superset.reloadIfShowing (dashboardId: number) => void Superset host tiptap.editor Editor from @tiptap/core Tiptap host presenton.api { fetch: typeof fetch; presentationId: string; afterIndex: number } Presenton host host.confirm (req: { title; body; danger? }) => Promise<boolean> any host with a dialog host.notify (n: { tone; message }) => void any host with toasts host.startContext () => HostContext \| null, the context sent when the run was submitted hosts whose apply checks for concurrent changes Hosts learn the outcome through emit: after every apply the controller calls host.emit?.("gck.applied", { result, artifact }). That is where a host shows a link, records telemetry or refreshes its own view.

The run controller's apply(mode, host) is the one function between a finished run and a host; GenerationRun.apply(mode) calls it with GckProvider's host. It runs the target's deterministic serializer, hands the native value to the adapter's apply, records the result on the run, and tells the host. gck/packages/core/src/controller.ts (excerpt: apply, as specified in React SDK and UI kit) A refused apply (ok: false) or a thrown error returns the run to ready, not failed: the artifact is still good, only the host refused it (permissions, a conflict, a closed editor), so the user can retry or choose another mode without paying for another generation. Two consequences for host code: a target reports expected refusals as ok: false with a coded warning ("conflict: ...", "no_markdown_selected: ...") instead of throwing, and the modes a user can pick come from the target's manifest.applyModes, narrowed by ApplyBar's modes prop. The patch mode of an edit run goes to the adapter's applyPatch with the run's block diff; the Tiptap target (Step 4) and the text target implement it, and the dashboard and slides targets do not list it in v1, so a "patch" request reaches them as replace with a patch_unsupported warning. In protocol 1.1 the doc above is withBindingState(doc, state): the artifact's binding definitions merged with the run store's latest binding.resolved state, so a value that resolved after the last artifact.patch still reaches the host, and adapters never fetch on their own. Right after a successful apply the controller seeds the host's BindingStore with stripRuntime definitions plus that state, which is the handoff rule 5 in Step 1.2 describes; from then on the host's RefreshController, not the run, keeps the content current (Live Superset data).

@gck/host-superset is an npm library; a deployment wraps it in a one-file .supx extension (publisher gck, name host-superset, so the extension id is gck.host-superset and its REST base is /extensions/gck/host-superset). The kit is bundled into the extension's remote: react, react-dom, antd and @apache-superset/core are shared singletons with import: false (the CLI template), and everything else, including @gck/*, ships inside the remote's own chunks. Superset master pins react and react-dom at ^18.3.0 (apache/superset: superset-frontend/package.json:196,202), so @gck/react's peer range must include 18.3. Gotcha: react-dom/client is a different shared module Module Federation shares by request string. The template shares react-dom, so import { createPortal } from "react-dom" resolves to the host's copy, but import { createRoot } from "react-dom/client" is not listed and gets bundled from the extension's node_modules, giving a second React DOM that cannot render components from the first. Inside Superset the kit never calls createRoot; it renders only inside views and panels the host mounts, and uses createPortal for modals.

docs.x: Two facts from the Superset source shape the apply code. First, chart membership (the dashboard_slices rows) is rebuilt from json_metadata.positions, not from position_json alone (set_dash_metadata, apache/superset: superset/daos/dashboard.py:820-847); the update command documents that "the frontend always sends them there" (apache/superset: superset/commands/dashboard/update.py:120-131). Second, there is no server-side conflict check on PUT: the last writer wins. 62's applyDashboard(n, host, mode, target?) handles the first fact: it always sends the layout inside json_metadata.positions (spreading every other metadata key), adds a generated artifact to an existing dashboard as one new tab with addAsTab (which keeps every existing id and wraps a flat grid into an "Overview" tab first), creates a new dashboard with POST /api/v1/dashboard/ when no target is given, and returns an undo that PUTs the previous layout back. The Superset host adds what is specific to a live, multi-user dashboard: the changed_on comparison against the context captured at submit (host.startContext), a confirmation through host.confirm, a filter_scope_review warning, a page reload through superset.reloadIfShowing, and an explicit, confirmed delete as the undo of a new dashboard. docs.t: 2.11 Keeping a generated tab live, and whose data it shows
docs.x: A generated tab holds no numbers at all: it holds CHART components (saved charts, plus the live-text charts of Step 2.7) and qualitative Markdown. Everything numeric is drawn by Superset's own frontend, so the dashboard host needs no refresh code; what it must get right is which events re-query and under whose identity. Trigger What happens Evidence The dashboard is opened every visible chart queries the chart data API with the viewer's session apache/superset: superset/charts/data/api.py:271 A native filter changes each chart reads the dashboard's dataMask and rebuilds its form data with getFormDataWithExtraFilters, then re-queries; charts outside the filter's scope do not move apache/superset: superset-frontend/src/dashboard/components/gridComponents/Chart/Chart.tsx:461,481-491 The user clicks the dashboard's Refresh every chart re-queries with force: true, bypassing the cache forceRefresh, apache/superset: superset-frontend/src/dashboard/components/Header/useHeaderAutoRefresh.ts:343-357, wired at .../Header/index.tsx:660 Auto refresh json_metadata.refresh_frequency (seconds, apache/superset: superset/dashboards/schemas.py:215) is read on load (apache/superset: superset-frontend/src/dashboard/actions/hydrate.ts:411) and re-queries on that period; the kit writes it only for new dashboards and never below 60 apache/superset: superset/config.py:2045-2058 Viewer scope follows from the same fact. Each query runs as the person looking at the dashboard, so dataset access and row-level security apply per viewer, and Superset's data cache key includes the viewer's RLS clauses (get_rls_cache_key, apache/superset: superset/security/manager.py:6304), so two viewers never share cached rows. The author's numbers are never stored in the tab: the snapshot the run resolved exists only in the run's event log and the chat preview. Two scopes meet on a generated tab, and the host keeps them apart on purpose. The charts follow the filter bar live, because that is how Superset dashboards work. The artifact (what the chat preview, a Tiptap copy or an exported narrative show) keeps the filters captured at submit: each binding's filter_context carries the masks and the permalink key from Step 2.6 with mode: "captured", so a refresh next month still reads the selection the text was written about. A kit view that should follow the filter bar instead uses mode: "follow_host" and a

@gck/target-text turns an Artifact into Markdown, plain text or an HTML snippet: render(artifact, profile, options) with the profiles markdown, plain, html and email, and toMarkdown(artifact, options) as the Markdown shortcut (Artifact Spec and targets, Step 10). Its adapter, textTarget, has the native value { markdown: string }. For the Superset text surfaces its manifest allows only text blocks, so the engine's response schema cannot even contain a chart. gck/packages/target-text/src/adapter.ts (new, excerpt) Tokens are resolved with resolveToken from @gck/core, the same d3-format rules every renderer uses, never with Intl.NumberFormat or by reading snapshot[field]; a binding without a snapshot, or with status forbidden or error, renders as n/a instead of a number. The target emits Markdown only, never raw HTML. Superset sanitizes Markdown HTML by default (HTML_SANITIZATION = True, apache/superset: superset/config.py:1646), but the kit does not rely on a host's sanitizer: links are kept only for http, https and mailto URLs (safeHref), and Markdown punctuation in plain segments is escaped before any markup is added. Text is live only while the kit renders it. In the kit's own text preview and in the <gck-data> and <gck-artifact> elements (Step 6.4) the numbers come from a RefreshController and re-resolve as the viewer on open, on Refresh, on an opt-in interval and on parameter or filter changes. Once text leaves the kit as a string (Markdown copied out of SQL Lab, a dashboard Markdown component, an email) it is a snapshot, and the text target says so: protocol 1.1 adds TextOptions.dataAsOf ("footer" by default, "inline", "none"), and with the default toMarkdown appends "Data as of UTC", computed by dataAsOf(artifact) from @gck/core over the bindings the text actually uses, plus "Some values could not be refreshed" when one of them is stale. "inline" writes "(as of ...)" after each token instead, which is what the dashboard target uses for any number left in Markdown (Step 2.7). Every text host below picks one of these two outcomes explicitly: live through the kit, or stamped.

docs.t: 3.2 Writing into a dashboard Markdown component
docs.x: The Markdown flow registers the dashboard context provider and, after it, a second provider that contributes selection: { kind: "dashboard_component", componentId } from a picker over the MARKDOWN nodes of layoutOutline; its baseContext sets surface: "dashboard_markdown". It registers textTarget with a Superset apply: the manifest and serializer stay the text target's, only the commit changes. ApplyBar gets modes={["replace", "append"]}: replace overwrites meta.code, append adds below the existing text. An edit run on a component the kit wrote earlier ("make this shorter", submit({ intent: "edit", baseArtifact }), where the base is the artifact the flow kept from that apply's gck.applied event, since Markdown is not read back into blocks) needs no extra apply code. With these modes, ApplyBar preselects replace, because patch is not offered; a host that calls run.apply("patch") directly reaches the spread textTarget.applyPatch, which calls this.apply(..., "replace"), the wrapper below, so both paths overwrite meta.code. A Markdown component cannot run a query (Step 2.7), so this flow is where live data is hardest, and the flow is built so that it never writes a bare number. Its manifest's promptHints ask for qualitative text, so most narratives contain no tokens at all. When the result does contain tokens, toNative renders them with dataAsOf: "inline" ("revenue of 1.2M (as of 2026-11-03 09:00 UTC)"), the apply result carries a stale_number_in_markdown warning, and the apply bar offers a second action, "Insert as live text", which runs the dashboard target's planLiveText and createLiveTextCharts (Step 2.7) for those blocks and places the resulting Handlebars or Big Number chart in a new row directly below the component, keeping the Markdown qualitative. That chart re-queries as each viewer and follows the dashboard's native filters; the Markdown never changes after the apply, which is why it must not carry the numbers. gck/packages/host-superset/src/markdown/markdownTarget.ts (new)

docs.t: 3.3 An SQL Lab panel that narrates the current result set
docs.x: SQL Lab is the one place where the extension framework hands the kit real data: onDidQuerySuccess delivers QueryResultContext with executedSql, remoteId (the backend Query id) and result: {columns, data} (apache/superset: superset-frontend/packages/superset-core/src/sqlLab/index.ts:190-232,401). Each column carries name, column_name, type, type_generic and is_dttm (apache/superset: superset-frontend/packages/superset-core/src/common/index.ts:31-56); type_generic is 0 for numeric columns (GenericDataType, .../common/index.ts:128-134). No binding source in protocol 1.1 reads a SQL Lab result (superset_chart, superset_dataset and superset_metric all read saved Superset objects), and a run request carries no bindings of its own. Until protocol 1.2 the panel therefore sends a small aggregate summary of the result (row count, per-column min, max and sum for numeric columns, top values for low-cardinality text) as context.document, through a context provider. Because the model may write numbers only as data tokens that reference a binding (the validator's I5_NUMBERS_IN_TOKENS), the narrative is qualitative until a binding source for query results exists. That source is superset_sql, planned for protocol 1.2 behind GCK_SQL_SOURCES_ENABLED (off by default) and specified in Live Superset data. It never trusts the browser's rows: the binding carries { type: "superset_sql", database_id, sql, catalog, schema } built from the result event's executedSql and the tab's databaseId, catalog and schema (apache/superset: superset-frontend/packages/superset-core/src/sqlLab/index.ts:58-87,209), or { type: "superset_sql", saved_query_id } for a saved query, and the model refers to it only by binding key, never writing SQL. Every resolve re-executes that SQL inside Superset as the viewer: the data token needs scope ai_slides:sql, which the token exchange grants only to users holding can_execute_sql_query on SQLLab (SqlLabRestApi.class_permission_name = "SQLLab", apache/superset: superset/sqllab/api.py:87), and a statement that mutates data is rejected (sql_mutation_rejected). So a narrative saved from SQL Lab with 1.2 refreshes like any other binding, and a viewer without SQL Lab access sees forbidden, not the author's numbers. Until then the panel's output is qualitative text plus the copy action below. gck/packages/host-superset/src/sqllab/SqlLabNarrativePanel.tsx (new) Gotcha:

Alerts and Reports deliver text through notification plugins, and its Webhook recipient is the only "data changed" signal Superset has (see Superset landscape). A narrative for an alert has no browser and no user at the keyboard, so it is the one host where the kit runs headless: @gck/client, @gck/core and @gck/target-text are DOM-free and run in a small Node worker next to the engine. gck/apps/alert-narrator/src/handler.ts (new, sketch) GckClient is the transport from Run protocol and client; engineUrl never contains /v1, the client appends /v1/runs. runToCompletion from @gck/core (React SDK and UI kit) starts the run, reads the stream (which reconnects with Last-Event-ID on its own) into an artifact store, throws a GckError on run.failed, and resolves with { artifact, events }, where artifact already has the resolved bindings merged in, so toMarkdown renders real numbers. Unlike a browser run, aborting it cancels the run on the engine, so the timeout above does not leave a run burning tokens. A headless narrative has no viewer, so its identity is the schedule's executor, chosen by Superset's own report rules: ALERT_REPORTS_EXECUTORS (default [ExecutorType.EDITOR] on master, apache/superset: superset/config.py:2838), per-schedule "Run As" behind ALERT_REPORT_DYNAMIC_EXECUTOR (apache/superset: superset/config.py:741, default False), resolved by get_executor (apache/superset: superset/tasks/utils.py:58). The Superset-side scheduler mints the engine token for that user with the same signer as the engine-token endpoint (Step 2.9), and the engine exchanges it for a data token like any other, so the alert's numbers are exactly what the executor may see. An email is read after it is sent, so its numbers are a snapshot by nature: toMarkdown stamps them (Step 3.1). What keeps a recurring narrative current is re-rendering it per send, which needs no model call: the stored artifact's binding definitions are re-resolved as the executor and re-rendered by the engine's text target. Validation enforces the split: on the alert and report surfaces a data token is allowed only when the schedule re-renders per send; otherwise the engine rejects it (I5_NUMBERS_IN_TOKENS, variant tokens_not_live) and the narrative must be qualitative. gck/apps/alert-narrator/src/rerender.ts (new, sketch) Regenerating the words (a new runToCompletion) stays a separate, explicit choice; a

Tiptap is the host where frontend detail matters most: the kit writes directly into a live document that the user is typing in, possibly with collaborators. The design goals are: stream visibly, never fight the user's cursor, undo the whole generation with one keystroke, and keep the shared document clean during collaboration.

docs.t: 4.1 Negotiate the manifest from the editor schema
docs.x: Every Tiptap host has its own schema. Presenton's slide text editor, for example, disables headings, lists, blockquotes, code blocks, horizontal rules and links in StarterKit and adds its own runStyle mark and latexRun node (servers/nextjs/components/slide-editor/text/TiptapInlineTextEditor.tsx:49-50,86-87,266-280). A generator that emits a heading into that editor produces a schema error. So the manifest is computed from the editor's schema when the adapter is created, createTiptapTarget(editor), not hard-coded. Its serializer (toProseMirror), reverse import (fromProseMirror), one-transaction apply (applyToEditor) and in-place patch (patchEditor) are in Artifact Spec and targets (Step 8); the factory ties them to one editor. The parts a host relies on: gck/packages/target-tiptap/src/index.ts (excerpt, defined in Artifact Spec and targets) "patch" is offered only when the editor registers GckBlockIds (part of gckNodes), the extension that stores each top-level node's block id in a gckBlockId global attribute; without it there is nothing to find blocks by, and an edit run applies with replace. Gotcha: Tiptap schema differences between hosts Node and mark names are a per-host contract: StarterKit calls them bulletList, listItem, horizontalRule, other setups use bullet_list or custom names, and attributes differ (heading level ranges, image src rules). Three rules keep the kit safe: (1) compute the manifest from editor.schema as above, so the engine never asks for a missing block; (2) convert IR to ProseMirror JSON with toProseMirror and let ProseMirror check it (schema.nodeFromJSON(...) plus Node.check()) before dispatching, as applyToEditor does; (3) keep kit data in the kit's own node types, and limit what the kit adds to host nodes to the one gckBlockId global attribute, which GckBlockIds declares only on the node types the target emits, with a null default, keepOnSplit: false and a data-gck-block-id HTML attribute (62, Steps 8.1 and 8.2). Every editor that opens the document, including read-only viewers and server-side generateHTML, must register it, or the ids are dropped on load and the next edit can only replace. One more limit: toProseMirror writes every section title as a level 2 heading, so for a schema without heading the prompt hints ask for untitled sections.

Three pieces are needed in the document: a transient placeholder that holds streamed content, the data nodes and a provenance mark. The data nodes are 62's gckChart, gckMetric, gckDataTable and gckToken (gckNodes, whose React node views live in the @gck/target-tiptap/react subpath); this chapter adds two kit-internal types, which need no React. gck/packages/target-tiptap/src/transient.ts (new) The provenance mark is how an editor can later show "AI-generated" highlights, filter generated text out of training exports, or let a reviewer jump to every passage from one run. Marks only cover text. The data nodes are atoms without text, so they carry no run id; they keep the artifact's block id in gckId, and like every top-level node the target writes they also get gckBlockId from GckBlockIds, which is the id an edit run patches by. Provenance and block ids answer different questions (which run wrote this text, which artifact block is this node), so the kit keeps both.

The extension is framework-agnostic: it imports nothing from React and talks to the kit through a small RunDriver interface that the React layer provides (Step 4.5). It owns the slash command, the run bookkeeping, the streaming transactions, the commit and cancel logic, and the history behavior. gck/packages/target-tiptap/src/GckGenerate.ts (new) fragmentFor reuses the Tiptap target's deterministic serializer, toProseMirror (Artifact Spec and targets), with the same options createTiptapTarget uses, then lets ProseMirror validate the result with schema.nodeFromJSON and Node.check(). A streamed frame that fails the check (a block type the schema lacks, a structure that is still half built) is skipped and the previous frame stays on screen; a final artifact that fails it is discarded with the reason schema_check_failed rather than inserted half-valid. Generated text carries the gckProvenance mark, and every top-level node carries its block id in gckBlockId, which toProseMirror writes and GckBlockIds declares. The three intents take three paths through the same command: Intent Started by Sent to submit Streams into Applied by generate /ai, the composer prompt, document digest through the context provider the placeholder commit, one undo step transform bubble actions (gckTransformSelection) selection: the selected blocks, read back with the target's fromHost logic (readBack) the placeholder, after the selection commit with replace over the mapped selection, one undo step edit "Edit page" (gckEditPage) baseArtifact: pageArtifact with its sections re-read from the whole document; apply: "patch" the run store only, the document is untouched while streaming ApplyBar, through RunController.apply("patch"), which calls the target's applyPatch (patchEditor), one undo step An edit run does not stream into the document, because its patches describe the whole page: the extension finishes its own bookkeeping at ready and leaves the result with the run, where the host shows the block diff (run.diff) and an ApplyBar with patch preselected (Step 4.5). The user can keep typing meanwhile; patchEditor finds blocks by id, not by position, and refuses with patch_anchor_missing if the user deleted a block the edit changed. Gotcha: an edit run needs the page's bindings fromProseMirror reads blocks back, not bindings: a chart node holds only its bindingId. The base of an edit run

docs.t: 4.4 Why this undoes in one step
docs.x: Tiptap 3's UndoRedo extension (formerly History, now in @tiptap/extensions, https://tiptap.dev/docs/editor/extensions/functionality/undo-redo) wraps ProseMirror's history plugin. That plugin groups adjacent changes made within newGroupDelay (default 500 ms) and skips any transaction whose addToHistory meta is false; closeHistory(tr) "will prevent further steps from being appended to an existing history event" (https://github.com/ProseMirror/prosemirror-history, src/history.ts). A run streams for many seconds, so without intervention it would leave dozens of undo events, some interleaved with the user's own typing. Transaction addToHistory Effect on undo Insert placeholder false invisible to undo Every streamed frame (replace placeholder content) false invisible to undo; history still maps its positions Unwrap: delete placeholder false document back to the pre-run shape Commit: insert (or replace selection with) final content, closeHistory default (true) exactly one new event Seal: empty transaction with closeHistory n/a the next keystroke starts a new event Undo after a commit removes the generated content (or restores the selected text in replace mode, which is how a transform applies), and redo puts it back. An edit run never touches these rows: its id stamping is a single addToHistory: false transaction, and its patch apply is one ordinary transaction built by patchEditor, so it is exactly one undo event as well. The user's own edits made elsewhere during streaming stay separate events, because the history plugin maps unrecorded steps instead of grouping them. Gotcha: setContent and full-document replacement break the scheme Some hosts sync external state by calling editor.commands.setContent(...); Presenton does this with emitUpdate: false (servers/nextjs/components/slide-editor/text/TiptapInlineTextEditor.tsx:503). A full replacement during a run deletes the placeholder, and findPlaceholder then returns null: the stream stops rendering and commit falls back to inserting at the mapped anchor. Hosts that do this must pause their sync while editor.storage.gckGenerate.runs.size > 0.

The React layer, in the @gck/target-tiptap/react subpath, supplies the GckProvider for the editor, the driver, the slash menu, the composer popover, the bubble menu and 62's node views. Tiptap 3 moved BubbleMenu to @tiptap/react/menus and replaced tippy.js with Floating UI (https://tiptap.dev/docs/guides/upgrade-tiptap-v2). GckConfig requires a host and the targets, and here both need the editor (createHost("tiptap", { "tiptap.editor": editor }) and createTiptapTarget(editor)), so the component creates the editor first and renders the provider around the editor chrome. gck/packages/target-tiptap/src/react/GckTiptapEditor.tsx (new) The driver is the only file that touches the core run API, so a change there stays local: gck/packages/target-tiptap/src/react/driver.ts (new) Two details of the core API shape the driver. submit(input) takes the whole submission (prompt, intent, selection, base artifact, apply mode), so the bubble actions run as real transform runs (submit({ intent: "transform", selection }), applied with replace) and "Edit page" as a real edit run (submit({ intent: "edit", baseArtifact, apply: "patch" })); the engine streams the edit's artifact.patch ops against the base, which the run store holds as version 0. And the driver subscribes only after submit has synchronously moved the machine to submitting (the first await comes after that), so a ready left over from the previous run is not mistaken for the end of this one. Keeping the partial result on cancel ("Keep what is there") is handled entirely inside the extension, which already holds the latest artifact; it applies to generate and transform runs, since an edit run has nothing in the document to keep. The review strip appears only for edit runs. It reads run.diff (block ids added, removed and changed, computed by the controller once the run is ready) for its summary, and its ApplyBar offers patch, preselected because submit recorded apply: "patch", and replace as the fallback for edits that reorder blocks or whose anchors are gone. patch calls patchEditor through the target's applyPatch, one transaction and one undo step; on success the host's emit hands the applied artifact to rememberPage, so the next "Edit page" starts from it. A run resumed after a reload has diff: null, so the strip shows no counts and patch falls back to the adapter's own handling. The data nodes need no code here

With @tiptap/extension-collaboration, the document lives in a Yjs Y.Doc that a provider (for example Hocuspocus) syncs to every peer. Three facts change the design: The Collaboration extension brings its own undo, and UndoRedo must be disabled (StarterKit.configure({ undoRedo: false }), per the Tiptap 3 upgrade guide and https://tiptap.dev/docs/editor/extensions/functionality/collaboration). Yjs-based undo is scoped to the local client, so one peer cannot undo another's changes, and the y-prosemirror binding honors tr.setMeta("addToHistory", false) to keep programmatic changes out of undo (https://github.com/yjs/y-prosemirror). Tiptap 3 uses its fork @tiptap/y-tiptap; that the fork keeps the same behavior is expected but was not verified for this chapter. Every streamed frame written into the shared document would be broadcast to every peer, persisted by the server, and replayed in its update log: dozens of throwaway updates per run. Remote changes arrive as transactions from the sync plugin, which can rewrite large parts of the document, so a plain ProseMirror position is not a stable anchor across them. So in collaborative mode (collaborative: true) the extension never writes the placeholder. It streams into a local-only widget decoration, anchors it with a Yjs relative position, and writes to the shared document exactly once, at commit. gck/packages/target-tiptap/src/collab.ts (new) During the run the extension also publishes awareness so peers see who is generating where: provider.awareness?.setLocalStateField("gck", { runKey, status: "generating" }), cleared in finish. Use the Suggestion shouldShow option with isChangeOrigin(transaction) so a remote peer typing / does not open your slash menu (example on https://tiptap.dev/docs/editor/api/utilities/suggestion). Live data adds one rule to collaboration: the shared document holds definitions only, and every peer refreshes as itself. The Y.Doc replicates the data nodes' binding attributes, never a snapshot or a token's text, so nothing a peer resolved is broadcast, persisted by the collaboration server or replayed from its update log. Each peer's editor wraps its own GckBindingsProvider with live, so each peer runs its own RefreshController and calls the engine with its own engine token: two peers with different row-level security on the same dataset see different numbers in the same paragraph, and a peer

A deck is the one target whose content is stored with values in it: Template v2 slide content holds chart series, metric text and table cells, because Presenton's renderer and exporter read them from the slide. So "live" in a deck means Part VIII's model, unchanged: every bound element has a slide_data_bindings row holding its definition and the owner's latest snapshot, and Part VIII's refresh service rewrites the element from Superset as the viewer (Story 1, dynamic data and refresh). Protocol 1.1 closes the gap that GCK-generated slides had no rows, so Part VIII's refresh never touched them. Some hosts cannot load third-party scripts at all (locked-down CMSs, strict CSP without a nonce, sandboxed admin consoles). For them the deployment serves an embed page next to the engine, /gck/embed?target=text (a host-specific page, not part of the run protocol), that contains <gck-generate> and speaks a small postMessage protocol, the same pattern and origin rules as Part VIII's Presenton frame (Story 5). Message Direction Payload gck:ready frame to host { v: 1 } gck:init host to frame { v: 1, context, data, mode } gck:token-request frame to host { v: 1, request_id } gck:token host to frame { v: 1, request_id, token } gck:resize frame to host { v: 1, height } gck:apply frame to host { v: 1, target, mode, native } (no artifact: keep it small) gck:applied host to frame { v: 1, result } host page snippet for the iframe fallback (new) The embed page sends Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors with the allowed host origins (configured per deployment, never *), checks event.origin and event.source === window.parent on every message, and keeps the token only in memory. Only text and slides previews make sense in a frame; Tiptap and Superset hosts always use the in-page integrations. Data in the frame is live on the same terms as in the element: the frame's kit resolves through the engine with the token the host page hands over in gck:token, so it is the host page's user who must have a Superset identity; whatever the host commits from gck:apply is a stamped snapshot (Step 3.1).

Reads: servers/fastapi/utils/llm_calls/generate_presentation_outlines.py, servers/fastapi/utils/llm_calls/generate_presentation_structure.py, servers/fastapi/utils/llm_calls/generate_slide_content.py, servers/fastapi/utils/llm_utils.py, servers/fastapi/utils/schema_utils.py, servers/fastapi/templates/v2/schema.py, servers/fastapi/api/v1/ppt/endpoints/presentation.py, servers/fastapi/services/database.py, servers/nextjs/app/(presentation-generator)/outline/hooks/useOutlineStreaming.ts, servers/nextjs/lib/template-v2-json-to-html.ts, servers/nextjs/proxy.ts · Builds on: Architecture, Prompts and schemas, Smart mode · Time: ~55 min The earlier Part IX chapters define what the Generative Content Kit (GCK) is: an Artifact Spec, target manifests, a run protocol and a React kit. This chapter answers the practical question that follows: which Presenton code becomes that kit, which code has to change, and in what order you can do the work without breaking AI Slides. You will classify every relevant backend and frontend module, map Presenton's three LLM steps onto target-aware GCK steps (with the real prompts before and after), write the run event log and the /v1/runs router, carve @gck/* packages out of servers/nextjs, choose a repository layout that keeps upstream rebases cheap, check the licensing, and finish with a checkpointed migration plan and a risk table. How to read the code in this chapter Excerpts titled with a repository path and "(excerpt)" are real Presenton code and match the snapshot exactly. Blocks titled "NEW:" are proposed GCK code. They are designs, not code that exists in the repository, and they are written against the real Presenton helpers they import.

Presenton is one product with two servers. FastAPI owns the pipeline, the database and the LLM calls; Next.js owns the pages, the Redux store and the slide renderer. Everything is shaped around a presentations row and its slides rows. GCK keeps the useful machinery and moves the slide-specific parts behind a slides target. The four classes used throughout this chapter: Class Meaning Typical action Keep as is Already host-agnostic; GCK imports it unchanged Import from the engine module, add tests that pin behavior Generalize Right idea, wrong coupling (to slides, to a row, to EventSource) Add a parameter or a thin wrapper; rewrite only when the coupling is structural Slides only Correct for the slides target, meaningless for others Stays in Presenton; reached through @gck/target-slides Drop Not part of the kit Leave in Presenton, do not port

docs.t: Step 3: Map the pipeline to target-aware steps
docs.x: Presenton's Standard pipeline runs three LLM steps, each written for slides (Standard generation pipeline). GCK keeps the three steps and makes each one read the target manifest instead of slide assumptions. Presenton function GCK step What changes Events generate_ppt_outline (generate_presentation_outlines.py:252) A: plan_sections Response is a section list, not Markdown; count bounded by limits.maxSections; data catalog in the prompt plan.proposed generate_presentation_structure (generate_presentation_structure.py:157) B: choose_section_layouts Runs only when the manifest has a layoutCatalog; answers with layout ids from an enum instead of integer indexes folded into plan.proposed _normalize_presentation_structure (presentation.py:384-407) B: normalize_layout_hints Deterministic fallback instead of random.randrange run.warning when repaired get_slide_content_from_type_and_outline (generate_slide_content.py:229-275) C: generate_section_blocks Schema assembled from manifest and layout slots; output is IR blocks artifact.patch process_slide_and_fetch_assets (process_slides.py:173) D: resolve_assets Walks IR image blocks, not SlideModel.content artifact.patch Part VIII binding refresh (Story 1 BindingRefreshService, new code in Part VIII) E: resolve_bindings Same resolution and the same mappers, keyed by Artifact.bindings instead of slide_data_bindings rows; input is binding definitions with their scope (filter_context, pinned overrides, parameter values); identity is a data token from a token exchange (or Presenton's session data token when the engine is mounted in Presenton); 25 items per Story 8 call, 4 calls in parallel; a slow or failed call leaves the binding pending or stale instead of failing the run (Step 3.4) binding.resolved with status ok, stale, error or forbidden The order differs from Presenton in one deliberate way. Presenton chooses layouts in /prepare, after the user has reviewed outlines (Standard generation pipeline). GCK runs Step B before the review so that plan.proposed can show each section's layoutHint, and after review it re-runs Step B only for sections the user changed.

docs.t: 3.1 Step A: from outline to plan
docs.x: The outline system prompt is written for decks. Its content rules turn a chart request without supplied data into invented numbers: servers/fastapi/utils/llm_calls/generate_presentation_outlines.py (excerpt) (generate_presentation_outlines.py:104-116.) The opening lines fix the vocabulary to slides: "Generate presentation title and content for slides." and "Generation settings are authoritative." (generate_presentation_outlines.py:122-126). The voice rules ban "this presentation", "this slide", "this deck" (generate_presentation_outlines.py:42-48). Most of this is worth keeping; three things must change: the noun (from the manifest), the chart rule (bindings instead of invented tables), and the output (structured sections instead of Markdown blobs). NEW: servers/fastapi/gck_engine/prompts/plan.py The user prompt keeps Presenton's "Generation Settings (authoritative)" block (generate_presentation_outlines.py:200-215) and adds two sections: Host Context: (a compact rendering of context, for example the dashboard title and native filters) and Data Catalog: (one line per allowed chart: binding id, chart name, viz type, metrics, dimensions). Reusing DIRECT_CONTENT_VOICE_RULES by import, rather than copying it, means an upstream improvement to the voice rules reaches GCK on the next rebase. The dashboard's native filters in Host Context: are there so the model can describe the scope in words, not so it can filter. The filter state itself travels as data: the host captures it as RunRequest.data.scope (the dashboard's dataMask plus a dashboard permalink), and the engine copies it onto every binding created in that context as filter_context with mode: "captured", so the narrative and every later refresh use the same selection (Live Superset data). When the prompt names a filter value ("for EMEA") that is a known value of a filterable column and no binding in that section carries it, the engine adds a scope_mismatch warning with the block id instead of trusting the prose.

docs.t: 3.2 Step B: from layout index to layout hint
docs.x: servers/fastapi/utils/llm_calls/generate_presentation_structure.py (excerpt) (generate_presentation_structure.py:66-75.) The catalog it reads is PresentationLayoutModel.to_string(): index, name and description per layout (templates/presentation_layout.py:49-62), and the answer is a list of integers whose length is pinned by get_presentation_structure_model_with_n_slides (get_dynamic_models.py:32-40). GCK keeps the content-driven mapping, rewords it per target, and changes the answer from integers to ids: NEW: servers/fastapi/gck_engine/prompts/layout.py The response schema is {"layouts": {"type": "array", "minItems": n, "maxItems": n, "items": {"enum": [<layout ids>]}}}. An enum of ids removes the out-of-range class of errors that _normalize_presentation_structure repairs today (presentation.py:384-407), and the catalog text adds each layout's slot list (Step 4) so the model can match data to slots. Gotcha Presenton repairs a short or invalid structure with random.randrange(layout_count) (presentation.py:399, presentation.py:404). That is acceptable for a deck, but it makes a GCK run non-reproducible: replaying the same event log through a fresh engine must yield the same artifact, and golden tests must be stable. normalize_layout_hints picks the first catalog layout whose slots accept the section's bound block types, and emits run.warning with code layout_repaired.

docs.t: 3.4 Step E: resolve bindings by reusing Part VIII's data code
docs.x: Presenton itself has no data binding code: chart values are model output (Step 5). The binding and refresh code the engine needs is the code Part VIII adds to Presenton for AI Slides (Story 1, dynamic data and refresh) and to the analytics backend (Story 8, analytics refresh APIs and MCP). docs.t: Step 4: Assemble the response schema from a TargetManifest
docs.x: Presenton derives the slide-content schema from a template layout: get_template_schema builds one JSON Schema per layout from its components (templates/v2/schema.py:257-279, :585-639), and _prepare_response_schema strips asset URL fields, forces type: object, adds __speaker_note__ and fixes arrays (generate_slide_content.py:203-226). GCK does the same thing one level up: the schema is assembled per run from the TargetManifest (allowed block types, limits, layout catalog) and the data catalog (allowed binding ids). The builder itself is canonical and lives in the engine module: build_response_schema(manifest, catalog: list[CatalogEntry]) in gck_engine/schema/response_schema.py, with stamp assigning ids afterwards (Artifact Spec and targets, Step 6). It produces the schema for a whole draft (title plus sections). Step C writes one section per LLM call, so inside Presenton the engine adds a thin wrapper that takes the section item of that schema, narrows it, adds the slides-only speaker note, and finishes with Presenton's own schema_utils: NEW: servers/fastapi/gck_engine/schema/section_schema.py The canonical builder already does the important work: a data block type whose kind has no catalog entry is dropped from the anyOf (no data, no chart, so the model cannot invent one), bindingId is an enum of catalog keys per kind, and every object is strict with nullable optionals. speakerNote must be popped before stamp, because the Pydantic Artifact forbids extra fields; whether slides get a Section.notes field is an open question for protocol 1.1. Three design choices are worth stating: Block ids are not in the schema. The engine assigns id to every section and block (stamp) before emitting artifact.patch. If the model chose ids, a repair round could rename blocks and break patch paths and host-side selection. No link mark. The Artifact Spec allows link, and the canonical builder offers it, but generated text never gets one, so the wrapper removes it and pins href to null. This mirrors Presenton's outline rule "Do not include URLs, hyperlinks, citations, footnotes, references, or source lists in slide outlines." (generate_presentation_outlines.py:159). Links enter an artifact only from existing host content: the selection of a transform or the base artifact of an edit. maxCharsPerBlock is only partly a JSON Schema keyword. The builder puts it on each segment's text

docs.t: 4.1 The slides target: slots from Template v2
docs.x: For the slides target the engine builds layoutCatalog itself from the template, because the full catalog is large and the engine already has the code. It calls the same _build_template_layout_model that /prepare uses (presentation.py:410-470), which runs get_template_schema and returns SlideLayoutModel(id, name, description, json_schema) per layout. Each top-level property of a layout schema becomes a slot: Template v2 leaf (from _content_schema_for_element, schema.py:361-423) Slot accepts Limits carried over text string with minLength/maxLength heading or paragraph maxLength image object with image_prompt image none image with is_icon (icon_query) not offered in v1 icons stay slides-only text-list array list maxItems, item maxLength chart object (_chart_content_schema, schema.py:1490-1534) chart chart_type enum, intersected with ChartKind table (array of arrays of strings) table only when a table binding exists maxItems rows and columns infographic not offered in v1 layout excluded from the catalog when it is required When a slides run reaches Step C, the section schema is narrower than the generic one: an object keyed by slot id, each value constrained to the block type that slot accepts. The materializer can then write slot k to component key k with no guessing. Gotcha Template v2's CHART_TYPE_VALUES has twelve entries, including bubble, horizontal_stacked_bar and polar_area (templates/v2/schema.py:23-36), while the IR ChartKind has nine. Intersect the two when you build a chart slot's enum. If you pass the Template v2 list straight through, the model can pick a chart type that @gck/target-tiptap or @gck/target-superset-dashboard cannot render, and the artifact stops being portable between targets. Gotcha Presenton sends strict=False schemas everywhere except slide content, and never enables ensure_strict_json_schema (Prompts and schemas). The IR block list is a discriminated union (anyOf of objects with a const type). How each llmai provider adapter treats anyOf, const and strict=True is not visible in this repository and is not verified here. Test every provider you support before relying on provider-side enforcement; the server-side jsonschema validation catches violations either way.

The Artifact Spec rule is that the model may write numbers only inside tokens that reference bindings (Artifact Spec and targets). Presenton does the opposite in three places: the outline prompt asks for invented datasets (generate_presentation_outlines.py:113-116), the content prompt asks the model to "populate the requested labels, series, and values" (generate_slide_content.py:47-49), and the Template v2 chart schema contains series[].values arrays of numbers (templates/v2/schema.py:1509-1521). GCK enforces the rule in four layers: Layer Mechanism Where Prompt Plan and blocks prompts forbid numeric literals outside tokens Steps 3.1 and 3.3 Schema Chart, metric and table blocks have bindingId and display options only; no value fields exist Step 4 Validator Digits in text segments without a token are reported as I5_NUMBERS_IN_TOKENS before stamping and fed back through the repair loop; validate_artifact repeats the check on the stamped artifact below Adapter Values are written from DataBinding.snapshot by deterministic code, never by the model, and refreshed as the viewer after apply Part VIII binding resolution (Step 3.4) The validator plugs into the existing repair loop. Today generate_structured_with_schema_retries validates only against the JSON Schema and appends structured_validation_feedback_user_message when errors remain (llm_utils.py:362-387). The generalization is one keyword argument: NEW: change to servers/fastapi/utils/llm_utils.py (generate_structured_with_schema_retries) NEW: servers/fastapi/gck_engine/number_discipline.py generate_section_blocks passes extra_validator=numbers_in_tokens_hook. The hook applies exactly the rule that validate_artifact applies to the stamped artifact (I5_NUMBERS_IN_TOKENS, Artifact Spec and targets): outside tokens, digits are allowed only as calendar labels such as "2026", "Q3", "H1" or "FY26", so "revenue grew 14%" is rejected. Running the same rule before stamping only moves the failure into Presenton's repair loop, where it costs one round trip instead of a failed run; validate_artifact stays the final check. A count the user typed, such as "top 5", fails too, which is why the blocks prompt asks for such counts in words: widening the allowlist here without changing validate_artifact and its @gck/core twin validateArtifact would let the hook accept drafts that the final check rejects. Gotcha Do not strip

docs.t: Step 6: Persist runs as an event log
docs.x: Presenton has two persistence patterns that GCK merges into one: Async task rows. AsyncTaskModel stores status, message, error, data and a hidden payload, owner-scoped (models/sql/async_task.py:16-56). Statuses are only pending, completed and error (servers/fastapi/enums/async_task_status.py:4-7), and fail_interrupted_async_tasks marks pending rows as failed at startup because background tasks die with the process (services/async_tasks.py:22-52, called from api/lifespan.py:62). Smart checkpoints. Smart mode commits each accepted slide in its own session before emitting it (presentation.py:2075-2115), and on reconnect replays saved slides as slide_html frames before resuming (presentation.py:1941-1985) (Smart mode). Both are special cases of an append-only event log: a run row with the current state, plus every emitted event with a gapless sequence number, so that replay is "send every event with seq greater than Last-Event-ID". The event table, RunEventRow (gck_run_events, primary key (run_id, seq), with type, data, progress, ephemeral and created_at), and the EventLog that appends to it under a per-run lock are specified in Run protocol and client (Step 13). What the log needs beside it, and what Presenton lacks, is the run row: the generalization of AsyncTaskModel. NEW: servers/fastapi/gck_engine/models.py How the old fields map onto the run row and the log: Presenton today GCK Notes AsyncTaskModel.status (3 values) gck_runs.state The engine states from the run protocol: queued to completed, plus failed, cancelled, expired AsyncTaskModel.message progress on the latest event Replaces free-text status frames AsyncTaskModel.data (created_slides, remaining_slides) progress.completed and progress.total; completedSections and totalSections on run.failed Derived from artifact.patch events, not stored twice AsyncTaskModel.payload (excluded from responses) gck_runs.request The original RunRequest, kept for the run task and for resubmitting after a retryable failure; GET /v1/runs/{id} returns a RunSummary, which does not include it Smart slides rows as checkpoints gck_run_events rows Replay by sequence instead of by slide index (none) gck_runs.artifact, artifact_version Snapshot served by GET /v1/runs/{id}/artifact and used for compaction fail_interrupted_async_tasks fail_interrupted_runs Same startup sweep: every non-terminal run gets run.failed with retryable:

Run protocol and client (Step 13) gives the engine side of the protocol: RUNS_ROUTER = APIRouter(prefix="/v1/runs"), the events and cancel handlers, run_guard (which turns any failure into run.failed) and stream_run_events. Three pieces are specific to running inside Presenton: creating the run row with Presenton's session and owner, starting the task with the owner context, and authorizing reads with Presenton's principal. NEW: servers/fastapi/gck_engine/runs/create.py A repeated identical decision (a client retry after a dropped response) is answered with 202 again; only a different body for an input that was already answered gets 409 input_already_resolved, as the run protocol requires. Every error leaves the engine in the protocol's shape, {"error": {"code", "message", "retryable"}}, through one exception handler for GckHttpError registered on the app next to the router (Step 7.1). The run task body is execute_run, which run_guard awaits. It is a plain coroutine on the event loop, the same mechanism Smart mode uses for generate_smart_presentation (presentation.py:2128): NEW: servers/fastapi/gck_engine/runs/execute.py (excerpt) The intent changes the inputs, not the pipeline. build_context puts a transform's context.selection (Artifact blocks from the target's fromHost) into the planning prompt as the content to rewrite, and validates an edit's context.document as an Artifact, which becomes ctx.base_artifact. For edit, start_from sets the patcher's version to 0 without emitting anything, because the client already holds the base as version 0, and set_blocks then emits replace and remove ops only for blocks that changed and add ops with new ids for new ones; the client diffs the result by block id and applies it with the target's patch mode (Run protocol and client). In this sketch plan_sections plans the changed sections for an edit; that edit planning prompt is new engine work (roadmap work package 2.3), modeled on the per-slide edit prompts listed in Step 1. generate_all_sections runs Step C with a bounded asyncio.Semaphore and yields sections as they finish. That sits between Presenton's two existing policies: the web UI stream generates one slide at a time (presentation.py:2366-2381), and the one-shot API runs batches of 10 with asyncio.gather (presentation.py:2985). Because patches address sections by id, finishing out of order is harmless.

Four layers decide whether a request for /api/gck/... reaches the engine with an identity: Layer Today Change FastAPI app Routers are included one by one (api/main.py:68-74) app.include_router(RUNS_ROUTER, prefix="/api/gck"), so {engine} is /api/gck and the runs endpoint is /api/gck/v1/runs; one exception handler renders GckHttpError as {"error": {...}} Docker nginx Only /api/v1/ and /api/v2/ are proxied to port 8000 (nginx.conf:45-69); everything else goes to Next.js (nginx.conf:29-30) Add location /api/gck/ with the same 30-minute timeouts plus proxy_buffering off; Next.js proxy.ts (Electron and dev) isFastApiApiPath matches only /api/v1 and /api/v2 (proxy.ts:25-32); a Bearer header is forwarded only for sk-presenton- API keys, anything else must carry a session cookie (proxy.ts:146-171) Match /api/gck and forward its requests to FastAPI without the cookie check; FastAPI authenticates them FastAPI auth SessionAuthMiddleware requires a principal for any /api/ path (api/middlewares.py:44-53); a principal comes from the session cookie or a Bearer API key (api/v1/auth/principal.py:22-57) Accept a short-lived Bearer JWT as well (below) The last row matters because @gck/client sends credentials: "omit" and an Authorization header from its token provider (Run protocol and client), and an API key must never reach a browser. The fix reuses Presenton's own JWT machinery: a small endpoint, behind the normal cookie session, returns await get_jwt_strategy(lifetime_seconds=300).write_token(user) (get_jwt_strategy takes the lifetime as a parameter, api/v1/auth/users.py:176-182), and resolve_request_principal tries Bearer values that are not API keys as JWTs before giving up. Presenton's getToken callback calls that endpoint. Gotcha If you add only the FastAPI router, the Docker image still serves /api/gck/... from Next.js through the catch-all location /, and in development proxy.ts rejects the cookie-less request with 401 before FastAPI sees it. Either way you debug an auth error on the wrong server. Change nginx, proxy.ts and the principal resolution in the same commit as the router. Gotcha With DISABLE_AUTH (the Electron runtime), SessionAuthMiddleware calls the next handler before it sets request.state.auth_principal (api/middlewares.py:59-72). Code that reads request.state.auth_principal directly raises AttributeError there; read it with getattr(..., None) as

docs.t: Step 8: Keep the slides target on Template v2 and export
docs.x: The slides target must produce exactly what the Presenton editor and exporter already understand: a presentations row whose layout is a Template v2 payload and slides rows whose content and ui are hydrated. The materializer, run in the engine at the end of a slides run, reuses Presenton's own functions: Resolve the template with _resolve_prepare_layout(layout, sql_session), which extracts the template id from the layout reference and returns the layout payload, the PresentationLayoutModel and fonts (presentation.py:1448-1470). For each IR section, convert blocks back to the layout's content shape by slot key (heading or paragraph segments to text, with bold and italic as Markdown emphasis so _template_text_runs_from_markdown can parse it, presentation.py:1157; list items to text-list; chart blocks to {chart_type, categories, series} filled from the binding snapshot, the shape Part VIII resolution produces (Story 1, dynamic data and refresh); image blocks to image_prompt plus the resolved image_url). Build SlideModel(layout_group=<template reference>, layout=<layout id>, index=i, speaker_note=<popped speakerNote>, content=..., ui=_template_slide_ui(...)) as the stream does (presentation.py:2383-2391), then _hydrate_template_slide_ui (presentation.py:309-319). Persist the bindings (new, the step that keeps a GCK deck live): for every filled chart, metric and table slot, add a slide_data_bindings row in the same session with the binding's source, mapping, format, the snapshot and its status, resolving element_path after hydration with Story 1's element helpers, exactly as Story 1's persist_bindings_from_plan does for planner decks (Story 1, dynamic data and refresh). A slot whose binding is pending, error or forbidden is written empty (never template sample data and never the author's snapshot under forbidden), with the row status set to match. Commit the presentation, slides and binding rows in one transaction, store presentation_id on the run row, then run Story 1's resolve_new_bindings_inline so pending rows fill before the deck first opens. That path creates a new deck at the end of a run. From then on the deck behaves like any Part VIII deck: it refreshes on open as the viewer, "Refresh data" forces it, and an export refreshes first and stamps "Data as of" on slides whose refresh failed. docs.x: AI Slides (Part VIII) and the Presenton web UI call the existing endpoints. The extraction must not change their behavior, so the plan adds new code beside the old instead of rewriting it. Endpoint Until slides parity (M6) Optional bridge, behind a flag GET /api/v1/ppt/outlines/stream/{id} (outlines.py:84) unchanged translate plan.proposed into legacy chunk and complete frames POST /api/v1/ppt/presentation/prepare (presentation.py:1840) unchanged unchanged GET /api/v1/ppt/presentation/stream/{id} (presentation.py:2281) unchanged translate artifact.patch into legacy chunk and slide_assets frames POST /api/v1/ppt/presentation/generate and /generate/async (presentation.py:3169, :3240) unchanged run as a slides run, keeping the response and async_tasks contract POST /api/v2/ppt/presentation/generate/smart unchanged unchanged (Smart is not a GCK target) Part VIII routes (bindings, refresh, prompt library) unchanged; the deck-scoped refresh routes become the Presenton transport of @gck/data-superset (P4), while other hosts reach Story 8 through the engine's POST {engine}/v1/data/resolve, whose resolver reuses Story 1's mappers (as gck_data), refresh client and cache (Step 3.4) unchanged The rules that keep this safe: Shared functions change only additively. The extra_validator keyword in Step 5 defaults to None, so every existing caller of generate_structured_with_schema_retries behaves as before. Golden tests pin the legacy paths. servers/fastapi/tests/integration/test_presentation_generation_flow.py already covers the prepare normalization (test_presentation_generation_flow.py:891) and template-schema content generation (test_presentation_generation_flow.py:1066). Run it on every GCK change; add a test that a slides run and the legacy stream produce slides with the same layout, content keys and ui element types for a fixed fake LLM. The bridge is optional. Its flag defaults to off; if it never ships, the legacy endpoints simply keep their own code paths. Gotcha The legacy slide stream concatenates slide chunks without commas (presentation.py:2360-2363, presentation.py:2448-2451), and the browser relies on parsing each chunk on its own (Streaming (SSE)). A bridge must reproduce that framing byte for byte, including the opening { "slides": [ and closing ] } chunks, or usePresentationStreaming will silently drop slides.
