docs.t: Step 11: Make Presenton consume the kit (strangler pattern)
docs.x: The strangler pattern replaces a system piece by piece: new code grows around the old, callers move one at a time, and the old code is removed only when nothing calls it. Presenton is the first and best test host, because its outline page already does what OutlineReview does. The first cut keeps OutlinePage untouched. useOutlineStreaming keeps its signature and return shape (useOutlineStreaming.ts:18-21, :257-263) but gets a second implementation behind a build-time flag: NEW: servers/nextjs/app/(presentation-generator)/outline/hooks/useOutlineStreaming.ts (facade) setOutlines still runs limitOutlines (store/slices/presentationGeneration.ts:128-130), so every downstream component, including /prepare, sees the same {content} list as before. The stages after this: Stage Change in Presenton Old code removed when S1 Outline page plans through @gck/client behind NEXT_PUBLIC_GCK_OUTLINE; the run is cancelled at the review point the flag has been on by default for one release with no regressions S2 Template preview thumbnails render through @gck/target-slides/renderer (same code, new import path) lib/template-v2-json-to-html.ts is a re-export shim, then deleted S3 Outline page renders OutlineReview instead of OutlineContent OutlineContent, OutlineItem, useOutlineManagement have no importers S4 "Generate" answers the run's run.awaiting_input (no more cancel) instead of calling /prepare and the slide stream the presentation page can load a materialized deck by id (it already can, through GET /presentation/{id}) S5 AI Slides (Part VIII) moves to the same run API Part VIII's own release plan allows it Gotcha S1 is not invisible to users. The legacy hook highlights the outline card that is still being written, because it re-parses partial JSON on every chunk (useOutlineStreaming.ts:142-164); plan.proposed arrives whole, so the facade returns activeSlideIndex: null and the cards appear at once. Either accept that change explicitly when you turn the flag on, or have the engine emit plan.proposed with final: false more than once while Step A is still writing, and restore the highlight from the newest outline item. text.delta cannot carry the plan: it addresses a block of the artifact (blockId), and the plan is not part of the artifact. Gotcha Do not let S4 remove the legacy slide stream while usePresentationStreaming still handles Smart mode through the same URL

Two layouts are realistic. Concern A: packages inside the fork (presenton-os/packages/*) B: gck/ monorepo next to the fork Upstream rebase cost High: root package.json (no workspaces today, package.json:1-26), servers/nextjs/package-lock.json, Dockerfile, Electron build all change Low: the fork gains only dependency lines and the seam files below Docker build servers/nextjs is installed alone with npm ci from its own lock file (Dockerfile:42-44); file: links to ../../packages are outside that layer Unchanged; @gck/* come from a registry like any dependency Iteration speed One commit spans kit and Presenton Two commits; use a local registry or npm pack tarballs during development Other hosts (Superset extension, Tiptap apps) Must depend on a slides product repository Depend on a small, focused repository Protocol contract Easy to share The engine exports its Pydantic models as JSON Schemas and opens a pull request against @gck/protocol Recommendation: B for the frontend, plus an engine module inside the fork. The @gck/* packages live in gck/ (pnpm workspaces and Turborepo, per the blueprint). The GCK Engine is a generalized Presenton FastAPI, so its code lives in the fork, in a new directory servers/fastapi/gck_engine/ that upstream never touches. The protocol contract flows from the engine to the kit: the engine's Pydantic models (gck_engine.protocol) are the source of truth, as Presenton's own response schemas are (generate_presentation_outlines.py:362-365 derives one with model_json_schema()), and a script exports them into gck/packages/protocol/schemas/ through a pull request; Frontend engineering and quality shows the script and the contract tests on both sides. The kit consumes the engine the way Presenton consumes export-core, by a pinned version (package.json:4), never by reaching into the fork's tree. The fork's footprint outside servers/fastapi/gck_engine/ is a short list of seams, and this list is what you re-check on every rebase: Seam Lines changed servers/fastapi/api/main.py one include_router, one exception handler servers/fastapi/api/v1/ppt/endpoints/gck_slides.py new file: POST /api/v1/ppt/presentation/{id}/slides/from-content on PRESENTATION_ROUTER (Step 8), plus one import so the route registers servers/fastapi/services/database.py two entries in the create_all list, one in _STRICT_OWNER_MODELS servers/fastapi/alembic/versions/<new>.py new

Presenton is licensed under the Apache License 2.0 (LICENSE:1-3), with "Copyright 2025 presenton" in the appendix (LICENSE:190). Any @gck/* file that starts from Presenton code (the renderer, the chart loader, prompt text, schema helpers) is a Derivative Work. Section 4 of the license sets four conditions (LICENSE:90-122): Condition What it means for GCK 4(a) give recipients a copy of the License Ship LICENSE (Apache-2.0) in every @gck/* package tarball and in gck/ 4(b) modified files carry prominent change notices A header on each moved or adapted file: origin path, "modified by", date 4(c) retain copyright, patent, trademark and attribution notices Keep existing notices and vendored license headers 4(d) include the attribution notices from the NOTICE file See below Presenton's NOTICE is not a short attribution line. It is a 26,825-line list of third-party licenses with a PYTHON PACKAGES section (NOTICE:2) and a NODE PACKAGES section (NOTICE:3783), duplicated at servers/fastapi/NOTICE. Condition 4(d) excludes the notices "that do not pertain to any part of the Derivative Works" (LICENSE:107-111). So each package's NOTICE should contain a line attributing Presenton plus the third-party notices for what that package actually ships: for @gck/target-slides, at least Chart.js and the datalabels plugin, whose license files are vendored next to the scripts (servers/nextjs/public/vendor/chart-4.5.1-LICENSE.md, chartjs-plugin-datalabels-2.2.0-LICENSE.md), and KaTeX, which lib/math.ts imports (servers/nextjs/lib/math.ts:1) and which therefore moves with the renderer. Generate the third-party part from each package's lock file in CI rather than editing it by hand. Section 6 grants no right to use the licensor's names or marks (LICENSE:139-142), so name the kit GCK and describe Presenton only factually ("derived from Presenton"). You may add terms for your own modifications (LICENSE:124-129), but the Presenton-derived parts stay Apache-2.0, so licensing all of @gck/* under Apache-2.0 avoids mixed-license packages. This is an engineering reading of the license, not legal advice. Gotcha @presenton/export-core cannot be a dependency of any new target. It is installed as a prebuilt archive, presenton-export-core-opensource-<version>.tgz, downloaded from the presenton/presenton-export releases at a pinned version (scripts/sync-presentation-export.cjs:32-33, :170-172,

Reads: servers/nextjs/package.json, servers/nextjs/eslint.config.mjs, servers/nextjs/cypress.config.ts, servers/nextjs/cypress/security/dependencies.cy.ts, servers/nextjs/app/(presentation-generator)/components/SmartHtmlSlide.tsx, servers/nextjs/app/(presentation-generator)/components/useSmartChartInjection.ts, servers/nextjs/lib/chart-browser.ts, servers/nextjs/utils/mixpanel.ts, apache/superset: superset-frontend/webpack.config.js, apache/superset: superset-frontend/src/extensions/ExtensionsLoader.ts, apache/superset: superset-frontend/packages/superset-core/src/theme/*, apache/superset: superset/config.py · Builds on: Architecture, React SDK and UI kit, Host integrations · Time: ~50 min The previous chapters defined what the Generative Content Kit (GCK) does: the Artifact Spec, the run protocol, the React SDK, the host integrations and the extraction plan. This chapter is about how the kit is built, shipped and kept correct. You will lay out the gck/ monorepo file by file, write the package.json exports maps, build configs and bundle budgets, package the kit three ways (npm packages, a Module Federation remote inside a Superset extension, and a web component), and then work through theming, i18n, accessibility, performance, security, testing, release engineering and telemetry, each with concrete config and code. Where Presenton or Superset already does something relevant, the chapter cites the source so you can see which constraints are real and which are design choices. What is source and what is new Every code block whose title ends in "(new)" is design code for the GCK and does not exist in either repository. Blocks with a path title and no "(new)" are verbatim excerpts. Presenton paths are relative to the Presenton repository root at 571461f. Superset paths are prefixed apache/superset: and refer to master at cabd8d4.

The blueprint fixes the shape: one repository gck/, pnpm workspaces, Turborepo, the eleven @gck/* packages listed in Architecture. The tree below adds the folders every package needs to be built, tested and documented.

gck/ (new) engine/ is optional. If the GCK Engine lives in a separate repository (for example as a fork of Presenton's FastAPI server, see Extracting the engine from Presenton), the schema export in Step 10.2 runs there and opens a pull request against packages/protocol/schemas/.

gck/pnpm-workspace.yaml (new) gck/package.json (new) gck/turbo.json (new) Type checking runs once for the whole graph with tsc -b (Step 1.4), not per package through Turborepo, because project references already give incremental, ordered checking and a second layer of caching only adds confusion about which cache is stale.

Every published package is ESM-only, declares "type": "module", ships dist/ plus its own README, and resolves through an exports map with types listed first. Four manifests show the patterns. @gck/protocol has no runtime dependencies. Its JSON Schemas (schemas/artifact-1.schema.json and the run schemas of Step 10.2) and the Artifact fixture corpus (fixtures/valid/, fixtures/invalid/, see Artifact Spec and targets) are files, exposed through subpaths so that runtime code never imports them by accident: packages/protocol/package.json (new) @gck/react has two entry points and ships CSS. It depends on @gck/core, @gck/client and @gck/protocol (the provider constructs the GckClient); intl-messageformat is the ICU formatter proposed in Step 6.1. React is a peer that accepts both majors, because Superset master is on React 18.3 (apache/superset: superset-frontend/package.json:196) while Presenton is on React 19.2.6 (servers/nextjs/package.json:59): packages/react/package.json (new) @gck/target-tiptap supports Tiptap 2 and 3 through an internal compatibility module (src/compat/), so @tiptap/core is a peer with two ranges. Like every target, its main entry is React-free and DOM-free (createTiptapTarget, toProseMirror, fromProseMirror, applyToEditor, the GckGenerate extension); the React node views (gckNodes, GckChart, GckMetric, GckDataTable, GckToken) live in a /react subpath. The React peers are therefore optional, because the main entry also works with a vanilla Tiptap editor: packages/target-tiptap/package.json (excerpt, new) @gck/host-superset treats @apache-superset/core as an optional peer. The package exports two kinds of code: extension glue that only makes sense inside Superset (commands, views, context providers), and pure functions such as supersetThemeToGck() (Step 5) that an app embedding Superset dashboards through the Embedded SDK can call with its own antd tokens, without @apache-superset/core installed: packages/host-superset/package.json (excerpt, new) Gotcha: sideEffects: false deletes your CSS A bundler that trusts "sideEffects": false drops any import that binds no names, which is exactly what import "@gck/react/ui/gck.css" is. Packages that ship CSS must list it ("sideEffects": ["**/*.css"]). The same applies to @gck/element: customElements.define(...) is a side effect, so it lives in a separate define entry that is listed in sideEffects, while

gck/tsconfig.base.json (new) packages/core/tsconfig.json (new) The lib setting is the cheapest architecture test you will ever write: @gck/core is framework-agnostic and "no DOM" per the blueprint, so its tsconfig omits "DOM". Any accidental document.querySelector in core fails type checking. WebWorker is included because the patch worker (Step 8.4) lives there. UI packages extend a dom preset from tooling/tsconfig that adds "DOM", "DOM.Iterable" and "jsx": "react-jsx". The root tsconfig.json lists every package in references and has "files": [].

docs.t: 1.5 Building with tsup (and Vite library mode for the element)
docs.x: Libraries are built with tsup: ESM output, declaration files, and no bundling of dependencies or peers (tsup externalizes both by default, so no external list is needed). packages/react/tsup.config.ts (new) The "use client" banner matters for Next.js App Router hosts such as Presenton: without it, importing a hook-using component from a server component fails at build time. @gck/core, @gck/client and @gck/protocol use the same config without the banner and with platform: "neutral". Gotcha: tsup is in maintenance The tsup README now states that the project "is not actively maintained anymore" and points to tsdown, which has a "Migrate from tsup" guide (https://github.com/egoist/tsup, https://tsdown.dev/guide/). The options used above (entry, format, dts, platform, sourcemap, clean) are the basic set; check each against the migration guide before switching rather than assuming a one-to-one mapping. @gck/element is different: it must bundle React because its hosts (Angular, Vue, plain pages) do not provide one. Vite library mode suits that (https://vite.dev/guide/build.html#library-mode): with multiple entries the default formats are es and cjs, so restrict to es. packages/element/vite.config.ts (new)

The kit must look native in Superset (antd 6, Emotion), in Tiptap apps (often Tailwind or shadcn), in Presenton (Tailwind 3 plus a browser Tailwind 4 runtime for Smart slides, see Next.js architecture) and on plain pages. No single CSS-in-JS library is shared by all of them, so the kit uses none: Headless first. @gck/react primitives render no styles at all; hosts that want full control style them with their own system. One plain stylesheet for @gck/react/ui, gck.css. All selectors are prefixed .gck- and wrapped in @layer gck { ... }, so any unlayered host rule wins without !important. Every visual value is a --gck-* custom property (Step 5), set on the kit's root element (the .gck-root wrapper that GckProvider renders). Host theming is a mapping function into GckProvider's theme prop, not an override war. Logical properties only (margin-inline-start, padding-block), so RTL works without a second stylesheet (Step 6). No runtime style injection by default. Hosts import @gck/react/ui/gck.css through their bundler. For hosts that cannot (a Superset extension built with the stock template has no CSS loader, Step 4.2), a proposed helper injectGckStyles({ nonce }) in @gck/react/ui appends one <style> element with an optional nonce. Inside the web component, the stylesheet is adopted into the shadow root. CSS custom properties inherit through the shadow boundary, so --gck-* tokens set on the host page still apply.

Three rules keep the graph honest, enforced by an ESLint no-restricted-imports block per package in tooling/eslint-config: Rule Enforced by Why protocol, client, core never import React or the DOM tsconfig lib (Step 1.4) plus a lint rule banning react* imports the core must run in a worker, in Node tests and under any framework Targets depend on core, never on react, in their main entry; previews and node views live in a /react subpath reached through loadPreview lint rule a server-side or worker consumer of toNative() must not pull React Only host-* packages import host SDKs (@apache-superset/core) lint rule keeps every other package host-agnostic Presenton's lint config turns off sixteen rules, including @typescript-eslint/no-explicit-any and react-hooks/rules-of-hooks (servers/nextjs/eslint.config.mjs:10-27). Code extracted into the kit (Extracting the engine from Presenton) lands in packages with those rules on; fix violations during the move instead of copying the overrides.

The blueprint sets two numbers; the rest are proposals that follow from them and are labeled as such. Bundle Budget (gzip) Source Notes @gck/core incl. its @gck/client and @gck/protocol runtime < 15 kB blueprint includes jsonrepair (the store's format: "json" drafts) and d3-format (resolveToken); if the budget is exceeded, jsonrepair is the first candidate for a dynamic import() on the first JSON text.delta @gck/react + @gck/react/ui, excluding renderers < 40 kB blueprint React and react-dom excluded (peers) @gck/data-superset < 6 kB proposal a thin DataProvider over @gck/client; the binding store and refresh controller it feeds count against the @gck/core budget (Live Superset data) @gck/target-text < 5 kB proposal pure serializers @gck/target-tiptap (eager part) < 12 kB proposal Tiptap excluded (peer) @gck/target-slides (eager part: manifest + adapter) < 8 kB proposal renderer and Chart.js are lazy @gck/target-slides lazy preview chunk < 120 kB proposal see measurement below @gck/element full bundle < 110 kB proposal includes React, react-dom, core, ui Superset extension initial chunk (remoteEntry + ./index) < 60 kB proposal React, antd and @apache-superset/core come from the host The slides preview budget comes from what Presenton ships today: Chart.js 4.5.1 as a 208,522-byte UMD file (70,529 bytes gzipped at level 9), the datalabels plugin (5,275 bytes gzipped), both under servers/nextjs/public/vendor/, and the Template v2 renderer servers/nextjs/lib/template-v2-json-to-html.ts (4,145 lines, 191,674 bytes of unminified TypeScript). The UMD build registers every chart controller; importing only the controllers that ChartKind needs from the ESM build is the main lever. Measure the minified renderer chunk once it is extracted.

size-limit measures Brotli by default; "gzip": true switches to gzip so the numbers match the budgets. The import field measures the tree-shaken cost of what a consumer actually imports, and ignore keeps peers out of the total (https://github.com/ai/size-limit). gck/.size-limit.json (new) In CI (Step 11) pnpm size fails the job when any limit is exceeded, and the andresz1/size-limit-action@v1 step posts the diff against main on the pull request. A budget is raised only in the same pull request that explains why, reviewed like an API change.

A target adapter keeps its manifest and serializer eager (the engine needs the manifest on every run, see Artifact Spec and targets) and its preview lazy, behind TargetAdapter.loadPreview. The slides target loads its renderer and Chart.js only the first time a slides preview mounts: packages/target-slides/src/index.ts (excerpt, new) buildManifest, toSlides and applySlides stand for the manifest, toNative and apply code shown in Artifact Spec and targets. Chart.js itself is reached through the @gck/target-slides/charts subpath. Extracting the engine from Presenton first moves lib/chart-browser.ts there as is, with the script URLs turned into options; for hosts that do not serve Presenton's /vendor/ files (Superset, any bundled host), the subpath's loader becomes a module-scoped ESM import: packages/target-slides/src/charts/chart-runtime.ts (new) useTargetPreview wraps loadPreview in React.lazy (cached per adapter), and StreamingPreview renders it inside a Suspense boundary whose fallback is the same skeleton the streaming state already shows (React SDK and UI kit), so the lazy load never causes a layout jump. Gotcha: Presenton's chart runtime is a global script Presenton loads Chart.js by appending <script src="/vendor/chart-4.5.1.umd.min.js"> and caches the promise on window.__PRESENTON_CHART_BROWSER_RUNTIME__ (servers/nextjs/lib/chart-browser.ts:1-3, :58-96, :98-136). That works only where /vendor/ is served from the same origin and nothing else defines window.Chart. Inside a Superset extension the path does not exist, and a host that already uses Chart.js would share (or clobber) the global. Outside Presenton, the kit therefore uses the module-scoped ESM loader above, which webpack or Vite turns into a hashed chunk next to the rest of the bundle.

React hosts (Presenton, any Vite or Next.js app with Tiptap) install the packages they need and get one copy of React, Tiptap and the kit, deduplicated by their package manager: examples/react-vite-tiptap/src/GckRoot.tsx (excerpt, new)

docs.t: 4.2 A Module Federation remote inside a Superset extension
docs.x: Superset loads extension frontends as webpack Module Federation remotes. The host declares four shared singletons, all eager: apache/superset: superset-frontend/webpack.config.js:187-211 The extension template generated by the Superset extensions CLI mirrors this on the remote side with import: false, which means the remote ships no fallback copy and always uses the host's: apache/superset: superset-extensions-cli/src/superset_extensions_cli/templates/frontend/webpack.config.js.j2:44-64 At load time ExtensionsLoader builds a custom share scope in which @apache-superset/core resolves to window.superset with extensions.getContext pre-bound to that extension (apache/superset: superset-frontend/src/extensions/ExtensionsLoader.ts:204-220, :234-244), and window.superset itself is the host's real @apache-superset/core namespaces plus the host implementations (apache/superset: superset-frontend/src/extensions/ExtensionsStartup.tsx:56-68). Everything the kit needs from Superset therefore arrives through one import of the package root. apps/superset-extension is the .supx frontend. It bundles every @gck/* package it uses (they are not in Superset's share scope, so they cannot be shared) and takes React, react-dom, antd and @apache-superset/core from the host: apps/superset-extension/webpack.config.js (excerpt, new) apps/superset-extension/package.json (excerpt, new) Gotcha: the stock template references a peer it does not declare The template's webpack config reads packageConfig.peerDependencies["antd"] (webpack.config.js.j2:55-59), but the generated package.json.j2 declares only @apache-superset/core, react and react-dom as peers (package.json.j2:16-20), so requiredVersion for antd is undefined. Add antd to peerDependencies explicitly, as above, so webpack can warn about a mismatch with the host's antd ("antd": "^6.6.7" in apache/superset: superset-frontend/package.json:159). Gotcha: only the package root is shared webpack's Module Federation docs state that to share anything below a package's root you must "append / to the package name" in shared (https://webpack.js.org/plugins/module-federation-plugin/). Superset shares '@apache-superset/core' without the slash, so a runtime import of a subpath such as @apache-superset/core/theme is not resolved from the host scope and would be bundled from the extension's devDependency instead. Inside the extension, import

@gck/element defines <gck-generate> for hosts without React. Its attribute, property and event contract, and the full GckGenerateElement class, are in Host integrations (Step 6.1); this section only covers what matters for packaging it: Shadow root. The element renders the React kit into a gck-root mount inside an open shadow root, so host CSS cannot break it and its CSS cannot leak out. Inside, it renders GckProvider with only its documented props and composes the five @gck/react/ui components itself; there is no packaged "whole flow" component and no portalContainer prop. Stylesheet. The kit stylesheet (@gck/react/ui/gck.css) is written into the bundle as a string at build time (KIT_CSS from src/styles.generated.ts) and adopted on the shadow root with CSSStyleSheet.replaceSync, with a <style> element as the fallback. Properties, not attributes. context, tokenProvider (a TokenProvider from @gck/client) and data are objects or functions, so they are properties only. The connected callback re-applies values a framework set before the element was defined. Apply hand-off. The element applies nothing itself: it dispatches gck-apply with the native value and waits for the page to call reportApplied(result). No side effects in the class module. src/index.ts only exports GckGenerateElement; registration lives in a separate define entry, which is the one listed in sideEffects (Step 1.3) and the one pages import as @gck/element/define: packages/element/src/define.ts (new) The element emits gck-apply ({ target, mode, native, artifact }, the host commits native), gck-state and gck-error; composed: true lets them cross the shadow boundary. Never load @gck/element inside Superset or another React host: it carries its own React, which doubles the bundle and splits context. React hosts use the npm packages; Superset uses the remote in Step 4.2.

Hosts that cannot run third-party script at all mount the same standalone app in an iframe, the pattern Part VIII uses for AI Slides (Story 5, analytics menu and iframe). Context is posted in and apply results are posted out, with typed, origin-checked messages (Step 9.4). It is a fallback, not the default.

Package line Protocol React Host versions Tiptap Notes @gck/protocol 1.x gck.artifact/1, run API v1 none any none independent semver (Step 12) @gck/core, @gck/client 1.x 1.0 to 1.latest none any none sends GCK-Protocol: 1 on every request @gck/react 1.x 1.x 18.3, 19.x any React host none tested on both majors @gck/target-tiptap 1.x 1.x 18.3, 19.x (optional) any 2.10+, 3.x Presenton uses Tiptap 3.30.5 (servers/nextjs/package.json:40-44) @gck/host-superset 1.x 1.x 18.3 (host) Superset 6.1 and master none extension menus differ by version, see Host integrations @gck/element 1.x 1.x bundled 19.x any page none not for React hosts @gck/target-slides 1.x 1.x 18.3, 19.x Presenton 0.9.x Template v2 none renderer extracted from lib/template-v2-json-to-html.ts The matrix lives in the docs site and is generated from the e2e job's actual matrix, so it cannot drift from what CI tests.

All styled components read these properties and nothing else. Defaults live in gck.css under .gck-root (React SDK and UI kit); hosts override them through GckProvider's theme prop (Partial<GckTheme>, keys accent, bg, fg, border, danger, radius, font), which the provider writes as --gck-<key> on its .gck-root wrapper. Token Default (light, gck.css) GckTheme key From Superset theme token From a Tiptap host (shadcn variables) --gck-accent #1f6feb accent colorPrimary hsl(var(--primary)) --gck-bg #fff bg colorBgContainer hsl(var(--background)) --gck-fg #1c1c1c fg colorText hsl(var(--foreground)) --gck-border #e5e7eb border colorBorder hsl(var(--border)) --gck-danger #b42318 danger colorError hsl(var(--destructive)) --gck-radius 8px radius borderRadius (number, add px) var(--radius) --gck-font inherit font fontFamily computed font-family of the editor element --gck-space 8px none (stylesheet only) sizeUnit times 2 (number, add px) 8px The eight properties above are the 1.0 contract. The rest of this chapter (focus ring, target size, reduced motion) also relies on the following additions, proposed for a 1.x minor (new tokens are a minor change, Step 12.2); each extends GckTheme with the same key minus the --gck- prefix when it ships: Proposed token From Superset theme token From a Tiptap host --gck-fg-muted colorTextSecondary hsl(var(--muted-foreground)) --gck-accent-hover / --gck-on-accent colorPrimaryHover / colorTextLightSolid computed / hsl(var(--primary-foreground)) --gck-focus-ring controlOutline hsl(var(--ring)) --gck-warning / -success / -info colorWarning / colorSuccess / colorInfo defaults --gck-font-mono fontFamilyCode default --gck-font-size / --gck-line-height fontSize (number) / lineHeight (unitless) computed font-size / line-height --gck-control-height controlHeight (number) 2.25rem --gck-shadow-popover boxShadowSecondary default --gck-motion-duration motionDurationMid default --gck-z-overlay zIndexPopupBase host z-index scale Every Superset name in both tables is in Superset's allowlist of antd tokens that make up SupersetTheme (apache/superset: superset-frontend/packages/superset-core/src/theme/types.ts:277-500, type at :511), so the mapping uses the public theme contract rather than antd internals.

packages/host-superset/src/theme.ts (new) packages/host-superset/src/useSupersetGckTheme.ts (new) GckProvider writes the theme values as inline custom properties on its <div className="gck-root" style={{ display: "contents", ...vars }}> wrapper (React SDK and UI kit). React applies the style prop through the CSSOM, which a CSP style-src without 'unsafe-inline' does not block, so token values work under strict policies too.

Dark mode in Superset. Superset's dark theme already has dark values for colorBgContainer, colorText and the rest, so the bridge needs no separate dark table. Because it re-derives the theme object whenever the Emotion theme object changes, a user switching Superset between light, dark and system mode (ThemeMode, types.ts:56-60) re-themes the kit without a reload. isThemeDark(theme) is tinycolor(theme.colorBgContainer).isDark() (apache/superset: superset-frontend/packages/superset-core/src/theme/utils/themeUtils.ts:55-57), exported from the theme namespace; a host can use it to set color-scheme on its own container so native scrollbars and form controls match. Dark mode elsewhere. The gck.css defaults are light. A host with its own dark mode passes dark values through theme; class-based hosts (Presenton's Tailwind config uses darkMode: ["class"], servers/nextjs/tailwind.config.ts:4) derive them from their own state. A default dark set under @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) for hosts that pass nothing is a proposed stylesheet addition; GckConfig has no colorScheme prop. Density. antd's compact algorithm (ThemeAlgorithm.COMPACT, types.ts:43-47) produces smaller sizes. --gck-space is not a GckTheme key, so a host maps density with an unlayered stylesheet rule on .gck-root (for example sizeUnit times 2 in px), which wins over the layered gck.css default and tightens every padding defined as a multiple of --gck-space; the proposed --gck-control-height would follow controlHeight the same way. Gotcha: antd numbers and shadcn triplets are not CSS values antd tokens such as fontSize, borderRadius, controlHeight and sizeUnit are numbers, and lineHeight is a unitless ratio; writing --gck-radius: 6 produces an invalid length that silently falls back. shadcn-style hosts, including Presenton's own stylesheet, store colors as bare HSL components (--background: 0 0% 100%;, servers/nextjs/app/globals.css:40), which must be wrapped as hsl(var(--background)). The mapping functions own these conversions so components never do. For Tiptap hosts without design tokens, a proposed helper themeFromElement(editor.view.dom) in @gck/target-tiptap/react (it reads the DOM, so it cannot live in the React-free main entry) reads getComputedStyle() of the editor element (font family, text and background colors) once on mount and returns a Partial<GckTheme>, so generated content previews

In 1.0, every kit string has a typed key (MessageKey), defaultMessages in src/messages.ts holds the English text, and GckContextValue.t(key, vars) substitutes {name} placeholders (React SDK and UI kit). That is enough for English and breaks on plurals. The proposal for 1.x keeps the keys and the t signature and swaps the formatter: messages become ICU MessageFormat strings in per-locale JSON catalogs inside @gck/react, formatted with intl-messageformat. ICU gives plurals, selects and number formatting that work across languages, which Presenton's UI does not need today (its chrome is English-only) and Superset handles with gettext through Jed. packages/react/src/i18n/en.json (excerpt, new, proposal) The variables are the ones the components already pass: completed and total come from the event's progress, n from the section count. packages/react/src/i18n/format.ts (new, proposal) Catalogs for locales other than English are loaded with dynamic import() so that only the active locale ships. Hosts can override any message key through GckProvider messages={...} (a Partial<Messages>, already in 1.0), which is how a host aligns wording with its own product.

Host Where the locale comes from Normalization Superset the language pack the page bootstraps into window.__SUPERSET_LANGUAGE_PACK__ and that @apache-superset/core's translator reads (apache/superset: superset-frontend/packages/superset-core/src/translation/TranslatorSingleton.ts:39-59); its locale_data.superset[""].lang is a Superset Locale (translation/types/index.ts:26-72) Superset uses underscores (pt_BR, zh_TW, sr_Latn); convert to BCP 47 (pt-BR, zh-TW, sr-Latn) before calling Intl Tiptap app GckProvider locale from the app's i18n library already BCP 47 in most apps Presenton the presentation's language field for content; the UI stays English content language and UI locale are separate Web component locale attribute, else document.documentElement.lang as given The window global is an implementation detail, not a documented extension API, so @gck/host-superset reads it only as a fallback, and one Superset e2e project (Step 10.5) runs in French to catch a change.

Two directions coexist: the UI direction (from the UI locale) and the artifact direction (from Artifact.language, which the engine sets from the prompt or context.locale). An Arabic user can generate an English report, and the reverse. The kit sets dir and lang separately on the chrome and on the preview root: packages/react/src/i18n/direction.ts (new) Superset's own catalog list includes two RTL locales, ar and fa (translation/types/index.ts:27, :33), so RTL is a real requirement, not a hypothetical. Because the stylesheet uses logical properties only (Step 1.6), flipping dir is all the layout needs. Streaming text in a mixed-direction paragraph is wrapped in <bdi> per data token so that a number or an English product name inside Arabic prose does not reorder its neighbors.

The kit makes these rules systematic.

docs.t: 7.2 Announcing a stream without flooding the screen reader
docs.x: A live region that receives every text.delta makes a screen reader read fragments forever. The kit announces state transitions immediately and progress at most every five seconds: packages/react/src/a11y/useRunAnnouncer.ts (new) Components call it with run.state from useGenerationRun and t from useGckContext(). The preview container carries aria-busy="true" while the run is in generating or resolving_data, so assistive technology does not read half-built content as final. Failures use a separate role="alert" region, the only assertive announcement the kit makes.

Focus moves only when the user caused the transition. After Apply, focus goes to the applied content in the host, and the ApplyBar announces apply.done with the target's undo hint (apply.undoNote, for example "Undo with Ctrl+Z"): Target Focus after apply tiptap-doc editor.chain().focus().setTextSelection(insertedRange.to).scrollIntoView().run(): caret at the end of the inserted range, inside the same undo group slides the first new slide's thumbnail in the side panel superset-dashboard the new tab's title (or the dashboard title for a new dashboard) after navigation text the Markdown component that received the text When a run finishes generating while the user is typing elsewhere (for example in the outline review), focus stays where it is; the status region announces readiness instead.

Key Context Action /ai then Enter Tiptap editor open the composer at the cursor (GckGenerate slash command) Mod+Enter composer submit Escape composer, review, preview cancel the run if running, else close; focus returns to the invoker Alt+ArrowUp / Alt+ArrowDown outline row move the section up or down Enter outline review approve the outline Mod+Shift+Enter preview apply with the default mode Mod+Z host, after apply undo the whole application (one undo step, see React SDK and UI kit) Shortcuts are registered on the kit's root element, not on window, so they never collide with host shortcuts.

packages/react/src/ui/gck.css (excerpt, new) The JavaScript side honors the same preference: scrollIntoView({ behavior: "auto" }) instead of "smooth" when matchMedia("(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)") matches, and the preview does not auto-scroll to follow the stream unless the user has scrolled to the bottom.

The engine can emit dozens of artifact.patch and text.delta events per second. Re-rendering after each one is wasted work, because the screen can only show one frame per refresh. Presenton debounces outline Markdown rendering with a 60 ms timer (servers/nextjs/app/(presentation-generator)/outline/components/OutlineItem.tsx:120-140); the kit generalizes that into the artifact store of @gck/core (React SDK and UI kit). createArtifactStore(schedule?) applies every patch to its snapshot immediately and batches only the notification: the first change in a frame calls schedule(emit), later changes in the same frame do nothing, and the default schedule is requestAnimationFrame behind a typeof guard, with a 16 ms setTimeout where it does not exist (Node tests, old workers). One frame, one notification, one React render. requestAnimationFrame does not fire in background tabs, so subscribers hear about patches only when the tab becomes visible again. @gck/core cannot check document.hidden (it never touches the DOM), so a visibility-aware scheduler belongs in @gck/react. Passing it needs a schedule option on RunControllerOptions, which the 1.0 controller does not have (it calls createArtifactStore() with the default); this is proposed for 1.x: packages/react/src/schedule.ts (new, proposal) Gotcha: data is current, subscribers are not store.getSnapshot() always reflects every event received so far, so the controller's apply() never sees an artifact missing its last patches. What lags by up to a frame is React: a value captured in a render can be one frame old. Code that acts on what the user sees (custom apply buttons, tests asserting on rendered output) calls store.flush() first, which delivers the pending notification synchronously; tests can also pass (fn) => fn() as schedule.

The IR store applies JSON Patch with structural sharing: unchanged sections and blocks keep their object identity. React components subscribe per block through useArtifact (which wraps useSyncExternalStore) with a selector that returns one block, so a patch to block 37 re-renders block 37 only: packages/react/src/use-block.ts (new) Presenton's presentation stream does the opposite: each chunk dispatches a whole new presentationData into Redux (servers/nextjs/app/(presentation-generator)/presentation/hooks/usePresentationStreaming.ts:482-502), and every subscriber of that slice re-renders. That is acceptable for 50 slides with block-level content; it does not scale to a 200-page Tiptap document.

The preview list virtualizes once an artifact has more than 40 sections. Two levels are used: content-visibility: auto with contain-intrinsic-size on each section, which costs nothing and skips layout and paint for off-screen sections. A windowed list (for example TanStack Virtual) for the StreamingPreview and the slides thumbnail strip when the count is large enough that DOM node count itself is the problem. Measured heights are cached per section id so a streaming section that grows does not make the scroll position jump. The slides preview renders a Template v2 slide to HTML only when its thumbnail intersects the viewport (IntersectionObserver), and Chart.js canvases are created only for visible slides and destroyed when they leave, the same cleanup Presenton does on re-render with Chart.getChart(canvas)?.destroy() (servers/nextjs/app/(presentation-generator)/components/TemplateV2HtmlSlidePreview.tsx:309-317).

docs.t: 8.4 A worker for patch and repair
docs.x: Presenton repairs partial JSON by appending each chunk to a string and running jsonrepair plus JSON.parse over the whole accumulated text on every chunk: servers/nextjs/app/(presentation-generator)/outline/hooks/useOutlineStreaming.ts:133-137 The same pattern is in the presentation stream (usePresentationStreaming.ts:455, :482-483). The work per chunk grows with the document, so total work grows with the square of its length, all on the main thread. The kit keeps block-level artifact.patch as the primary channel (small, already valid JSON) and confines repair to text.delta events with format: "json", where ArtifactStore.applyTextDelta runs jsonrepair over one block's buffer only. When the artifact is large, the same store runs in a worker: packages/core/src/workers/patch.worker.ts (new) packages/core/src/workers/create.ts (new) The worker is used when the proposed patchWorker flag (Step 13.3) is "auto" (the default) and the artifact exceeds 200 blocks or 256 kB serialized; below that the structured-clone cost of posting snapshots exceeds the savings. In production the worker posts only changed sections, not the whole artifact; the excerpt posts snapshots for clarity. A "conflict" result is posted back so the controller can resync with getArtifact, exactly as it does on the main thread (React SDK and UI kit). Gotcha: workers and CSP Superset's production policy allows workers from 'self' and blob: (apache/superset: superset/config.py:3130), so a same-origin chunk served from the extension's publicPath loads. A host whose policy has no worker-src falls back to script-src (and then default-src) for workers; if neither allows the chunk's origin, the constructor throws or the worker fails to load, and the kit must keep working on the main thread. That is why createPatchWorker() returns null instead of throwing, and why the worker also listens for its own error event and the store falls back on the first failure.

The model output is untrusted, the host page is trusted, and the kit sits between them. The rules mirror the server-side design in Security, RLS, auth: never trust model text, never give the browser a secret it does not need, and fail closed. # Threat Vector Mitigation in the kit Test F1 XSS via model output model emits , javascript: links, or HTML inside a paragraph the IR has no HTML block; RichText is text plus marks; href allowlist (https:, http:, mailto:, host-relative); any HTML the kit renders goes through SafeHtml (DOMPurify) fuzzing with hostile strings (10.7), Storybook play tests, axe F2 Prompt injection rendering into the host injected instructions in data labels or documents come back as content content is content: adapters serialize only IR fields into host-native nodes; no adapter creates host commands, links to host admin routes, or embeds; the preview shows exactly what apply will write golden-file tests with an injection corpus F3 Script execution from generated slides an LLM-generated

docs.t: 9.2 Sanitization: what Presenton does and what the kit keeps
docs.x: Presenton already depends on DOMPurify ("dompurify": "^3.4.17", servers/nextjs/package.json:49) and uses it for Smart-mode HTML slides with an explicit profile: servers/nextjs/app/(presentation-generator)/components/SmartHtmlSlide.tsx:25-40 It is applied at SmartHtmlSlide.tsx:118 and the result is rendered with dangerouslySetInnerHTML at :197. The Cypress spec servers/nextjs/cypress/security/dependencies.cy.ts:3-22 checks that DOMPurify with the same USE_PROFILES setting (not the full SANITIZE_CONFIG) keeps headings, SVG and img src while removing <script>, onload, onerror and the href of a javascript: link. Reading the rest of the Next.js source shows three things the kit must not copy: Model-written scripts run in the page. SmartHtmlSlide passes the original, unsanitized html to useSmartChartInjection (SmartHtmlSlide.tsx:122-123), which parses it, takes the text of every <script>, wraps it in a scoped function and appends it to document.body as an inline script (servers/nextjs/app/(presentation-generator)/components/useSmartChartInjection.ts:41-100). Sanitizing the markup does not help when the script text is executed separately. This is the Smart-mode design (LLM-generated chart code), and it is incompatible with both the kit's threat model and any CSP without 'unsafe-inline'. The kit does not support Smart-mode HTML as a target. Markdown is rendered without sanitization. The outline cards render marked.parse(...) output with dangerouslySetInnerHTML (servers/nextjs/app/(presentation-generator)/outline/components/OutlineItem.tsx:129, :146, :155-158, :196, :201, :232), as do servers/nextjs/app/(presentation-generator)/documents-preview/components/MarkdownRenderer.tsx:17, :31 and servers/nextjs/app/(presentation-generator)/components/MarkdownInlineText.tsx:27, :51. marked does not sanitize. Outline text is LLM output, so the outline review UI that the kit reuses (Extracting the engine from Presenton) must route Markdown through SafeHtml. Template v2 HTML relies on escaping alone. templateV2UiToHtmlFragment() escapes every text and attribute with escapeHtml/escapeAttribute (servers/nextjs/lib/template-v2-json-to-html.ts:4105-4116) and stores chart configs as escaped JSON in data-chart-config (:1080-1086), which the preview hydrates with JSON.parse (TemplateV2HtmlSlidePreview.tsx:295-319). That design is sound and is what the slides target reuses, but the

Superset's production Content Security Policy is the strictest host on the list: Directive Superset value Consequence for the kit script-src 'self' 'strict-dynamic' plus a per-request nonce (apache/superset: superset/config.py:3156-3158) no inline scripts, no eval; dynamically loaded chunks are allowed because a trusted script loads them connect-src 'self' plus map tile hosts (:3131-3145) the engine must be reachable same-origin (a proxy route under Superset) or the operator must add its origin worker-src 'self' blob: (:3130) same-origin worker chunks load (Step 8.4) style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' plus theme font domains (:3147-3151) a runtime <style> works in Superset, but not on stricter hosts object-src 'none' no plugins, ever The kit's rules follow: no eval or new Function in the kit or its runtime dependencies (this excludes runtime JSON Schema compilers such as Ajv in the browser; validation in the browser uses Ajv's standalone, precompiled validators or none at all, and full validation happens in tests and in the engine); no inline event handlers; every chunk, worker and font is served from the bundle's own origin; and the proposed injectGckStyles({ nonce }) (Step 1.6) accepts a nonce for hosts that require one. Gotcha: Superset's development policy hides eval TALISMAN_DEV_CONFIG allows 'unsafe-inline' and 'unsafe-eval' in script-src (apache/superset: superset/config.py:3203), with the comment that React needs eval in dev mode. Code (or a dependency) that uses eval works in a Superset dev instance and fails in production. Run the Superset e2e project (Step 10.5) against the production Talisman config, and fail the test on any securitypolicyviolation event.

The browser never holds a provider API key. Every engine request carries a short-lived engine token as Authorization: Bearer with credentials: "omit", so no cookie reaches the engine (Run protocol and client). The host's own backend mints the token under its own session: in Superset the extension endpoint POST /extensions/gck/host-superset/v1/engine-token is called with the session cookie and X-CSRFToken from authentication.getCSRFToken() (Host integrations, Security, RLS, auth). The kit's contract is the TokenProvider type from @gck/client, (opts: { forceRefresh: boolean }) => Promise<string | null>, passed as GckProvider getToken. Caching is the host's job; a small wrapper does it: examples/react-vite-tiptap/src/engine-token.ts (new, host code) GckClient calls getToken({ forceRefresh: false }) before every request, including each SSE reconnect with Last-Event-ID, and on 401 token_expired calls it once with forceRefresh: true and retries once; a null token sends no Authorization header. Tokens are never written to localStorage, sessionStorage, URLs or telemetry. For the iframe fallback: packages/element/src/frame-bridge.ts (new)

Presenton's telemetry is a useful counterexample. Its Mixpanel setup defaults to enabled when the status endpoint fails (servers/nextjs/utils/mixpanel.ts:224-226) and initializes session recording for every session with text masking turned off: servers/nextjs/utils/mixpanel.ts:246-255 It does have good habits worth keeping: error messages are collapsed to one line and capped at 240 characters, and sizes are bucketed instead of exact (servers/nextjs/utils/analytics.ts:1-35). The kit's policy: the kit itself sends nothing anywhere; it calls the host's telemetry callback with typed events (Step 13) that contain ids, timings, counts and enum values only; no prompt text, no artifact text, no data values, no user names; and an absent callback means no telemetry, so failure is closed by construction. Session replay of the kit's UI is the host's decision, and the kit marks its preview root with data-gck-sensitive so hosts can block it in their replay tool.

Presenton's frontend tests today are node --test files, ESLint, a production build and Cypress component specs (nine *.cy.ts(x) files, three of them under servers/nextjs/cypress/security/) (.github/workflows/test-all.yml:98-111, servers/nextjs/cypress.config.ts:3-11); there is no browser end-to-end test against a running app (CI, tests, security). The kit needs more because it runs in hosts it does not control. Layer Tool Scope Runs Unit Vitest protocol helpers, client, run machine, JSON Patch, adapters, i18n every PR Contract Vitest + Ajv fixtures and recorded logs against engine-exported JSON Schemas every PR, and in the engine repo Component Storybook + MSW every component in every state, themes, locales every PR (build + play tests) Visual Playwright screenshots of Storybook pixel diffs per story every PR Accessibility axe (Storybook and Playwright) WCAG 2.2 AA rules every PR Fuzz fast-check adapters and patch apply with hostile and truncated input every PR (short), nightly (long) End-to-end Playwright real hosts: Tiptap demo, Presenton, Superset every PR (Tiptap), nightly and pre-release (all)

packages/core/test/machine.test.ts (new) The machine is a pure reducer (React SDK and UI kit), so the test needs no client, no timers and no mocks; events use the real envelope and the id patterns of the Artifact Spec.

docs.t: 10.2 Contract tests shared with the engine
docs.x: The engine's Pydantic models are the source of truth, as in Presenton, which already derives LLM response schemas with model_json_schema() (for example servers/fastapi/utils/llm_calls/generate_presentation_outlines.py:363). An export script writes the schemas into @gck/protocol, under the file names and $id the Artifact Spec fixes (artifact-1.schema.json, Artifact Spec and targets): engine/scripts/export_schemas.py (new) gck_engine.protocol holds RunRequest and OutlineDecision today (Extracting the engine from Presenton); GckEvent is a Pydantic discriminated union mirroring the TypeScript GckEvent of Run protocol and client, proposed here so that events get the full schema validation that isGckEvent (a structural guard only) does not give. The TypeScript types in @gck/protocol stay hand-written (src/artifact.ts, src/target.ts, src/run.ts); a type test generates declarations from the schema files with json-schema-to-typescript into src/generated/ (never exported) and asserts that both sides are mutually assignable, and CI fails when regenerating produces a diff, so a field renamed in Python breaks the frontend build in the same pull request. Pydantic v2 emits JSON Schema draft 2020-12, so the tests use Ajv's 2020 build. The contract test lives in @gck/core, because it replays patches through the real store and @gck/protocol must not depend on @gck/core: packages/core/test/contract.test.ts (new) The engine repository runs the mirror image: it loads the same fixtures/event-logs/ (published as a tarball artifact of @gck/protocol) and validates them with Pydantic, so neither side can drift alone.

docs.t: 10.3 A mock engine with MSW replaying recorded event logs
docs.x: Recorded runs are the kit's most valuable test data: real event timing, real patch sizes, real failure shapes. The engine already keeps a run event log for Last-Event-ID resume; an export command writes a run as JSONL, one GckEvent envelope per line (v, id, runId, ts, type, data, optional progress) plus t in ms since start, after scrubbing prompt and data values. MSW then replays the log through the real @gck/client, because the client uses fetch and MSW can return a ReadableStream body (https://mswjs.io/docs/http/mocking-responses/streaming). The handlers live in the private @gck/testing package, so msw never becomes a dependency of a published package: tooling/testing/src/replay.ts (new) The same handlers serve Vitest (through msw/node), Storybook (through the browser worker) and local development of host integrations without an engine or an LLM key. Variants inject faults: cut the stream after event N (tests reconnect), duplicate an event id (tests idempotence), return 401 token_expired once (tests the token provider's forceRefresh path), and emit run.failed {retryable: true} (tests Retry). Refresh streams get the same treatment: a replayRefresh handler answers POST */v1/data/resolve from recorded refresh logs (refresh.started, binding.loading, binding.resolved, refresh.completed), with one fixture per binding status (ok, stale with reason: "timeout", error with mapping_changed, forbidden), a snapshot whose meta.resolved_by belongs to another viewer (tests the redact skeleton), refresh.failed with rate_limited and data_token_expired (tests backoff and re-authentication), and a changed: true update (tests the narrative-outdated prompt). The data views (GckChartView, GckMetricView, GckTableView, GckEmbedView) get one story per status from those fixtures, and the contract tests of Live Superset data (Step 16) run in the same suite.

Every styled component has one story per run state (idle, composing, submitting, planning, awaiting_review, generating, resolving_data, ready, applying, applied, cancelled, failed retryable and not), plus cross-cutting variants: dark, compact, RTL (ar), long artifact (300 sections), forbidden binding, and slow network. Streaming stories use the replay handlers: packages/react/src/ui/StreamingPreview.stories.tsx (excerpt, new) The MSW integration uses msw-storybook-addon; its README documents mswLoader() with handlers passed in parameters.msw for CSF 3 (https://github.com/mswjs/msw-storybook-addon). The addon's API has changed across versions, so pin it and follow the README for the version you install.

e2e/playwright.config.ts (excerpt, new) Tiptap demo (examples/react-vite-tiptap, built twice with React 18.3 and 19): slash command, streaming insertion, one-step undo, apply at cursor and replace selection. Presenton: the AI Slides flow from Part VIII with the slides target, against Presenton's Docker image. Superset dev instance: Superset from its own docker-compose-light.yml with FEATURE_FLAGS = {"ENABLE_EXTENSIONS": True}, the production Talisman config, the .supx built from apps/superset-extension, and a fixture dashboard. Tests open the dashboard menu, generate a text artifact into a Markdown component and a superset-dashboard artifact into a new tab, and revert. Each test listens for securitypolicyviolation and fails on any. The engine in e2e is a real GCK Engine with a scripted LLM provider that replays recorded model outputs, the same idea as Presenton's regression test that feeds fixed chunks through a patched stream (CI, tests, security). No e2e test calls a real model.

A Playwright job loads every Storybook story (from storybook-static/index.json), waits for the replay to reach its last event (stories expose data-gck-settled="true"), and calls expect(page).toHaveScreenshot() in light, dark and RTL. Streaming stories are captured at fixed event ids, never at wall-clock times, so diffs are deterministic. Baselines are generated in the same Linux container CI uses, because font rendering differs across operating systems.

Adapters must survive anything a model can produce, including output that passed schema validation but is semantically odd. Property tests generate artifacts from the schema and mutate them: packages/target-tiptap/test/fuzz.test.ts (new) hostileText mixes

The Storybook test runner runs axe on every story, and Playwright runs axe on each host page after apply: e2e/tests/tiptap/a11y.spec.ts (new) axe cannot judge live-region verbosity or focus after apply; those get explicit e2e assertions on :focus and a manual VoiceOver and NVDA pass before each minor release.

.github/workflows/ci.yml (excerpt, new) Like Presenton's workflows, the default token is read-only (permissions: contents: read, for example .github/workflows/test-all.yml:10-11), and, as Presenton's CodeQL workflow does (.github/workflows/codeql.yml:34), the checkout does not persist credentials (CI, tests, security). Only the release workflow gets id-token: write (for npm provenance) and the npm publish token.

Every pull request that changes a published package adds a changeset (pnpm changeset) naming the packages and the bump. On main, the changesets action opens or updates a "Version packages" pull request; merging it publishes. gck/.changeset/config.json (new) fixed keeps the runtime packages a host installs together on one version number, so "which @gck/core goes with @gck/react 1.4?" has one answer. Targets, hosts and @gck/protocol version independently.

Package Major (breaking) Minor Patch @gck/protocol removing or renaming a field, event type or enum value; changing a field's meaning; gck.artifact/1 to /2 new optional fields, new event types, new block types, new enum values that old clients may ignore doc and schema description fixes @gck/client, @gck/core public API removal, state machine semantics change new options, hooks, events bug fixes @gck/react, @gck/element prop removal, DOM structure changes that styled hosts rely on (class names, data-gck-* attributes), token renames new props, components, tokens, messages visual fixes within the token contract targets toNative output change that alters existing host content on re-apply new block support, new apply modes fixes that make output match the documented mapping @gck/host-superset dropping a Superset version from the matrix supporting a new Superset version or contribution point fixes Two rules make protocol minors safe. Clients must ignore unknown event types and unknown fields (the test in Step 10.1). And the engine must accept every client within the current major, which the client advertises with the GCK-Protocol request header (PROTOCOL_VERSION, 1); a breaking change bumps v, and the engine rejects a client whose header is too old with invalid_request and details.minProtocol (Run protocol and client).

Deprecate in a minor: @deprecated JSDoc with the replacement, a changeset entry, and a one-time console.warn in development builds only. Keep it for at least one further minor and at least six months. Remove it in the next major, listed in a migration guide on the docs site. Protocol majors: the engine serves the current and the previous protocol major for at least twelve months after a new major ships, because embedded hosts (a Superset extension pinned in a customer deployment) upgrade slowly.

Every merge to main also publishes a snapshot under a dist-tag, so hosts can test unreleased changes without affecting latest. Changesets documents the two commands: changeset version --snapshot <name> produces versions such as 0.0.0-<name>-<timestamp>, and changeset publish --tag <name> publishes without moving latest (https://github.com/changesets/changesets/blob/main/docs/snapshot-releases.md): .github/workflows/release.yml (canary step, new) Longer pre-releases (a 2.0.0-next.N series) use changesets pre mode (changeset pre enter next). The Superset extension is released as a .supx attached to a GitHub release with a pinned set of @gck/* versions recorded in its manifest.

Docs site (apps/docs): host guides plus generated references (compatibility matrix, tokens from gck.css, message keys from defaultMessages, TypeDoc API, protocol from the JSON Schemas). Storybook, published per release, whose replay stories are live demos that need no engine. Examples (examples/*), private packages built in CI on every PR, so a change that breaks a real consumer setup (Next.js App Router, Vite, a plain page with the element) fails before release.

The kit's telemetry contract is the TelemetryEvent of @gck/core, { name, targetId, runId?, status?, code? }, passed through GckProvider telemetry to every controller. In 1.0 the controller emits one event name, gck.status, on every status transition, with the new RunStatus and, on failure, the protocol error code (React SDK and UI kit). There is deliberately no text and no timing in the event; the host's sink adds both clocks and context: examples/presenton-ai-slides/src/telemetry.ts (new, host code) From those transitions a host dashboard derives time to first content (ms at the first generating, p50 and p95), completion (ready), cancel (cancelled) and failure rates by code, outline review rate (awaiting_review), and apply success (applied) versus apply failure (applying followed by ready with a code). Revert rate within five minutes (a strong bad-output signal), resume count (a network or proxy signal) and long render frames are not visible in status transitions; they are proposed as further event names on the same TelemetryEvent shape (gck.apply_reverted, gck.resumed, gck.long_frame) for a 1.x minor. Gotcha: runId is the join key, not the user Telemetry events carry runId so the host can join them with the engine's server-side run log, which already knows the user under the host's own access rules. The kit never adds a user id, email or tenant id. If a host needs per-user analysis, it joins on its side, under its own privacy policy.

The kit has one error vocabulary, the protocol's GckErrorCode (Run protocol and client): transport failures throw GckError from @gck/client (code, retryable, status, retryAfterMs, details), and run and apply failures land in run.state.error as a GckErrorBody (an apply that returns ok: false becomes code: "conflict", a thrown apply error goes through the same conversion). Every styled component is wrapped in an error boundary that renders a compact failure state with Retry (StreamingPreview's preview boundary is the example in React SDK and UI kit). A host reports errors from the state it already has: examples/presenton-ai-slides/src/report-errors.ts (new, host code) run.failed.message from the engine is rendered as text (never HTML) and is not forwarded to the host's error tracker unless the host opts in, because an engine message can echo model output. Render exceptions caught by a boundary are kit bugs rather than protocol errors; an onError prop for them is a proposal, not part of GckConfig 1.0. Hosts forward reports to whatever they already use (Sentry, Superset's own logging, a console in development).

examples/presenton-ai-slides/src/GckRoot.tsx (excerpt, new) Flags are plain values owned by the host and driven by its own flag system. Defaults are conservative. Anything that changes what the engine sends travels in RunRequest.options, whose 1.0 fields are reviewOutline, maxSections and tone; a new switch there, such as asking the engine for text.delta token streaming, is a new optional field and therefore a protocol minor (Step 12.2). Every flag gets a removal date in Roadmap and tracker.

Reads: the earlier Part IX chapters · Builds on: Architecture, Part VIII (AI Slides delivery plan) · Time: ~15 min This chapter turns Part IX into a plan you can track. It covers five phases, each ending in something a user can try, with 44 work packages, effort estimates, dependencies and exit criteria. Each phase adds one new host or target, so the kit proves its "plug into any host" promise step by step instead of all at the end. Each phase also makes its target show live Superset data, fetched as the viewing user and refreshed after generation, so no phase ships a target that freezes numbers (Live Superset data). Download tracker (.csv)

Assumption Value Start After the AI Slides pilot is stable, or in parallel with a separate small team (see Step 5) Team 2 frontend engineers, 1 backend engineer full time (the live-data work doubles the backend share), QA support in phases 2 and 3 Effort unit Ideal person-days (d), including tests and review Capacity 4 focus-days per person per week Windows Indicative week ranges relative to the start date; convert them to Friday release trains when a start date is fixed, the same way as the AI Slides release plan in Part VIII Totals: about 130 d of frontend work, 69 d of backend work and 11 d of QA, 210 d in all. The 17 live-data work packages (1.8 to 1.13, 2.5 to 2.7, 3.6 to 3.8, 4.6 to 4.10) account for 65 d of it, 36 d of them backend. Two frontend engineers at 4 d per week deliver the frontend share in about 16 weeks of pure work, and one backend engineer at 4 d per week delivers the backend share in about 17 weeks, so 24 weeks leaves room for review, integration and surprises. P1 is the backend-heavy phase (30 d of backend work), which is why it is the longest; 1.8 depends only on the schema contract test (0.3), so the backend engineer can start it during P0.

Why this order: P0 first, because the protocol and core are the contract every host and target depends on. Changing them later is the most expensive change in the project. Text before Tiptap before dashboards. Text is the simplest target (no custom editor nodes, no layout), so it validates the engine and the kit with the least risk. Tiptap adds editor integration and undo. Dashboards add layout and real Superset objects. Slides last, because AI Slides already works through Part VIII. Moving it onto the kit is a refactor, not new value, and it is safest once the kit is proven on three other targets. docs.t: Step 3: Check each phase's exit criteria
docs.x: Phase Exit criteria (a demo a user can run) P0 A Storybook story streams a recorded run from the mock engine through @gck/core into a preview, and can be cancelled and resumed P1 In Superset, a user writes "summarize this dashboard for leadership" and every data token in the generated text comes from a binding resolved as the viewer, with the dashboard's native filters captured at submit; text the kit renders refreshes on open and on "Refresh data" with the same scope, and static outputs (a Markdown component, exported Markdown or email) carry "Data as of" (Live Superset data) P2 In a Tiptap page, /ai generates a page with a live chart node; selecting text and choosing "turn into chart" replaces the selection (transform); "Edit page" changes only the affected blocks (edit with patch); one undo reverts each of them. Reopening the page refreshes every data node as the viewer, "Refresh data" forces it, a viewer without access sees no numbers, copy-paste keeps nodes refreshable, and changing a parameter re-resolves only the nodes that depend on it P3 From a dashboard, "create an EMEA tab with revenue and churn" produces a new tab that uses existing charts, respects permissions and can be reverted; its charts are filtered to the prompt's scope and react to native filter changes, and numbers in its narrative are live charts (Handlebars or Big Number) or stamped P4 Presenton's own outline and streaming screens run on the kit with no user-visible regression; a GCK deck has slide_data_bindings rows, refreshes on open (Story 4 AC1 to AC6), bakes fresh data into export (Story 1 AC6) and its PPTX charts carry native data; the <gck-generate> web component works in a plain HTML page; version 1.0 is published

docs.t: Step 5: Decide how to run it alongside AI Slides
docs.x: Two workable options: Sequential (recommended for a small team). Finish the AI Slides pilot, then start P0 with the same people. The Part VIII code (bindings, refresh API, harness planner) becomes the engine's data layer, and nothing is built twice. Parallel. A separate pair of frontend engineers starts P0 and P1 while AI Slides continues. This works only if @gck/protocol and Part VIII share one binding shape and one person owns the protocol across both teams. The shapes are aligned field by field (a GCK DataBinding maps onto a slide_data_bindings row, see Extracting the engine from Presenton), both stores use the snapshot JSON produced by the shared gck_data mappers (1.8), and a contract test pipes one recorded Story 8 response through gck_data.map_result into Part VIII's write_value and GCK's resolveToken and asserts identical displays.

The tables above and the CSV download are generated by tutorial/scripts/gen_gck_roadmap.py from one work-package list. To re-plan, edit the list and regenerate: Paste the regenerated tables into this page. The script holds the short work-package names; the descriptions on this page add the package and API names from chapters 62 to 69 (for example RUNS_ROUTER or toPositions), so carry those over when you paste. IDs, areas, effort and dependencies must match the script exactly. The CSV has empty Owner, Start week and End week columns, ready to fill in the team sheet. Feature flags introduced by the kit (see Frontend engineering and quality) each get a removal date: record it in the tracker against the work package that introduces the flag.

Reads: apache/superset: superset/charts/data/api.py, apache/superset: superset/charts/data/dashboard_filter_context.py, apache/superset: superset/charts/schemas.py, apache/superset: superset/commands/chart/data/get_data_command.py, apache/superset: superset/common/query_context_processor.py, apache/superset: superset/security/manager.py, apache/superset: superset/config.py, servers/fastapi/templates/v2/models/elements.py · Builds on: Artifact Spec and targets, React SDK and UI kit, Story 8, analytics refresh APIs and MCP, Story 1, dynamic data and refresh · Time: ~60 min This chapter makes every number the Generative Content Kit (GCK) puts on a slide, a Tiptap page, a Superset dashboard or a text block a live value: fetched from Superset as the person viewing it, refreshed after generation on open, on demand, on an interval and when a filter or parameter changes, and never a frozen number or a screenshot presented as current. You will build the whole path: the binding sources that cover saved charts, datasets, saved metrics and (behind a flag) SQL; the four-layer scope merge for dashboard filters and viewer parameters; the Superset-side extension of Part VIII's Story 8 refresh API; the engine's /v1/data/resolve endpoint; the browser's DataProvider and @gck/data-superset; and the per-target behavior, security model, caches and tests that keep it honest. The chapter ends with the short list of outputs that must stay snapshots, and why. Code under gck/, gck_engine/, gck_data/ and ai_slides_superset/ is new (marked "(new)" in block titles). Superset paths prefixed apache/superset: cite the master clone at cabd8d4 (2 November 2026); where the 6.1.0 release differs, the text says so, relying on the 6.1.0 checks already made in Story 8. Presenton paths are the snapshot 571461f. Everything here ships as protocol 1.1: additive to gck.artifact/1, a minor bump of @gck/protocol, engine first.

docs.t: Step 1: The requirement, and where data used to freeze
docs.x: The requirement is short: every GCK target shows live Superset data, fetched as the viewing user, refreshed after generation, with honest fallbacks where a host cannot be live. Before protocol 1.1, the kit met it only during a run. An audit of chapters 61 to 68 found these places where numbers froze: Where data froze Why Fixed in Slides apply baked snapshot values and created no slide_data_bindings rows Part VIII's refresh-on-open only knows rows Step 12.1 Tiptap stored the author's value in gckToken.text getHTML() serialized the number Step 12.2 Dashboard Markdown carried numbers the Markdown component cannot query Step 12.3 No refresh API outside a run Story 8 needs a server-held data token Steps 7 to 9 stamp() wrote mapping: {} Part VIII mappers raise MappingError on it Step 2.3 Host filter context was lost after generation no field to keep it Step 4 Only saved charts could be sources no dataset or metric source Step 3 The fix rests on one rule: an applied artifact stores binding definitions, never values presented as current. Values live in a runtime overlay that is refilled as the viewer.

A DataBinding in protocol 1.1 is a definition plus runtime state: Part Fields Who writes it Persisted by hosts? Definition kind, source, mapping, format, params, refresh, generatedAgainst the engine at stamp time, editors later yes Runtime state snapshot, snapshotAt, status, error every resolve, as the current viewer no (optional offline seed, redacted for others, Step 14) BindingDefinition = Omit<DataBinding, "snapshot" | "snapshotAt" | "status" | "error"> is the type hosts save. stripRuntime(artifact) produces it; withBindingState(artifact, state) merges the overlay back before an adapter's toNative or apply reads it. Adapters never fetch.

docs.t: 2.2 The artifact gains three optional fields
docs.x: gck/packages/protocol/src/data.ts (new, protocol 1.1, excerpt)

docs.t: 2.3 Mapping is derived, never written by the model
docs.x: The engine derives mapping and format once per catalog entry, from a sample resolve (25 rows, force: false) through the same Story 8 call that later refreshes it. It reads the post-processed colnames and coltypes and uses the chart's form data only to pick roles (which column is the x axis, which are metrics). The rules per visualization are in Artifact Spec and targets; the two that matter for liveness are: a timeseries chart with a groupby gets series: ["*"], meaning "every numeric column except x", because the set of series (one per region, say) is itself data and can change between refreshes; a pop_kpi metric maps previous_column to "<metric>__<offset>", because Superset names time-offset columns by joining the metric and the offset with TIME_COMPARISON = "__" (apache/superset: superset/utils/core.py:148, used at apache/superset: superset/models/helpers.py:3348).

docs.t: 2.4 One snapshot shape for Part VIII and GCK
docs.x: Snapshots keep Part VIII's snake_case so one JSON blob serves the slide_data_bindings.snapshot column and the GCK overlay. Each carries meta: gck/packages/protocol/src/data.ts (new, excerpt) Every meta field has a Superset origin. applied_filters and rejected_filters are what _filter_status returns per query (apache/superset: superset/common/query_actions.py:81-103); from_dttm and to_dttm, the resolved time range, are in the same payload as queried_dttm and is_cached (apache/superset: superset/common/query_context_processor.py:423-444). coltypes are Superset's GenericDataType values 0 to 3 (numeric, string, temporal, boolean; apache/superset: superset/utils/core.py:251-259). Gotcha: ChartSeries.values cannot hold nulls Presenton's chart model declares values: list[float] (servers/fastapi/templates/v2/models/elements.py:176-178), so a missing month becomes 0 and is counted in meta.nulls_coerced. Views show "n gaps filled with 0" (data.gapsFilled) whenever the count is non-zero. Do not hide that hint: a zero is a claim about the data.

docs.x: DataBinding.source is a discriminated union on type. All four types resolve inside Superset under the viewer's identity, so RBAC and row-level security (RLS) apply unchanged. source.type Version What it reads Typical use superset_chart v1 a saved chart's query the chart the user is looking at, or one from the catalog superset_dataset 1.1 a query the engine builds from a dataset's columns and metrics "revenue by month for EMEA" when no chart exists superset_metric 1.1 (table), 1.2 (semantic view) one saved metric, optionally with a period comparison KPIs in prose and metric slots superset_sql 1.2, off by default a saved query or the user's SQL Lab text narratives over an ad hoc result
