docs.t: Step 2: Packaging: a Flask blueprint, not an extension @api
docs.p: Story 8: Analytics refresh APIs and MCP
docs.b: Part VIII: AI Slides delivery plan
docs.x: Two mechanisms can add REST endpoints to Superset. BLUEPRINTS config. Superset registers each Blueprint listed in config during init_app, before CSRF and the middlewares are configured: apache/superset: superset/initialization/__init__.py:1813-1820 The key is declared as BLUEPRINTS: list[Blueprint] = [] (apache/superset: superset/config.py:2431) and the call sits at apache/superset: superset/initialization/__init__.py:1434, followed by configure_wtf() at line 1435. Routes keep whatever URL prefix the blueprint declares, so url_prefix="/api/v1/ai_slides" yields exactly the contract paths. It works on 6.1.0 and master and needs no feature flag. Extension @api. superset_core.rest_api.decorators.api registers a RestApi class, but inside an extension context the base path becomes /extensions/{publisher}/{name}: apache/superset: superset/core/api/core_api_injection.py:189-207 That moves the endpoints to /extensions/analytics/ai-slides/..., contradicting the contract paths, and it requires ENABLE_EXTENSIONS (default False, development lifecycle) in every process. RestApi also subclasses FAB's BaseApi, which is CSRF-exempt by default, so a session-authenticated handoff would need csrf_exempt = False set explicitly (see Building the Superset extension). Recommended default: the blueprint. Use the extension mechanism for exactly one thing, the custom MCP tool in Step 8, where it is the only supported registration path. ai_slides_superset package layout (new) ai_slides_superset/__init__.py (new) superset_config.py (additions for Story 8, new) Gotcha: lazy imports everywhere in the blueprint superset_config.py runs while superset.config is still loading, and register_blueprints() runs before Flask-AppBuilder is configured (configure_fab() happens later, inside init_app_in_ctx, apache/superset: superset/initialization/__init__.py:1114). Module-level code in api.py and its imports may use Flask, PyJWT, cryptography and the standard library only. Import superset.* inside the view functions, which run at request time when appbuilder.sm, db and the event logger exist.

docs.t: Step 3: Signing keys and the JWKS endpoint
docs.p: Story 8: Analytics refresh APIs and MCP
docs.b: Part VIII: AI Slides delivery plan
docs.x: Superset already depends on PyJWT>=2.15.1 and cryptography>=50.0.2 (apache/superset: pyproject.toml:53, 104), so no new dependency is needed. Keys are RSA private keys in PEM form, generated once per rotation with openssl genpkey -algorithm RSA -pkeyopt rsa_keygen_bits:3072 and stored in the secret manager. They are never derived from SECRET_KEY: that secret signs Superset's session cookie and, through Flask-JWT-Extended, its own API tokens. The kid is the RFC 7638 thumbprint of the public key, so it is stable, unique and needs no bookkeeping. ai_slides_superset/keys.py (new) Rotation is a three-deploy procedure that never invalidates a live token: Phase AI_SLIDES_SIGNING_KEY_CURRENT ..._PREVIOUS Effect 0. Steady state K1 (empty) JWKS = {K1}; tokens signed with K1 1. Pre-publish K1 K2 JWKS = {K1, K2}; still signing with K1. Wait for verifier JWKS caches to expire (Presenton BE and FastMCP cache JWKS; budget 10 minutes) 2. Promote K2 K1 signing with K2; K1 still verifies tokens issued up to 15 minutes ago 3. Retire K2 (empty) after at least AI_SLIDES_DATA_TOKEN_TTL_SECONDS plus cache TTL

docs.x: The current user comes from Flask-AppBuilder, which sets g.user = current_user before each request, and the role names from security_manager.get_user_roles() (apache/superset: superset/security/manager.py:6066). Superset has no organization concept, so org_id comes from a deployment hook (recommended default: a constant, AI_SLIDES_DEFAULT_ORG_ID; a multi-tenant platform supplies AI_SLIDES_ORG_RESOLVER(user) -> str). ai_slides_superset/api.py (new, part 1 of 3) CSRF protection is automatic: configure_wtf() calls csrf.init_app(app) and exempts only the entries of WTF_CSRF_EXEMPT_LIST (apache/superset: superset/initialization/__init__.py:1792-1797), so a blueprint POST that is not listed requires the X-CSRFToken header that the host bridge sends. A JSON request with a bad token gets a 400 JSON error from Superset's CSRFError handler (apache/superset: superset/views/error_handling.py:229-247), which the bridge handles by fetching a fresh token and retrying once. Gotcha: a Bearer FAB token can also authenticate /handoff Superset's request_loader accepts Authorization: Bearer Flask-JWT-Extended tokens from /api/v1/security/login and sets g.user (apache/superset: superset/security/manager.py:2446-2470). Without further checks, a script holding such a token could mint AI Slides tokens. The CSRF requirement already blocks it (API clients do not carry the session-bound CSRF token), and the Sec-Fetch-Site check adds a browser-only signal. Do not add /handoff to WTF_CSRF_EXEMPT_LIST.

docs.p: Story 8: Analytics refresh APIs and MCP
docs.b: Part VIII: AI Slides delivery plan
docs.x: Three patterns exist in Superset, and the decorator reuses the third: Browser and FAB JWT requests. request_loader resolves the user per request (guest token first when EMBEDDED_SUPERSET is on, then a Flask-JWT-Extended Bearer token) and sets g.user (apache/superset: superset/security/manager.py:2446-2470). MCP tools. _setup_user_context() resolves the MCP principal and assigns g.user = user before the tool body runs (apache/superset: superset/mcp_service/auth.py:1108-1132). Background work. override_user(user, force=True) swaps g.user for the duration of a with block and restores it afterwards (apache/superset: superset/utils/core.py:1633-1660). The GTF chart-query task and the dashboard Excel export use it to run queries as the requester. Everything downstream reads g.user: can_access (apache/superset: superset/security/manager.py:2530-2545), raise_for_access, the DAO base filters, and get_rls_filters, which returns nothing when g.user is unset and caches per user and table in g._rls_filter_cache (apache/superset: superset/security/manager.py:6110-6131). Gotcha: Superset's request loader sees our Bearer token first Because the refresh call carries Authorization: Bearer <data token>, Superset's request_loader tries verify_jwt_in_request() on it, fails (our token is RS256 with a different issuer, not a Flask-JWT-Extended token signed with SECRET_KEY), and returns None, so the request starts anonymous (apache/superset: superset/security/manager.py:2460-2470). That is the desired outcome. Never "simplify" by minting data tokens as Flask-JWT-Extended tokens: they would then authenticate against every Superset API with full user rights, instead of only the scoped AI Slides endpoints.

docs.t: 6.1 What Superset does for a saved chart today
docs.p: Story 8: Analytics refresh APIs and MCP
docs.b: Part VIII: AI Slides delivery plan
docs.x: GET /api/v1/chart/<pk>/data/ is the closest built-in: it loads chart.query_context, overrides three keys, applies dashboard filter context (master), exposes the body to Jinja, builds the query context and runs ChartDataCommand: apache/superset: superset/charts/data/api.py:168-189 (excerpt) apache/superset: superset/charts/data/api.py:221-230 (excerpt) _create_query_context_from_form loads the body through ChartDataQueryContextSchema with a QueryContextFactory (apache/superset: superset/charts/data/api.py:760-780). ChartDataCommand.validate() is self._query_context.raise_for_access() and run() returns {"query_context", "queries"} after raising on any failed query (apache/superset: superset/commands/chart/data/get_data_command.py:36-108). Why not call that HTTP endpoint from Presenton? It takes one chart per call, it has no override input on 6.1.0, it requires a FAB token or session (not our scoped token), and on 6.1.0 with GLOBAL_ASYNC_QUERIES a Bearer client gets a 202 it cannot complete. Running the same command in-process inside our blueprint avoids all four.

docs.p: Story 8: Analytics refresh APIs and MCP
docs.b: Part VIII: AI Slides delivery plan
docs.x: query_context is produced in the browser by each plugin's buildQuery and saved from Explore, so old, imported or API-created charts can have NULL. Superset handles this three ways: The chart data GET returns 400 "Chart has no query context saved" (above). Explore backfills it the next time someone with write access opens the chart (apache/superset: superset-frontend/src/explore/components/ExploreChartPanel/index.tsx:235-254). On master, a server-side builder reconstructs one from params: build_query_context_from_form_data(form_data, datasource, viz_type=None) in apache/superset: superset/common/form_data_query_context.py:1801-1813, used by the dashboard Excel export and every MCP chart tool. MCP get_chart_data prefers the saved query_context ("Use the chart's saved query_context - this is the key!", apache/superset: superset/mcp_service/chart/tool/get_chart_data.py:768) and falls back to the form-data builder with a warning that numbers may diverge (apache/superset: superset/mcp_service/chart/tool/get_chart_data.py:905-929). The module does not exist in 6.1.0. Decision: prefer the stored query_context; on master fall back to build_query_context_from_form_data and report query_context_source: "rebuilt_from_form_data" so Presenton can show a subtle "re-save this chart in Superset for exact numbers" hint; on 6.1.0 return unsupported with code no_query_context. The catalog applies the same rule, so the planner never proposes such a chart on 6.1.0.

docs.x: Contract overrides (time_range, extra_filters) are converted to Superset's extra_form_data vocabulary, the same keys native filters publish (EXTRA_FORM_DATA_APPEND_KEYS and EXTRA_FORM_DATA_OVERRIDE_REGULAR_MAPPINGS, apache/superset: superset/constants.py:209-229). Two merge helpers exist: merge_extra_form_data(form_data) works on form data, before buildQuery (apache/superset: superset/utils/core.py:1184). Not applicable to a stored query context. apply_dashboard_filter_context(query_context, extra_form_data) works on an already built query context: it appends filters with isExtra: True to every query, copies extra overrides, maps time_range and time_grain_sqla, and marks existing time-range filters (apache/superset: superset/charts/data/dashboard_filter_context.py:365-408). It is exactly the merge we need, and it is what the chart data GET uses for filters_dashboard_id. Master only. On 6.1.0 the refresh service uses a small local equivalent (append filters, set time_range, rewrite TEMPORAL_RANGE filter values). Treat it as an approximation and cover each supported visualization type with a test. Gotcha: an override filter is a SQL surface A Superset filter's col may be an adhoc column with a sqlExpression. Accept only plain strings that name a column of the chart's dataset, and only operators from FilterOperator (apache/superset: superset/utils/core.py:329). Otherwise a Presenton binding edit could inject SQL that runs with the user's warehouse access.

docs.x: QueryObjectFactory replaces a row_limit of 0 with ROW_LIMIT (50000) and clamps to SQL_MAX_ROW (100000) (see Superset landscape). Slides need far less, so each query's row_limit is clamped to min(item.row_limit, AI_SLIDES_MAX_ROW_LIMIT) before loading the context. Caching is Superset's own: force: false lets QueryContext serve from the data cache (which is NullCache unless DATA_CACHE_CONFIG is set), force: true re-runs the query. The cache key already includes the user's RLS clauses through get_rls_cache_key (apache/superset: superset/security/manager.py:6304), so two users never share cached rows. Gotcha: the row cap applies before post-processing For timeseries charts with a groupby, rows are long-format (one row per time bucket and series) and the plugin's pivot post-processing turns them into wide columns afterwards. A cap of 50 on a 12-month by 10-series chart returns 50 of 120 rows and silently drops points. Keep the cap per binding (row_limit in the binding source), return truncated: true when rowcount reaches it, and let Story 1 surface it.

docs.x: Nothing in the refresh service mentions RLS, and that is the point. While building SQL for a dataset, SqlaTable.get_sqla_row_level_filters asks the security manager for the current user's filters and adds them to the WHERE clause: apache/superset: superset/connectors/sqla/models.py:1189-1199 The query builder appends those clauses to every query (apache/superset: superset/models/helpers.py:7543). Because the refresh body runs inside override_user(token_user), get_rls_filters resolves the token user's roles (master: subjects, which include roles and groups; 6.1.0: roles only, per Security, RLS, auth), so the deck shows exactly the rows that user would see on the dashboard. Jinja macros in RLS clauses, such as current_username(), render as that user too.

docs.p: Story 8: Analytics refresh APIs and MCP
docs.b: Part VIII: AI Slides delivery plan
docs.x: The harness talks to a dedicated, internal-only MCP deployment (http://superset-mcp:5008/mcp). Restrict it three ways, from strongest to weakest: Scopes in the token (master). When a JWT carries scopes, every tool call is checked against superset:<action> or superset:<resource>:<action> (apache/superset: superset/mcp_service/auth.py:195-235), with read and get mapping to read and write, update, delete, execute_sql_query mapping to write (apache/superset: superset/security/api_key_scopes.py:22-29). The data token carries only superset:chart:read superset:dashboard:read superset:dataset:read, so every mutating tool and execute_sql is denied even if it is registered. An allowlist policy (master). MCP_RESTRICTED_TOOL_POLICY(user) returns the set of callable tool function names, default-deny for anything else (apache/superset: superset/mcp_service/mcp_config.py:283-287, enforced in apache/superset: superset/mcp_service/auth.py:339-367). On a harness-only deployment, return the same allowlist for every principal. Removing tools (master). docs.t: Step 0: The story, its owners and its acceptance criteria
docs.b: Part VIII: AI Slides delivery plan
docs.x: # Story What it does Owners 9 [Infra] Deploy Presenton BE and FE alongside the analytics platform Deploys both Presenton services with routing, secrets, storage, harness connectivity, CI/CD and monitoring. Nitesh, Sourav Story 9 starts early with a dev environment (so Stories 1 to 8 can integrate against real routing and cookies) and finishes with the production rollout. Acceptance criteria: Given the analytics namespace, when the Helm chart ai-slides is installed, then presenton-fe and presenton-be Deployments run with at least 2 ready replicas each, as non-root, and presenton-migrate completed before any BE pod became ready. Given a browser on https://analytics.example.com, when it requests /ai-slides/, /ai-slides/api/v1/... and /ai-slides/app_data/images/..., then they reach the FE, the BE (with the prefix stripped) and the BE asset mounts respectively, and every other path still reaches Superset. Given a 25-minute SSE stream through the ingress, when no bytes flow for 60 seconds between events, then the stream is not cut and events arrive unbuffered. Given the secret store, when a secret is rotated, then the pods pick it up through a rolling restart with no manual edits, and no secret appears in a manifest, image layer or log. Given NetworkPolicies in place, when a BE pod tries to reach anything other than Postgres, Superset web, the harness, the FE, object storage, DNS or the approved LLM egress, then the connection is refused. Given a merge to the fork's release branch, when CI runs, then both images are built, tested, scanned (no critical CVEs), pushed by digest, deployed to dev automatically, to staging after approval, and to production through a 10 percent canary. Given production traffic, when the refresh success rate drops below the SLO or p95 open-to-fresh latency exceeds it, then an alert fires with a link to the runbook entry in Step 11.

docs.x: deploy/helm/ai-slides/templates/migrate-job.yaml (new, rendered) The module is the one Story 2 adds (servers/fastapi/scripts/ai_slides_migrate.py). It mounts /app_data because import_default_templates_on_startup copies template static assets into APP_DATA_DIRECTORY and refuses to run without it (servers/fastapi/templates/default_templates.py:295-299). Gotcha: hook ordering with External Secrets A pre-install hook runs before the chart's normal resources exist. If presenton-migrate-secrets is created by an ExternalSecret in the same chart, the first install's Job starts before the Secret exists and fails. Either make the ExternalSecret a hook with a lower weight (helm.sh/hook-weight: "-5") and wait for its Ready condition, or manage the ExternalSecret objects in the platform's secrets chart so they exist before ai-slides is installed. Migration ordering rule: every revision must be compatible with the previous BE image, because old pods serve traffic while new ones roll out and during the canary. Use expand and contract: add nullable columns and new tables in release N, start using them in N, backfill in a Job, and drop old columns no earlier than N+1. The Story 2 /readyz check compares the database revision with the image's REVISION_HEAD, so a new pod never takes traffic on an older schema, and old pods tolerate the newer schema because the change was additive.

docs.x: deploy/helm/ai-slides/templates/autoscaling.yaml (new, rendered) Generation is mostly waiting on the LLM (median CPU 3.70 percent in the load test), so CPU alone scales too late. The custom metric ai_slides_generation_inflight (Step 9) through prometheus-adapter scales on concurrent work; the target of 3 per pod is below the 4 concurrent workflows the load test ran without failures. The long scale-down window protects in-flight streams and background tasks: a scale-down sends SIGTERM to a pod that may be generating.

docs.t: 7.1 Keeping the fork in sync with upstream
docs.b: Part VIII: AI Slides delivery plan
docs.x: The fork tracks presenton/presenton with an upstream remote and keeps all AI Slides work on a branch that is rebased onto upstream release tags. fork sync (maintainer workstation or scheduled job) Rules that keep rebases cheap: new code in new files (api/v1/platform/, api/v1/auth/access.py, services/platform_*.py, deploy/), small flag-guarded edits in hot upstream files (services/database.py, api/middlewares.py, api/v1/auth/users.py), a separate Dockerfile.ai-slides instead of editing Dockerfile, and Alembic revisions that chain after the newest upstream revision (if upstream adds a revision after yours, re-point your down_revision during the rebase, or use an Alembic merge revision). Rebase at least monthly; a scheduled workflow can open the sync PR automatically and let CI report conflicts.

docs.x: .github/workflows/ai-slides-release.yml (new) The workflow pins actions by major version for readability; pin them by commit SHA in the real file, as the platform's supply-chain policy requires. Note that the upstream test-all.yml triggers on push and pull request; calling it with uses: requires adding workflow_call to its on: block, which is a one-line fork change. The ai-slides-canary release renders only a presenton-be-canary Deployment, Service and a copy of the API Ingress with nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary: "true" and canary-weight: "10". It shares the database and volume with the primary release. Promotion is a second manual job: after 30 minutes with the SLOs in Step 9 green, upgrade the primary ai-slides release to the same digests and uninstall the canary. The migrate Job runs in the canary release's pre-install hook, which is why every migration must be backward compatible (Step 3.5). Gotcha: canary by request, not by user ingress-nginx canary weights apply per request. One user's page load, its SSE stream and its export can hit different versions. That is fine only because the API is stateless and the schema is compatible both ways. If a release changes an SSE event shape (Story 4) or a payload the FE depends on, canary the FE and BE together with canary-by-cookie on a test cohort instead of a weight.

The team's direction was to use JSON as the base format and add an adaptor that converts to tiptap.json, changing only the adapter layer, with Presenton PPT and a Tiptap page both mapping to one Canonical IR. The follow-up requirement shapes everything below: "Today it is for Tiptap, tomorrow it might be for other modules, so the solution should be generic."

docs.t: Step 1: The decision in one paragraph
docs.x: Presenton slides and Tiptap pages meet in one target-agnostic Unified Document Model (UDM). The UDM is not a third format: it is the Part IX Artifact Spec (gck.artifact/1) shipped as protocol 1.3, a "UDM profile" in which nothing names a target. Every module is one adapter that implements the same contract: a capability manifest, a pure serialize (UDM to native), a pure deserialize (native to UDM), validateNative (the host's own rules), and optional host apply and patch. A core negotiate() function degrades a UDM deterministically to what a manifest supports and reports every loss; a registry makes adapters plug-ins; and one shared conformance kit gates every adapter. Presenton PPT (presenton.slides) and Tiptap (tiptap) are the first two adapters. Markdown, HTML, a Superset dashboard, DOCX, Confluence, Notion or email each need a new adapter only, never a change to the UDM core or the generation engine. Target-specific data, such as a Presenton slot path or layout id, lives only in a namespaced ext["<adapter-id>"] field that the core never interprets (negotiation may only drop foreign bags). Geometry, styling and theme never enter the UDM; they stay in the host.

This is the team's diagram, redrawn with the generation engine added. The six facets in the middle are views over UDM fields, not separate objects. The "PPT serializer" and "Tiptap serializer" boxes are the serialize halves of the two adapters. The arrows into the IR are their deserialize halves. In the prototype, the Presenton adapter reads and writes the Template v2 tree stored in slides.ui (servers/fastapi/models/sql/slide.py:30), and the Tiptap adapter reads and writes ProseMirror JSON checked against a real Tiptap 3.30.5 schema, the version Presenton already ships (servers/nextjs/package.json:40-44).

Part VIII's element_path (an RFC 6901 pointer into slides.ui) is the same location the PPT adapter records as its slot Intermediate representation Part IX: Artifact Spec v1, protocol 1.0 to 1.2, closed TargetId union Same spec as protocol 1.3 "UDM profile": open adapter ids, optional neutral fields for the six facets, ext namespaces Adapter contract Part IX: TargetAdapter with toNative and a host-bound fromHost serialize, deserialize, validateNative on every adapter, host apply and patch optional Fallbacks Part IX: each adapter degrades unsupported content its own way One core negotiate(udm, manifest) with fixed, ordered rules and a loss report Slides direction Part IX slides target writes per-layout content, no reverse direction presenton.slides deserializes from slides.ui and serializes back by patching slots Tiptap nodes Part IX: one atom per data kind (gckChart, gckMetric, gckDataTable, gckEmbed) plus GckBlockIds One generic dataBlock atom plus one udmAttrs global-attribute extension; the manifest is derived from the editor schema Testing Part IX: per-adapter golden files and round-trip tests One shared conformance kit (checks C0 to C11) that every adapter must pass Part X is the final, consolidated decision. "Presenton is JSON and Tiptap is JSON" holds, but it is not enough by itself: the two are schema-bound JSON with different shapes (slot-keyed, positioned slides versus an ordered flow tree), so the conversion has to go through the UDM with each adapter's rules in hand. First, targets that cannot carry block ids and ext (Markdown, a StarterKit-only editor) fall back to placing blocks by position, so documents going back to slides through them should be treated as "generate a new slide", not "update this slide". Second, the prototype does not cover live-data tokens, Smart-mode HTML slides, the Python side, or splitting a long document across several slides. Every adapter therefore validates its own output; no adapter relies on the host to clean up.

docs.t: Step 1: The four JSON forms of a Presenton deck
docs.x: A Presenton deck lives in two SQL tables, presentations and slides, and almost every column that matters is JSON. For the current product (version="v2-standard") a deck exists in four JSON forms at once. A fifth form, the Smart-mode HTML string, is not JSON and gets its own step (Step 7). # Form Where it lives Shape Written by Read by 1 Outline presentations.outlines (servers/fastapi/models/sql/presentation.py:51), plus presentations.structure (:66) {"slides":[{"content":"<markdown>"}]} (servers/fastapi/models/presentation_outline_model.py:8-28) and a layout index per slide outline and structure LLM calls slide content generation 2 Content slides.content (servers/fastapi/models/sql/slide.py:26) a dict keyed by component id and element name, shaped by the layout's JSON schema (servers/fastapi/templates/v2/schema.py:257), plus __speaker_note__ and asset keys get_slide_content_from_type_and_outline (servers/fastapi/utils/llm_calls/generate_slide_content.py:229) the hydrator, once 3 UI tree slides.ui (servers/fastapi/models/sql/slide.py:30) the Template v2 element tree: components, elements, runs, chart data, infographic data, positions _apply_template_content_to_ui (servers/fastapi/api/v1/ppt/endpoints/presentation.py:575), the editor, chat tools the HTML renderer, the editor, export 4 Editor deck browser memory the editor's Deck (servers/nextjs/components/slide-editor/types.ts:675) adaptGeneratedTemplateV2PresentationToDeck (servers/nextjs/components/slide-editor/importing/template-v2-import.ts:135), the "presentation adapter" Presenton uses today the Konva editor Two details shape the adapter design. The deck response that the frontend receives drops layout and structure (servers/fastapi/api/v1/ppt/endpoints/presentation.py:343-344), and outlines is not a field of that response, so a client never sees the template payload together with the deck. And legacy v1 decks are refused by the frontend (servers/nextjs/app/(presentation-generator)/presentation/hooks/usePresentationData.ts:33-41), so an adapter needs to support only the v2 ui tree. Here is one card from the dynamic template's center_title_cards_4771 layout in forms 2 and 3. The content form below is an illustration built from the schema that get_template_schema produces for this layout; the UI form is a real excerpt. slides.content for the card (illustration; keys from get_template_schema)

docs.t: Step 2: Tiptap JSON in one page
docs.x: Tiptap stores a document as ProseMirror JSON. The root is {"type":"doc","content":[...]}, every node has a type that must exist in the editor's schema, formatting is a list of marks on text nodes rather than wrapper elements, and attributes live in attrs. StarterKit 3.x provides paragraph, heading (levels 1 to 6), bulletList, orderedList, listItem, blockquote, codeBlock, horizontalRule and hardBreak, plus the marks bold, italic, strike, code, underline and link. Tables (table > tableRow > tableHeader | tableCell > paragraph) and images come from separate packages. Presenton already ships Tiptap 3.30.5 (servers/nextjs/package.json:40-44) and already converts its text runs to and from Tiptap JSON: textRunsToTiptapContent (servers/nextjs/components/slide-editor/text/TiptapInlineTextEditor.tsx:751) and tiptapContentToTextRuns (:798), with a custom runStyle mark (:50) and a latexRun inline node (:87). That editor turns off headings, lists and blockquotes (:267), so it uses Tiptap as an inline-run profile: one paragraph of styled runs inside a slide element. A Tiptap page is a different schema profile of the same format, with headings, lists, tables, images and block nodes. This is why the Tiptap adapter takes its extension list as input and derives its capabilities from it (tutorial/prototypes/udm/adapters/tiptap/index.mjs:13), instead of hard-coding one schema.

docs.t: Step 3: Why "it is all JSON" is necessary but not sufficient
docs.x: JSON on both sides removes the hard parts of an integration: no binary formats, no parsing of rendered output, and conversion as a pure function on the server. That part of the team's intuition holds. It is not sufficient, for five reasons. Both sides are schema-bound. A Template v2 element is one member of a Pydantic union (servers/fastapi/templates/v2/models/elements.py:624) with type-specific fields. A Tiptap document must match the schema built from the editor's extensions. The prototype confirmed Tiptap's behavior on bad input with seven negative controls (tutorial/prototypes/udm/scripts/validate.mjs): an unknown node type is rejected, text directly inside doc is rejected, a list item that starts with a heading is rejected, an empty text node is rejected, a code mark combined with bold is rejected, a heading level of 9 passes the schema check and needs an explicit range check, and an attribute the schema does not know is silently dropped. JSON that "looks right" is not enough; the output must be checked against the real schema. Positioned layout versus flow. A slide is a 1280 by 720 canvas (servers/nextjs/lib/template-v2-json-to-html.ts:153-154). Element positions are relative to their parent, and flex and grid children have no position at all. Reading order is not stored anywhere: it has to be computed. A Tiptap document is an ordered sequence, and order is the structure. Slot-keyed versus sequence. The content form is keyed by component id and element name, and every slot has capacity limits (max_length, min_length, item and row limits). A document has no slots and no limits. Going from a document to a slide means choosing a layout and assigning blocks to slots. Styling versus marks. Presenton text is a list of runs, each with a full font (family, size, color, bold, italic, underline, spacing). Tiptap has a few boolean marks. Size and color differences inside one element have no neutral home. Implicit versus explicit semantics. Presenton has no heading level. "This is a title" must be inferred from element names (main_heading, card_title), font size rank and position. Charts carry their data inline in the slide; Tiptap has no chart node at all. So the mapping is schema to schema, not JSON to JSON. Going through a canonical model with explicit semantics, plus one adapter per side that knows its own schema, is what makes the conversion predictable.

docs.t: Step 6: Which Presenton form the adapter must read
docs.x: The presenton.slides adapter reads and writes slides.ui. The other forms are hints at most. ui is what users see and change. It is rendered, edited and exported. The Konva editor writes it back through PATCH /slide_update (servers/fastapi/api/v1/ppt/endpoints/presentation.py:2585), and chat tools edit it directly through servers/fastapi/services/chat/slide_ui_helpers.py. content goes stale. It is copied into ui once by the hydrator. After an edit on the canvas or through chat, content no longer matches the slide. Chat also has a second hydration implementation (servers/fastapi/services/chat/memory_layer.py:3321, :3382), so content is not even produced by one code path. ui carries the semantics the UDM needs. Element type, name, decorative, is_icon, text runs with fonts, the list marker, the table header row, chart data and infographic data are all in ui. The content form drops decorative elements and per-run fonts. The prototype proves it. Reading ui captured 100% of 3,582 text elements, 607 images, 113 charts, 51 infographics, 35 lists and 7 tables, and produced a valid UDM for 383/383 layouts. The other forms still help. The outline becomes Section.summary and the speaker note becomes Section.notes. The layout's content schema (from get_template_schema) is the natural source of slot limits for fitting text. The editor Deck is a frontend view model derived from ui and is not a stable persisted form, so no adapter reads it. Gotcha This differs from Part IX, where the slides target writes per-layout content and has no reverse direction (see Artifact Spec and targets, Step 7). Writing content is still a valid way to generate a new slide through Presenton's existing hydrator. For round trips, the adapter must patch ui, because that is the only form that survives edits.

Smart mode does not produce structured slides. generate_smart_presentation (servers/fastapi/utils/llm_calls/generate_smart_presentation.py:733) returns HTML, and each slide is stored with layout_group="smart-html", content={"title": ...} and the full HTML in html_content (servers/fastapi/api/v1/ppt/endpoints/presentation.py:2060-2067). Edits go through POST /slide/edit-html (servers/fastapi/api/v1/ppt/endpoints/slide.py:135), which rewrites the HTML. slides.ui is null for these slides. Options for an adapter: Option What it means Status Treat Smart decks as out of scope for the UDM Offer "convert to a standard deck" by regenerating, or export only No new code One-way import by parsing the HTML Parse html_content into UDM blocks (headings, paragraphs, lists, images); charts drawn in HTML would not come back as data Unverified; the prototype does not cover Smart mode Round trip UDM back into free-form HTML slides Not feasible without an LLM call; there is no slot structure to patch Verdict: Smart-mode slides stay outside the round-trip guarantee. If a one-way import is needed, it is a separate deserializer inside the presenton.slides adapter (or a separate adapter) and must report its losses like any other.

docs.t: Step 8: The prototype and its method
docs.x: The prototype in tutorial/prototypes/udm/ was built to answer one question with measurements rather than opinions: can one target-agnostic model carry Presenton slides and Tiptap pages both ways, and does a third and fourth target need only an adapter? It touches no Presenton server code. It runs in Node 22 with Tiptap 3.30.5 (the version Presenton ships), marked 17.0.5 and TypeScript 5.9.3 for a strict type check of the UDM types and the adapter contract. Corpus run (scripts/validate.mjs). Every one of the 383 layouts in the 16 bundled templates becomes a one-slide deck with the layout's own sample content. The core was not untouched while the first three adapters were built: the tests forced five changes there, none specific to a target. The 383/383 identical round trip through Tiptap is partly by design. When a block comes back unchanged, the Presenton serializer leaves its slot untouched (tutorial/prototypes/udm/adapters/presenton/to-presenton.mjs:30 computes the comparison key, and the write loop skips equal blocks). The edit test is the real proof that each block finds its way back. The serializer assigns blocks to slots in a fixed order: the slot recorded in ext["presenton.slides"].slot, then a table matched by exact shape (so a chart that a target turned into a table finds its chart slot again), then the next free slot of the same block type in reading order, then any compatible slot (:99-120). With provenance intact, 100% of edits landed: 3,228 text, 354 titles, 35 lists, 7 tables and 113 charts. All 3,582 edited slots kept the slot's base font. Four findings limit the claim. Per-run highlights flatten. 44 elements have a second color or size inside one text element; none kept it after an edit. A neutral highlight mark in the UDM would close this. That is a proposal, not something the prototype did. Slot length. 2,477 edited slots exceed the slot's max_length, because the scripted edit adds 9 characters to each. validateNative reports them as warnings. This chapter specifies the Unified Document Model (UDM), the "Canonical IR" in the team's diagram that Presenton slides, Tiptap pages and every later module map to. You will see why the UDM is not a new format but the Part IX Artifact Spec (gck.artifact/1) shipped as protocol 1.3, a target-agnostic profile; how the diagram's six facets (Content, Sections, Structure, Semantics, Media, Metadata) map onto concrete fields; the full TypeScript and Pydantic types; a field-by-field mapping from Artifact 1.2 to UDM 1.3 so there is exactly one canonical format; and the rules for ids, provenance, extension bags, versioning, data bindings and number tokens. Every JSON example is copied from the runnable prototype in tutorial/prototypes/udm/examples/, which converted all 383 bundled Presenton layouts into a valid UDM.

docs.t: Step 1: One canonical format, not a third one
docs.x: The team's diagram has two producers (Presenton PPT, Tiptap Page), one Canonical IR in the middle, and one serializer per output. The user's follow-up makes the middle the important part: "Today it is for Tiptap, tomorrow it might be for other modules, so the solution should be generic." A model that only knows slides and pages would be rebuilt for the third module. So the decision is: The Unified Document Model is the Artifact Spec gck.artifact/1 from Part IX, shipped as protocol 1.3, a target-agnostic profile. It is not a third format. Anything a single target needs lives only in a namespaced ext["<adapter-id>"] bag that the engine never interprets and every other adapter passes through. Presenton slides and Tiptap are the first two adapters; Markdown, HTML, a Superset dashboard, DOCX, Confluence, Notion or email are later adapters, each one a new adapter and nothing else. Part IX already argued for an intermediate representation plus deterministic adapters (one validation path, one safety model, whole-block streaming, pure testable adapters; see Artifact Spec and targets, Step 1). A separate UDM would need its own JSON Schema, Pydantic models, invariants, versioning and a converter back to the Artifact, which is exactly the "competing third format" the team wants to avoid. Keeping one format also keeps the wire id gck.artifact/1 and the package @gck/protocol; protocol 1.1 and 1.2 are already taken by the data sources, so the UDM profile is 1.3. Every arrow in the team's diagram is one function of the same adapter contract (Tiptap adapter and Adding any new target cover the contract in full): Diagram arrow Contract function Presenton PPT to Canonical IR presenton.slides.deserialize(native) (PPT adapter) PPT serializer presenton.slides.serialize(negotiate(udm, manifest).udm), then Presenton's existing export for the .pptx file Tiptap Page to Canonical IR tiptap.deserialize(doc) Tiptap serializer tiptap.serialize(negotiate(udm, manifest).udm) "only the adapter layer should change" the core (@gck/protocol, negotiate, registry, conformance kit) and the engine never name a target; adapters register themselves The prototype proves the "no target in the core" claim mechanically: core.lock.json records sha256 hashes of every core file after the Markdown adapter was written; the plain-text adapter was written afterwards, and npm run validate reports "Core files
