Container start: ensurePresentationExportRuntime() runs --check-only, and in development falls back to --force; in production a failed check aborts startup with "presentation-export runtime is missing in this container image" (start.js:444-466). Set ENSURE_PRESENTATION_EXPORT_RUNTIME=false to skip. Electron: electron/scripts/sync-export-runtime.cjs runs the root script, then copies presentation-export/ to electron/resources/export/ and re-validates (electron/scripts/sync-export-runtime.cjs:55-73). CI: see Step 14. Gotcha: do not run a plain sync inside the production container The runtime stage of the image copies only sync-presentation-export.cjs and export-permissions.cjs into /app/scripts (Dockerfile:136-137); scripts/run-presentation-export.mjs exists only in the assets-builder stage (Dockerfile:67). --check-only never touches the runner, so container startup works. But a plain node scripts/sync-presentation-export.cjs (no flags) on a valid runtime takes the "refresh the runner" branch and calls fs.copyFileSync(sourceRunner, targetRunner) (scripts/sync-presentation-export.cjs:371), which fails with ENOENT because the source file is absent. Rebuild the image instead of syncing in
Every caller ends up executing the same file with the same contract. If you want to replace export-core, this is the seam.

Input: one positional argument, a JSON task file. Missing argument throws Usage: run-presentation-export.mjs <task.json> (scripts/run-presentation-export.mjs:102-105). Output: the runner writes the response next to the task, replacing a trailing .json with .response.json (scripts/run-presentation-export.mjs:128-129). So export_task.json produces export_task.response.json. Exit code: 0 on success; any thrown error is printed with console.error("[presentation-export]", error) (so stderr gets the prefix followed by the error and its stack) and sets process.exitCode = 1 (scripts/run-presentation-export.mjs:132-135). process.umask(0o027) is set first (scripts/run-presentation-export.mjs:7), so anything export-core creates is at most rwxr-x---.

The runner strips three keys before handing the task to export-core: scripts/run-presentation-export.mjs (excerpt) So export-core never sees the raw cookie header; it receives cookies only through urlConfigs (below). It does receive an extra __taskFilePath with the absolute task path. No caller in this repository sends slide_concurrency; the runner discards it either way. The task types that callers in this repository send: type Extra fields Caller Response used export url, format (pptx or pdf), title servers/fastapi/services/export_task_service.py:437-447, servers/nextjs/lib/run-bundled-presentation-export.ts:181-188, electron/app/ipc/export_handlers.ts:83-90 path pptx-to-html pptx_path, get_fonts servers/fastapi/services/export_task_service.py:464-471 path to a JSON manifest pptx-to-json pptx_path servers/fastapi/services/export_task_service.py:691-700 path to a JSON file with layouts html-to-image html, width, height servers/fastapi/services/export_task_service.py:533-541 path html-to-images htmls, width, height servers/fastapi/services/export_task_service.py:644-652 file_paths json-to-image data, width, height, optional fonts servers/fastapi/services/export_task_service.py:561-573 path json-to-images jsons, width, height, optional fonts servers/fastapi/services/export_task_service.py:598-610 file_paths The runner also mentions html-to-any when choosing an output directory (scripts/run-presentation-export.mjs:49), but nothing in this repository sends it.

buildSafeExportFileName() (servers/nextjs/app/(presentation-generator)/presentation/components/PresentationHeader.tsx:62-94) turns the title into a download name: Default to presentation, trim, strip a trailing .pdf or .pptx. Replace every run of characters outside [a-zA-Z0-9\s_-] with -, whitespace with -, collapse repeated -/_, trim separators. If window.electron?.exportPresentation exists, the header calls it over IPC (servers/nextjs/app/(presentation-generator)/presentation/components/PresentationHeader.tsx:209-224, 253-254) and the Electron main process takes over (Step 11). On success the response is: The header then creates an <a href=path download=fileName rel="noopener">, clicks it, and removes it (servers/nextjs/app/(presentation-generator)/presentation/components/PresentationHeader.tsx:426-434). Condition Status Body Not authenticated 401 {"detail":"Unauthorized"} Empty, non-object or invalid JSON body 400 {"error":"Invalid export request JSON body"} Missing or blank id 400 {"error":"Missing Presentation ID"} format not pdf/pptx 400 {"error":"Invalid export format"} Runtime missing 500 {"error":"presentation-export runtime is not available. Run scripts/sync-presentation-export.cjs to install it.","success":false} Child failed, output outside exports, and so on 500 {"error":"<message>","success":false} Note that the route never checks that the presentation exists or belongs to the caller. docs.x: servers/nextjs/lib/run-bundled-presentation-export.ts (excerpt) So the caller's entire Cookie header is copied three ways: exportSession=<value of presenton_session> in the query string (extractSessionTokenFromCookieHeader() uses the regex /(?:^|;\s*)presenton_session=([^;]+)/, servers/nextjs/lib/run-bundled-presentation-export.ts:27-38). #exportCookie=<whole cookie header> in the URL fragment. cookieHeader in the task, which the runner turns into urlConfigs cookies for the page origin. In Docker that request goes through nginx, and nginx.conf does not configure access_log, so nginx's default access logging applies to it. The token values above are placeholders.) The title is passed through sanitizeFilename() (servers/nextjs/app/(presentation-generator)/utils/others.ts:61-110), which removes null bytes, .., the characters ?<>\:*|", control characters, Windows reserved names and trailing dots or spaces. It deliberately keeps forward slashes (it was written for paths), so a client that posts a raw title containing / passes that slash through to export-core; the editor never does, because buildSafeExportFileName() has already replaced it. The child is spawn(process.execPath, [entrypoint, exportTaskPath], { cwd: appRoot, stdio: ["ignore", "pipe", "pipe"], env: process.env }) (servers/nextjs/lib/run-bundled-presentation-export.ts:200-205), so it runs with the same Node binary as Next.js and inherits Next's entire environment. stdout and stderr go into BoundedTextBuffers that keep only the last 8192 characters (servers/nextjs/lib/runtime-limits.ts:1-21). A non-zero exit becomes Export process exited with code N[ signal S]. <stderr> stdout: <stdout>. Gotcha: no timeout on the Next.js path FastAPI kills the export child after 300 seconds (Step 6.5). The Next.js path has no timeout at all: a page that never finishes loading keeps the HTTP request, the Node child and its Chromium alive until export-core gives up on its own (its internal timeouts are not visible here). nginx's proxy_read_timeout 30m on location / (nginx.conf:41) is the outer bound in Docker.

normalizeExportOutputPath() (servers/nextjs/lib/run-bundled-presentation-export.ts:76-123) accepts, in order: an absolute path; a relative path (resolved against APP_DATA_DIRECTORY, stripping a leading app_data/); a file:// URL (with the Windows /C:/ prefix fix in normalizeExportFileUrlPathname()); or a /app_data/... URL. Then ensureExportFileReadable() confirms it is a file and runs chmod 0o755 on its directory and chmod 0o644 on the file (servers/nextjs/lib/run-bundled-presentation-export.ts:63-64, 125-133). The work directory is removed in finally. Gotcha: two different permission policies The runner's finalizeExportPermissions() sets the export to 0o640 and its directory to 0o750 (Step 10.2). Immediately afterwards, the Next.js path widens the file to 0o644 and its directory (the shared exports/ root, since the move has not happened yet) to 0o755, both world-readable, and only then does fs.rename move the file into exports/users/<id>/. The FastAPI path does not widen anything. If you are hardening a multi-user host, this is the place to align the two.

docs.t: 6.2 Why the export browser needs a logged-in session
docs.x: The headless Chromium is a new, empty browser. To render the deck it must (a) load /pdf-maker, (b) fetch the presentation JSON from FastAPI, and (c) load every slide image from /app_data/images/.... In Docker, (b) is behind the FastAPI auth middleware and (c) is behind nginx auth_request /_auth_check (nginx.conf:133-142, 159-165). An API key cannot be used for those browser requests: Next.js's proxy explicitly refuses Bearer sk-presenton-... on anything that is not /api/v1 or /api/v2 (servers/nextjs/proxy.ts:146-156). So FastAPI has to hand the export browser a cookie. build_export_cookie_header() (servers/fastapi/api/v1/ppt/endpoints/presentation.py:1473-1496) decides which one: servers/fastapi/api/v1/ppt/endpoints/presentation.py (excerpt) Situation Cookie handed to the export browser Electron (PRESENTON_ELECTRON=true and a token) incoming cookies plus presenton_desktop_session=<token> (servers/fastapi/api/v1/auth/desktop.py:18-22) Browser session (the request already had a Cookie header) that exact header API key request presenton_session=<JWT minted by the middleware>; the auth middleware writes request.state.internal_session_token for every api_key principal (servers/fastapi/api/middlewares.py:123-126) MCP the MCP server mints a one-hour JWT (MCP_INTERNAL_SESSION_TTL_SECONDS, servers/fastapi/mcp_server.py:35-39) and forwards it as a Cookie (servers/fastapi/mcp_server.py:393-404), so the "browser session" row applies Auth disabled, no cookie None (no cookie needed) The unit tests in servers/fastapi/tests/unit/test_export_cookie_header.py:22-50 pin the precedence: the internal token beats a bearer key, a browser cookie beats both, and a desktop-token header produces the desktop cookie. Gotcha: async exports reuse a cookie captured at request time /generate/async captures build_export_cookie_header(request_http) when the request arrives and passes it to the background task (servers/fastapi/api/v1/ppt/endpoints/presentation.py:3264-3271); export happens only after all slides are generated. The JWT minted for API keys uses the default 30-day lifetime, but a browser session that is logged out (or an MCP token, one hour) in the meantime will make the export browser unauthenticated, and the export fails at the very end of a long, paid generation. POST /{id}/export exists precisely to retry that last step (its docstring,

servers/fastapi/utils/export_utils.py (excerpt) Compared with the Next.js path: no format and no exportSession in the query; the cookie travels only in the fragment and in cookieHeader. _get_next_public_url() defaults to http://127.0.0.1 (servers/fastapi/utils/export_utils.py:18-19). In the Docker image that is nginx on port 80 inside the container, which proxies /pdf-maker to Next.js on port 3000 (nginx.conf:29-43). Gotcha: running FastAPI outside Docker If you run FastAPI and Next.js directly on your machine (see Running it locally), nothing listens on http://127.0.0.1:80, and every API export fails inside the headless browser. Set NEXT_PUBLIC_URL (for example http://127.0.0.1:3000) in FastAPI's environment. The file name is computed as safe_export_basename(sanitize_filename(name)), where name is the trimmed title or a random UUID (servers/fastapi/utils/export_utils.py:58-62). sanitize_filename comes from the pathvalidate package; safe_export_basename() (servers/fastapi/utils/filename_utils.py:6-18) keeps names up to 200 UTF-8 bytes unchanged and otherwise truncates to 191 bytes (on a character boundary) plus _ plus the first 8 hex characters of the MD5 of the full name. The test servers/fastapi/tests/unit/test_filename_utils.py:22-25 asserts that the result plus .pptx fits the 255-byte file name limit. That test only makes sense if export-core uses title as the output file's base name, which is the strongest evidence in this repository for how the engine names its output (the engine itself is not available to confirm it).

docs.t: 7.1 The proxy turns exportSession into a cookie
docs.x: servers/nextjs/proxy.ts is Next.js's request proxy (middleware). Requests to /pdf-maker are always handled by it, even though other pages pass straight through (servers/nextjs/proxy.ts:103-105): servers/nextjs/proxy.ts (excerpt) The export browser therefore ends up with a normal presenton_session cookie on the Next.js origin, and the token disappears from the visible URL. Browsers carry the original fragment across a redirect whose Location has none, so #exportCookie=... survives. Outside Electron the proxy does not authenticate /pdf-maker itself (it returns NextResponse.next()); the page is useless without a valid cookie, because the data fetch is what FastAPI authorizes. The root ConfigurationInitializer also special-cases the route: no startup splash, no user-config fetch and no LLM provider revalidation for paths starting with /pdf-maker (servers/nextjs/app/ConfigurationInitializer.tsx:56, 75-83, 205-209), so an export never stalls on settings checks. In Electron mode the desktop transport guard runs first (servers/nextjs/proxy.ts:98-99), and servers/nextjs/tests/desktop-security.test.mjs:59-63 checks that /pdf-maker?exportSession=arbitrary and /api/export-presentation-data/id return 401 without the desktop token.

docs.t: 7.3 Fetching the deck through the data bridge
docs.x: With a cookie, the page calls its own Next.js route rather than FastAPI directly, using fetch(..., { cache: "no-store" }) (servers/nextjs/app/(export)/pdf-maker/PdfMakerPage.tsx:206-222): servers/nextjs/app/api/export-presentation-data/[id]/route.ts:17-62 returns 401 if x-export-cookie is missing, then forwards it as a real Cookie header to <FAST_API_INTERNAL_URL or NEXT_PUBLIC_FAST_API or http://127.0.0.1:8000>/api/v1/ppt/presentation/<id> and relays FastAPI's status, body and content type with Cache-Control: no-store. In Docker, start.js:485-487 sets FAST_API_INTERNAL_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8000. This route is on the proxy's auth-exempt list (servers/nextjs/proxy.ts:87-95) because it authenticates with the header instead of the request's own cookies, and FastAPI performs the real check. (The route has its own copy of getFastApiBaseUrl(); servers/nextjs/lib/fastapi-internal.ts exports an identical function plus getFastApiAuthHeaders(), but only app/api/user-config/route.ts imports that file, and nothing imports getFastApiAuthHeaders().) FastAPI's GET /api/v1/ppt/presentation/{id} (servers/fastapi/api/v1/ppt/endpoints/presentation.py:1551-1569) returns the presentation plus slides ordered by SlideModel.index. See Data model for the fields. Without a cookie (the Electron IPC path, or auth disabled), the page uses DashboardApi.getPresentation() with credentials: "include" (servers/nextjs/app/(presentation-generator)/services/api/dashboard.ts:70-82); in Electron the runner's header rule adds x-presenton-desktop-token to those requests.

After the fetch, fetchUserSlides() (servers/nextjs/app/(export)/pdf-maker/PdfMakerPage.tsx:175-204): Runs normalizeBackendAssetUrls() over the whole JSON, rewriting every asset-like string (/app_data/..., /static/..., local file: URLs, absolute URLs pointing at this backend) to the runtime-appropriate form (servers/nextjs/utils/api.ts:292-343, 371-416). In Docker that is a same-origin path served through nginx. With fastapiUrl in the query, it becomes an absolute FastAPI URL, but only if that origin equals the configured NEXT_PUBLIC_FAST_API origin or the page's own origin (servers/nextjs/utils/api.ts:56-78), so a crafted export link cannot redirect credentials elsewhere. Dispatches the data to Redux. Calls useFontLoader(fonts), which fires ensureTemplateFontLoaded() for each font without awaiting it (servers/nextjs/app/(presentation-generator)/hooks/useFontLoad.tsx:7-11). Applies the presentation theme to #presentation-slides-wrapper, ignoring errors so a theme problem cannot block an export (servers/nextjs/app/(export)/pdf-maker/PdfMakerPage.tsx:186-196). Themes are covered in Themes and fonts. PDF_PRINT_STYLE (servers/nextjs/app/(export)/pdf-maker/PdfMakerPage.tsx:26-100) pins the geometry: servers/nextjs/app/(export)/pdf-maker/PdfMakerPage.tsx (excerpt) and, for printing: servers/nextjs/app/(export)/pdf-maker/PdfMakerPage.tsx (excerpt) Slides stack vertically with no gap, each exactly 1280x720 CSS pixels, each one printed page. The test servers/nextjs/tests/pdf-maker-export-layout.test.mjs:10-19 reads the source and fails if align-items: flex-start !important disappears, if the wrapper loses the items-start class, or if align-items: center !important appears. Gotcha: centering a slide breaks PPTX geometry The comment above is the only description in the repository of export-core's measurement: it uses a 3000px-wide viewport. If you center the 1280px slide (the natural thing to do for a pretty preview), every element's x coordinate shifts by 860px relative to the clipping rectangle and shapes land in the wrong place. Never restyle #presentation-slides-wrapper without running that test. Gotcha: nothing on the page waits for fonts Fonts are loaded fire-and-forget (void ensureTemplateFontLoaded(font)), images are ordinary /CSS loads, and the page sets no "ready" flag of its own (only the Template v2 chart flag above). The skeleton placeholders shown while loading are also 1280x720 (servers/nextjs/app/(export)/pdf-maker/PdfMakerPage.tsx:261-271), and because isLoading is contentLoading || slides.length === 0 (servers/nextjs/app/(export)/pdf-maker/PdfMakerPage.tsx:224-225), a deck with zero slides keeps showing two gray skeletons forever instead of .main-slide elements. Any waiting for network idle, document.fonts.ready or chart completion must therefore be done by export-core, and its exact policy cannot be verified from this repository. If you add a slide element that loads asynchronously, assume the exporter may capture it before it is ready unless you can confirm otherwise.

docs.x: The engine is a closed box from this repository's point of view. The install script calls it the "open-source release" (scripts/sync-presentation-export.cjs:1-3) and the archive name contains opensource, but its source is in a different repository (presenton/presenton-export) and no copy exists in this checkout, so nothing below about its internals is verified.

A natural question is how each kind of DOM element becomes a PowerPoint shape. Without the engine's source or dist, none of these can be answered from this repository: Question Status How text runs, font families, weights, sizes and colors become a:r/a:rPr runs not verifiable Whether images are embedded at source resolution or re-encoded (Sharp is present, which suggests image processing) not verifiable Whether rectangles, borders and rounded corners become native preset shapes not verifiable Whether HTML tables become native PowerPoint tables not verifiable Whether Chart.js canvases become native charts or pictures not verifiable; the DOM only contains a <canvas> plus its JSON config in data-chart-config for Template v2 slides How SVG icons (including /api/update-svg URLs) are embedded not verifiable How backgrounds and z-order are mapped not verifiable How KaTeX math is converted not verifiable (KaTeX is a dependency) PDF: whether it uses Chromium printing with the page's @page size, and what it waits for before printing not verifiable For orientation only: OOXML uses 914,400 EMU per inch, so at 96 CSS pixels per inch one pixel is 9,525 EMU, and a 1280x720 px slide would be 12,192,000 x 6,858,000 EMU (13.333 x 7.5 inches, PowerPoint's standard 16:9 size). That is arithmetic, not a statement about what export-core writes.

A PDF export takes the same path as PPTX; only format differs. What the page guarantees for PDF: Page box: @page { size: 1280px 720px; margin: 0; }, which is 13.333 x 7.5 inches. One slide per page: break-after: page on every .main-slide except the last, and break-inside: avoid. No margins or gaps anywhere (html, body margins and the wrapper's padding are forced to 0, servers/nextjs/app/(export)/pdf-maker/PdfMakerPage.tsx:27-40). overflow: hidden on each slide clips content that overflows the 1280x720 box. Whether export-core honors these print rules (for example by printing with the page's CSS page size) or uses its own page size, viewport and waiting strategy for PDF cannot be confirmed here. The file route serves it as application/pdf (servers/nextjs/app/api/export-presentation/file/route.ts:8-12).

Stage Path export-core output (runner outputDirectory) <APP_DATA_DIRECTORY>/exports/<title>.<ext> After owner scoping (FastAPI or Next.js) <APP_DATA_DIRECTORY>/exports/users/<owner uuid>/<title>.<ext> Auth disabled (no owner) stays at <APP_DATA_DIRECTORY>/exports/<title>.<ext> Electron moved to the OS Downloads folder (Step 11) Task scratch files <TEMP_DIRECTORY>[/<owner>]/export-task-XXXX/ (FastAPI) or <TEMP_DIRECTORY>/export-XXXX/ (Next.js), deleted afterwards In Docker, APP_DATA_DIRECTORY=/app_data (Dockerfile:82), and the image pre-creates /app_data/exports among other roots (Dockerfile:123-124). Gotcha: same title, same file Because the base name comes from the title, two exports with the same title target the same path in exports/ before they are moved. Whether export-core makes names unique is not visible here. If it does not, two users exporting "Quarterly Review" at the same moment could race, and a second export by the same user replaces the first file in exports/users/<id>/ (os.replace and fs.rename both overwrite an existing destination).

The same algorithm exists in Python (servers/fastapi/utils/export_permissions.py:1-86, used by FastAPI) and JavaScript (scripts/export-permissions.cjs:1-66, used by the runner). The goal, in the docstring's words, is to grant the app and proxy group access without granting other OS users access. Constant or rule Value Directory mode 0o750, keeping any existing setgid/sticky bits (stat.st_mode & 0o3000) File mode 0o640 Group (export_reader_gid()) when running as root: the www-data group, else nginx; otherwise the process's own group (servers/fastapi/utils/export_permissions.py:9-20, scripts/export-permissions.cjs:4-16) Symlinks never followed or changed Boundary walks up from the file's directory, fixing each ancestor, and stops at the longest configured root that contains it; raises Export artifact is outside managed storage if no configured root contains it (servers/fastapi/utils/export_permissions.py:47-76) Ancestors (every directory from the output's directory up to the boundary) processed in "legacy" mode: regrouped to the reader group, mode reduced to stat.st_mode & 0o7770 (existing bits kept, "other" bits removed), and EACCES/EPERM ignored (servers/fastapi/utils/export_permissions.py:23-44) The output's own directory and file strict: directory 0o750, file 0o640; errors are raised, except that a directory owned by another user (when not running as root) is downgraded to legacy handling (servers/fastapi/utils/export_permissions.py:28-33) servers/fastapi/utils/export_permissions.py (excerpt) In the Docker image, the processes run as root (there is no USER instruction) and nginx runs as www-data (nginx.conf:1), so exports end up root:www-data 0640: nginx can read and serve them, other users cannot. The tests scripts/export-permissions.test.mjs:19-60 and servers/fastapi/tests/unit/test_export_permissions.py:17-110 cover modes, group ownership, private (0o700) and group-writable (0o2770) roots being preserved, symlink non-following, and the outside-storage error.

GET /api/export-presentation/file?name=<relative path> (servers/nextjs/app/api/export-presentation/file/route.ts:58-107) first requires an authenticated session (401 otherwise), then validates name with getSafeExportName(): servers/nextjs/app/api/export-presentation/file/route.ts (excerpt) So a user can only fetch users/<own id>/<file>; legacy files directly in exports/ are admin-only; with auth disabled any relative name is allowed. Rejections return 400 {"error":"Invalid export file name"}. After that the route: Resolves real paths of exports/ and the file and returns 403 Access denied if the file escapes (for example through a symlink). Streams the file with Content-Type from a three-entry table (.pdf, .pptx as application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.presentationml.presentation, .zip; anything else application/octet-stream), Content-Length, Cache-Control: no-store, and Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="<ASCII fallback>"; filename*=UTF-8''<encoded name>, where the fallback replaces every character outside [a-zA-Z0-9._-] with _ (servers/nextjs/app/api/export-presentation/file/route.ts:53-56). Maps ENOENT to 404 {"error":"Export file not found"} and any other error to 500 {"error":"Failed to download export file"}.

The FastAPI response's path is an absolute filesystem path, for example /app_data/exports/users/<id>/Q3 Review.pptx. That works as a URL only because the Docker image sets APP_DATA_DIRECTORY=/app_data, so the filesystem path and the URL path are identical, and nginx serves that prefix: nginx.conf (excerpt) /_auth_check is an internal subrequest to FastAPI GET /api/v1/auth/verify that forwards Cookie, Authorization and X-Original-URI (nginx.conf:133-142). verify_session() (servers/fastapi/api/v1/auth/router.py:81-107) resolves the principal (session cookie or API key) and then checks is_app_data_path_authorized(X-Original-URI), which for the private roots (images, exports, uploads, pptx-to-html, pptx-to-json) allows only users/<own id>/..., or legacy root files for admins (servers/fastapi/api/v1/auth/assets.py:10-17, 106-123). The code in this snapshot produces /app_data/exports/users/<owner id>/<title>.pptx (or /app_data/exports/<title>.pptx with auth disabled). docs.b: Part VI: Auth, infra and ops
docs.x: Reads: servers/fastapi/api/v1/auth/*.py, servers/fastapi/api/middlewares.py, servers/fastapi/api/v1/admin/router.py, servers/fastapi/services/api_keys.py, servers/fastapi/services/database.py, servers/nextjs/proxy.ts, servers/nextjs/utils/serverAuth.ts, servers/nextjs/lib/server-auth-role.ts, nginx.conf · Builds on: FastAPI app and startup, Data model · Time: ~45 min Presenton ships a complete, self-contained account system: a username and password login backed by a database user table, a signed JWT session cookie, admin-issued API keys for REST and MCP clients, a per-user data partition enforced at the ORM layer, and a separate "desktop transport guard" that protects the auth-less Electron build. This chapter walks through every request path in execution order: how the first administrator is created, what the login endpoint writes into the cookie, how each incoming request is turned into a principal, how that principal silently scopes every SELECT, how nginx authorizes static files it serves directly, and how the Next.js server double-checks the same state before rendering pages.

docs.x: Before reading code, fix the moving parts in your head. Authentication happens in four places, in this order on a Docker deployment: Layer File What it decides nginx auth_request nginx.conf:133 Whether nginx may serve a private file under /app_data/ (images, exports, uploads, pptx-to-html, pptx-to-json) straight from disk SessionAuthMiddleware servers/fastapi/api/middlewares.py:29 Who the caller is (cookie JWT or API key), whether the path is admin-only, which owner ID scopes the request Route dependencies servers/fastapi/api/v1/auth/users.py:211, :219 Per-route get_current_user / get_current_admin checks (admin router, settings) Next.js proxy and layouts servers/nextjs/proxy.ts:97, servers/nextjs/utils/serverAuth.ts:94 Whether Next.js API routes and pages may run; they ask FastAPI /api/v1/auth/status Everything is owned by FastAPI. Next.js never verifies a JWT itself; it forwards the browser's cookie to GET /api/v1/auth/status and trusts the answer. The topology itself (which process listens where, how start.js supervises them) is covered in Runtime topology. Here we only follow credentials.

docs.x: The JWT signing secret does not come from an environment variable. It lives in userConfig.json (the file at USER_CONFIG_PATH, which start.js sets to $APP_DATA_DIRECTORY/userConfig.json, see start.js:481). servers/fastapi/api/v1/auth/config.py (excerpt) get_or_create_auth_secret (servers/fastapi/api/v1/auth/config.py:71) lazily creates a 32-byte, base64url secret on first use and merges only the three AUTH_CONFIG_FIELDS into the file through update_user_config_file (a lock-file plus atomic-rename writer, mode 0600, see CI, tests, security). persist_admin_credentials (config.py:95) writes AUTH_USERNAME and AUTH_PASSWORD_HASH next to the secret. This is a "rollback/recovery credential copy": the database is the source of truth, but the file keeps a hash that the bootstrap code can migrate from (Step 3). With rotate_secret=True the function also replaces AUTH_SECRET_KEY, which invalidates every JWT ever issued, for every user. Gotcha: the signing secret is read on every token operation get_jwt_strategy() (servers/fastapi/api/v1/auth/users.py:176) builds a new VersionedJWTStrategy and calls get_or_create_auth_secret() each time a token is read or written, so it reads userConfig.json per request. Deleting AUTH_SECRET_KEY from the file logs everyone out at once; deleting the whole file also drops the recovery hash. The README explicitly warns against editing these fields by hand. Gotcha: API key ciphertext depends on the same secret _api_key_cipher derives a Fernet key from sha256(AUTH_SECRET_KEY) (servers/fastapi/services/api_keys.py:39). Rotating the secret makes every stored token_encrypted undecryptable, so reveal_api_key returns None and the admin endpoint answers 409 "This API key cannot be revealed". Rotation through RESET_AUTH or AUTH_OVERRIDE_FROM_ENV deletes all keys anyway (Step 3.2), so this only bites if you rotate the secret some other way.

docs.x: app_lifespan calls bootstrap_database_admin() after migrations and create_db_and_tables and before the app accepts requests (servers/fastapi/api/lifespan.py:58). The function (servers/fastapi/api/v1/auth/bootstrap.py:43) reads four variables: Variable Parsed by Effect AUTH_USERNAME .strip() Username for creation, rotation or recovery; must be at least 3 characters if set, or startup raises RuntimeError AUTH_PASSWORD raw Must be at least 8 characters when it is used RESET_AUTH _truthy (1/true/yes/on) Recover the existing primary admin AUTH_OVERRIDE_FROM_ENV _truthy Rotate the existing primary admin's credentials The decision tree, in code order: The rotation branch is the interesting one: servers/fastapi/api/v1/auth/bootstrap.py (excerpt) Four things happen at once: the hash changes, auth_version increments (killing the admin's JWTs even before the secret rotation), every API key in the database is deleted (not only the admin's), and the signing secret is regenerated (killing every other user's JWT). The admin's id is preserved, so owned rows keep pointing at the same account. Gotcha: RESET_AUTH and AUTH_OVERRIDE_FROM_ENV are not one-shot Both flags are evaluated on every startup. If you leave RESET_AUTH=true in your compose file, every container restart rotates the secret, deletes all API keys and logs out every user. The README tells operators to remove the flag after a successful startup. The two flags are behaviorally identical in code; they differ only in intent. Gotcha: plain AUTH_USERNAME/AUTH_PASSWORD only matter on an empty database Without one of the two flags, the env credentials are used only when no user exists at all (bootstrap.py:91 onward). Changing AUTH_PASSWORD on a running deployment does nothing until you also set AUTH_OVERRIDE_FROM_ENV=true for one start.

docs.x: Older Presenton releases had a single account stored only in userConfig.json as AUTH_USERNAME plus an AUTH_PASSWORD_HASH of the form pbkdf2_sha256$<iterations>$<salt>$<digest>. Bootstrap picks those up through get_legacy_admin_credentials (config.py:84) and inserts them as the primary admin without rehashing. Two cooperating pieces make that work: LegacyAwarePasswordHelper.verify_and_update (servers/fastapi/api/v1/auth/users.py:31) recognises the pbkdf2_sha256$ prefix, verifies with verify_legacy_password_hash (config.py:50, hmac.compare_digest on a PBKDF2-SHA256 digest), and returns a modern replacement hash. Login then stores the replacement (router.py:176), so the legacy hash disappears after the first successful sign-in. LoginCredentialsRequest allows passwords of 6 characters (schemas.py:45) because the legacy system did; new passwords still need 8. Finally _backfill_legacy_ownership (bootstrap.py:128) claims all orphaned data for the admin: servers/fastapi/api/v1/auth/bootstrap.py (excerpt) The owned models are presentations, slides, async tasks, async presentation generation tasks, chat history, image assets and webhook subscriptions. This runs on every startup when an admin exists, so any row created with a NULL owner (for example while DISABLE_AUTH was on) is adopted by the admin on the next boot. Gotcha: toggling DISABLE_AUTH off hands desktop data to the admin Rows written while auth was disabled have owner_id = NULL. The next startup with an admin present runs the backfill, and they all become the primary admin's private data. Normal users never see them.

docs.t: 5.4 resolve_request_principal: cookie first, then API key
docs.b: Part VI: Auth, infra and ops
docs.x: servers/fastapi/api/v1/auth/principal.py (excerpt) The resolution order is: presenton_session cookie, if present and valid, wins. method = "jwt". Otherwise an Authorization: Bearer ... header is treated as an API key. method = "api_key". Otherwise no principal. AuthPrincipal (principal.py:14) is a frozen dataclass of user_id, username, is_admin and method. Note the type annotation: method is Literal["jwt", "api_key"]. There is no third "internal" method. Internal callers (the export browser, background tasks, the MCP server) authenticate by presenting a normal presenton_session JWT that the server minted for them (Step 7). Gotcha: a valid cookie always beats a bearer header If the cookie is present but invalid, the code falls through to the bearer branch, so a client that sends both a stale cookie and a valid API key still authenticates with the key. If the cookie is valid, the bearer header is ignored entirely, even if it names a different user.

docs.x: Isolation is enforced by two global SQLAlchemy ORM event listeners, not by hand-written WHERE clauses: servers/fastapi/services/database.py (excerpt) Reads. _scope_owned_selects (database.py:67) adds with_loader_criteria(model, owner_id == current) for the seven strict models on every ORM SELECT, including joins and aliases. docs.t: Step 12: Presenton OAuth (the cloud provider, not a login)
docs.b: Part VI: Auth, infra and ops
docs.x: PRESENTON_OAUTH_ROUTER (servers/fastapi/api/v1/auth/presenton_oauth.py:29) is mounted under /api/v1/auth/presenton. Despite the folder, it does not sign anyone into Presenton. It links the installation to Presenton Cloud as a text-generation provider using the OAuth 2.0 device authorization grant (DEVICE_GRANT_TYPE = "urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code"). The issuer and client ID are constants: https://api.presenton.ai and ptc_presenton_open_source (servers/fastapi/utils/get_env.py:7). Endpoint Guard Upstream call GET /status any authenticated principal none; returns enabled, issuer, linked, can_manage, and the linked email only to managers POST /device/start admin cookie or DISABLE_AUTH POST {issuer}/oauth/device_authorization with client_id, device_name (max 120) POST /device/poll admin cookie or DISABLE_AUTH POST {issuer}/oauth/token, then GET {issuer}/oauth/userinfo, then store credentials POST /logout admin cookie or DISABLE_AUTH revoke and clear; if LLM == "presenton", set LLM to None Details worth knowing: Every upstream call goes through _provider_request (presenton_oauth.py:77) with a 15-second timeout and follow_redirects=False. device/start validates that all six RFC fields are present, then overwrites verification_uri_complete with the plain verification_uri so the user code never appears in a URL, browser history or logs (presenton_oauth.py:204). Responses carry Cache-Control: no-store. device/poll maps authorization_pending and slow_down to 202 {"status": "pending", "error": ...}, validates the profile with PresentonUserInfo, defaults expires_in to 30 days when absent, and in a finally block revokes the fresh access token if storing it failed (presenton_oauth.py:310). How the stored credential is used for generation is covered in Configuration and LLM providers.

docs.t: 2.1 A pip-less virtual environment managed by uv
docs.b: Part VI: Auth, infra and ops
docs.x: Dockerfile (excerpt) The venv is created without pip; uv is installed into the base interpreter and pointed at the venv with --python /opt/venv/bin/python. Only /opt/venv is copied to the runtime stage, so neither pip nor uv exists at runtime. UV_COMPILE_BYTECODE=1 compiles .pyc files at install time, so the first import in the container does not pay that cost. UV_LINK_MODE=copy avoids hard links into the cache mount, which would dangle once the cache is unmounted. uv export --frozen --no-dev --no-emit-project turns uv.lock into a fully pinned requirements file without the dev group (pytest, pytest-cov) and without the project itself. --frozen means the lock is used as-is; a lock that disagrees with pyproject.toml is not silently re-resolved. Copying only pyproject.toml and uv.lock first means dependency layers are reused when only application code changes.

docs.t: 2.4 Baking FastEmbed weights, then proving they work offline
docs.b: Part VI: Auth, infra and ops
docs.x: Dockerfile (excerpt) servers/fastapi/scripts/warm_fastembed_cache.py initializes three models: the icon-search embedding index through ICON_FINDER_SERVICE.ensure_initialized() (the docstring names AllMiniLML6V2), the Mem0 dense embedder (MEM0_EMBEDDER_MODEL, default BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5, warm_fastembed_cache.py:28) and the Qdrant/bm25 sparse model (warm_fastembed_cache.py:49). The first RUN downloads them into normal image layers. The second RUN repeats the warm-up with networking disabled and HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1: if any weight is missing, initialization tries the network, fails, and the build stops. This is the image's offline guarantee for embeddings. Gotcha: changing the embedder model at runtime defeats the bake Only the default BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 (or whatever MEM0_EMBEDDER_MODEL was at build time) is cached. Setting a different MEM0_EMBEDDER_MODEL in compose makes the container download weights on first use, which fails in air-gapped deployments. The Dockerfile declares no ARG or ENV for MEM0_EMBEDDER_MODEL in the fastapi-builder stage, so to bake a different model you must add one before the warm-up RUN lines and rebuild.

docs.t: 5.2 Pinned Chromium from a Debian snapshot
docs.b: Part VI: Auth, infra and ops
docs.x: Dockerfile (excerpt) The export engine's rendering is sensitive to the browser build, so the image does not take "whatever Chromium trixie-security has today". It adds a snapshot.debian.org source frozen at 20260625T180000Z, disables Valid-Until checks (snapshot metadata is old by design), installs exactly 149.0.7827.196-1~deb13u1 (with --allow-downgrades in case the live mirror is newer), and holds the packages. The same build ID (149.0.7827.196) is pinned for the desktop app in electron/package.json:6, so Docker and Electron export with the same browser revision. The rest of the package list provides nginx, fontconfig, imagemagick, zstd, curl, the Chromium shared libraries (libgtk-3-0t64, libnss3, libgbm1 and others), and fonts. Node.js 22 comes from the NodeSource setup script, not from Debian.

docs.x: Dockerfile (excerpt) Every system font whose filename does not start with Noto is deleted and the fontconfig cache rebuilt. This makes font fallback during export deterministic: when a slide requests a font the image does not have, Chromium falls back to a Noto family rather than whichever font a dependency happened to pull in. Template fonts are loaded separately (see Themes and fonts). docs.t: 8.2 Bind mounts versus named volumes in development
docs.b: Part VI: Auth, infra and ops
docs.x: docker-compose.yml (excerpt) The whole repository is mounted at /app so source edits reload live. Three named volumes are mounted on top of paths inside that bind mount; they shadow whatever the host has there. This keeps Linux-built native modules (sharp, the export engine) inside Docker-managed storage, isolated from a macOS or Windows host's node_modules. This is also why installRuntime clears the contents of /app/presentation-export rather than deleting the directory: deleting a mount point fails with EBUSY (scripts/sync-presentation-export.cjs:296). The root test package-metadata.test.mjs asserts that presenton_presentation_export:/app/presentation-export appears exactly twice in the compose file and is declared under top-level volumes: (scripts/package-metadata.test.mjs:56). The production service's read-only templates mount replaces the image's servers/fastapi/templates package with the host copy. FastAPI is started as python server.py from /app/servers/fastapi (start.js:521), so that directory is first on sys.path and the mounted package is the one imported.

docs.x: Every service forwards roughly 110 variables using the pattern - NAME=${NAME:-default}. Most defaults are empty, which forwards an empty string. Two mechanisms make empty values harmless: start.js seeds userConfig.json from the environment through scripts/user-config-env.cjs. envValue treats both undefined and "" as "not set" (scripts/user-config-env.cjs:130), so an empty compose variable never erases a value saved in the UI. setupUserConfigFromEnv (start.js:490) writes the file only if it is empty or at least one recognised key is non-empty; otherwise it leaves a UI-managed configuration alone. Non-empty compose defaults worth knowing: Variable Compose default Effect MIGRATE_DATABASE_ON_STARTUP true (hard-coded, not ${...:-true}, so a shell variable cannot override it) Run Alembic at startup (otherwise create_all on a fixed table list) PRESENTATION_GENERATION_MODE both Standard and Smart generation PRESENTON_COMMUNITY_ENABLED true Community gallery on START_OLLAMA false No in-container Ollama ENABLE_PARALLEL_IMAGE_GENERATION true MAX_OUTLINE_WORDS 100 MEM0_LLM_MODEL ${OLLAMA_MODEL:-llama3.1:latest} Mem0 points at Ollama by default MEM0_LLM_BASE_URL ${OLLAMA_URL:-http://host.docker.internal:11434} MEM0_EMBEDDER_MODEL, MEM0_EMBEDDING_DIMS BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5, 384 Matches the baked weights LITEPARSE_DPI, LITEPARSE_NUM_WORKERS 120, 1 Document parsing cost PUPPETEER_EXECUTABLE_PATH /usr/bin/chromium Authentication variables (AUTH_USERNAME, AUTH_PASSWORD, AUTH_OVERRIDE_FROM_ENV, RESET_AUTH) are forwarded by all four services; their semantics are in Auth and multi-user. DISABLE_AUTH is not forwarded by compose, which keeps accounts on for Docker unless you add it yourself. Gotcha: two different host-port variable names The port mapping uses PRESENTON_HTTP_HOST_PORT, but the environment block forwards PRESENTON_HOST_HTTP_PORT (note the word order), defaulting to 5001 (and to 5000 in production-gpu). Inside the container that value only feeds the startup banner (scripts/presenton-terminal-banner.mjs:97). If you only set PRESENTON_HTTP_HOST_PORT=8080, the app works on 8080 but the banner still prints 5001. Gotcha: platform defaults to linux/amd64 Every service sets platform: ${PRESENTON_DOCKER_PLATFORM:-linux/amd64}. On Apple Silicon or ARM servers, compose builds and runs an emulated amd64 image unless you export PRESENTON_DOCKER_PLATFORM=linux/arm64.

docs.x: .github/workflows/docker-release.yml runs on release: published and on workflow_dispatch: .github/workflows/docker-release.yml (excerpt) Check out the release tag (or the dispatched ref). Set up QEMU and Buildx (both actions pinned by commit SHA), log in to ghcr.io with secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN (the job has packages: write). Tag: ghcr.io/presenton/presenton:<release tag> for releases, ghcr.io/presenton/presenton:dev (MOVING_TAG) for manual runs. Build both platforms in one Buildx invocation with the GitHub Actions cache backend. docker buildx imagetools inspect the pushed tag and grep for both linux/amd64 and linux/arm64. The concurrency group keys on the tag with cancel-in-progress: false, so two releases never cancel each other. Gotcha: CI never moves latest The workflow pushes only the release tag or dev. The latest tag used by docker run ghcr.io/presenton/presenton:latest and by the DigitalOcean template is promoted by hand, following docs/multi-docker-build.md step 4.

docs.x: docs/multi-docker-build.md describes the alternative used when building natively on two machines: build on macOS (arm64) and Linux (amd64), tag the local image presenton-3-production:latest as ghcr.io/presenton/presenton:<version>-arm64 and -amd64, push both, then stitch them with docker buildx imagetools create -t ghcr.io/presenton/presenton:<version> <amd64> <arm64>, promote with a second imagetools create -t ...:latest ...:<version>, and verify that both manifests list linux/amd64 and linux/arm64. Native builds avoid QEMU emulation, which matters for a build that compiles Python bytecode, installs Chromium and warms ONNX models. Because Buildx runs the assets-builder stage once per platform, each architecture gets its own @img/sharp-linux-<arch> native package, and validateSharpRuntime checks the right one.

docs.x: .do/deploy.template.yaml (excerpt) The template deploys the prebuilt latest image to one apps-s-1vcpu-2gb instance on port 80, sets MIGRATE_DATABASE_ON_STARTUP=true and START_OLLAMA=false, and alerts on DEPLOYMENT_FAILED and DOMAIN_FAILED. It declares no volume and no DATABASE_URL, so the SQLite database, userConfig.json (with the JWT signing secret) and all generated assets live on the container filesystem under /app_data. If the platform does not persist that filesystem across deploys, every redeploy resets accounts and data; add a managed database through DATABASE_URL and check your provider's storage options before relying on it.

docs.x: No Helm chart or manifest ships in the repository. What the code does provide is tolerance for volumes owned by an arbitrary UID: start.js (excerpt) At startup start.js creates the seven asset directories with mode 0755 (start.js:93), applies chmodBestEffort to them and to userConfig.json/.bak (0600, :104), and normalizes permissions under exports, pptx-to-html and pptx-to-json with legacy: true (start.js:89). In legacy mode an existing directory keeps its owner and group bits and only loses world access (stat.mode & 0o7770) instead of being forced to 0750; a non-root process also switches to legacy mode on its own for any directory it does not own (scripts/export-permissions.cjs:24). When running as root, exported files are re-grouped to www-data (or nginx) and set to 0640 so the nginx worker (user www-data;, nginx.conf:1) can read them without making them world-readable (exportReaderGid, scripts/export-permissions.cjs:4). Gotcha: one replica only start.js runs FastAPI, the MCP server, Next.js and nginx inside one container, async generation tasks are in-process BackgroundTasks that are marked failed after a restart (servers/fastapi/api/lifespan.py:60), and assets are on local disk. Nothing in the repository coordinates multiple replicas; run one instance per data volume.

docs.x: nginx.conf (excerpt) Location Upstream Body limit Timeouts Forwarded headers / Next.js :3000 100M read/connect 30m Host $http_host, X-Real-IP, X-Forwarded-For, mapped X-Forwarded-Proto/-Host, WebSocket upgrade /api/v1/ FastAPI :8000 110M, 413 returns {"detail":"File size must be less than 100MB."} read/send/connect 30m same (no upgrade) /api/v2/ FastAPI :8000 100M 30m same /mcp, /mcp/ MCP :8001 145M 30m Host localhost:8001 (FastMCP host allowlist) plus mapped forwarded headers /docs, /openapi.json FastAPI 100M 30m Host $host, X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme /static/ alias to /app/servers/fastapi/static/ public, Cache-Control: public, immutable /app_data/* alias to /app_data/* see Auth and multi-user The 30-minute timeouts exist for long SSE generation streams and exports. Host $http_host (not $host) keeps the port, which the comment at nginx.conf:34 says Next.js needs for redirects and absolute URLs. Downstream, the forwarded headers drive three behaviors: the Secure flag on the session cookie (_secure_request, servers/fastapi/api/v1/auth/router.py:39), MCP result links (absolute_mcp_url, servers/fastapi/utils/mcp_public_urls.py:17) and the /pdf-maker session cookie in servers/nextjs/proxy.ts:126. Gotcha: nginx trusts incoming X-Forwarded-* The map blocks pass any client-supplied X-Forwarded-Proto or X-Forwarded-Host through unchanged. When nginx is directly exposed (no outer proxy), a client can set them. Put a proxy in front that overwrites these headers, or set PRESENTON_PUBLIC_URL so generated links do not depend on them.

docs.x: get_database_url_and_connect_args (servers/fastapi/utils/db_utils.py:57) decides the runtime URL: Input Runtime URL Alembic URL (to_sync_sqlalchemy_url, :103) unset sqlite+aiosqlite:///$APP_DATA_DIRECTORY/fastapi.db (default /tmp/presenton/fastapi.db) sqlite:///... sqlite://... sqlite+aiosqlite://..., parent directory created sqlite:///... postgresql://... postgresql+asyncpg://... postgresql+psycopg://... mysql://... mysql+aiomysql://... mysql+pymysql://... anything else unchanged unchanged All three drivers are in pyproject.toml (aiosqlite, asyncpg, aiomysql, psycopg[binary]). For server databases, services/database.py:38 adds pool settings from get_pool_kwargs (db_utils.py:34): DB_POOL_SIZE (5), DB_MAX_OVERFLOW (10), DB_POOL_TIMEOUT (30 s), DB_POOL_RECYCLE (1800 s), DB_POOL_PRE_PING (true). servers/fastapi/utils/db_utils.py (excerpt) Gotcha: every query parameter is dropped The only query parameter that is interpreted is sslmode on PostgreSQL, which turns into a default ssl.SSLContext unless it equals disable. The whole query string is then removed, so options like ?charset=utf8mb4 or ?sslrootcert=... never reach the driver. Gotcha: postgres:// is not rewritten Only the postgresql:// prefix is mapped to asyncpg. A postgres:// URL (common in hosted database dashboards) is passed through unchanged and will not select the async driver. Rename the scheme before setting DATABASE_URL. Moving to Postgres or MySQL does not move userConfig.json (signing secret, provider keys) or the asset directories; /app_data still needs persistent storage. How migrations run at startup is covered in FastAPI app and startup.

docs.x: docs/presenton-resource-usage.md reports a controlled k6 test of a single container. The workflow it exercised is exactly the standard pipeline described in Standard generation pipeline: Order Request setup POST /api/v1/auth/login once per test account (Testuser1 to Testuser4), sequentially 1 POST /api/v1/ppt/presentation/create 2 GET /api/v1/ppt/chat/conversations?presentation_id={id}&presentation_type=standard 3 GET /api/v1/ppt/outlines/stream/{id} (SSE) 4 POST /api/v1/ppt/presentation/prepare 5 GET /api/v1/ppt/presentation/stream/{id} (SSE) The load shape was four waves with a 60-second cooldown; in each wave four virtual users ran one workflow each (10, 20, 30 and 40 slides), for 16 workflows, 96 HTTP requests and zero failures over a 51 minute 50 second window sampled every 2 seconds (1,551 samples). PPTX export was deliberately excluded. Metric Start Median P95 Max End CPU (100% = one core) 0.53% 3.70% 43.27% 1,087.09% 579.11% Memory utilization 17.42% 20.19% 21.36% 37.09% 37.09% Available memory 6,031.36 MB 5,828.61 MB 5,985.28 MB 6,031.36 MB 4,594.69 MB "Heap" (sum of process VmData) 2,670.32 MB 3,170.68 MB 3,273.54 MB 11,866.22 MB 11,086.41 MB The report's conclusions: CPU is bursty with a near-empty run queue (zero in 97.4% of samples); memory grew slowly during the run (+4.07 points, about +601 MB of VmData before 18:19:13); and about four minutes after the last k6 wave finished, a one-minute burst drove average CPU to 337.87%, memory to 37.09% and VmData to 11.9 GB. The capture ended during that burst, so the report cannot say which process caused it or whether memory was released. The report notes that heap_memory_mb is not a managed-runtime heap counter but the sum of Linux VmData across the container's processes, to be read as aggregate data/heap allocation rather than resident memory. For sizing, the start and end rows are consistent with a host of about 7.3 GB total memory (derived arithmetic: 6,031.36 / (1 - 0.1742) and 4,594.69 / (1 - 0.3709) both give roughly 7,300 MB). That implies roughly 1.3 GB in use at the start and 2.7 GB at the peak, so the 2 GB DigitalOcean template leaves little headroom for concurrent generation. The report itself recommends repeating the test with stage markers, a recovery period, and OOM and swap counters.

docs.x: Reads: electron/package.json, electron/build.js, electron/tsconfig.json, electron/app/main.ts, electron/app/utils/*.ts, electron/app/ipc/*.ts, electron/app/preloads/index.ts, electron/scripts/*.cjs, servers/fastapi/server.spec, servers/fastapi/api/v1/auth/desktop.py, servers/nextjs/lib/desktop-auth.ts, servers/nextjs/tests/desktop-security.test.mjs, docs/macos/dev/*.md, .github/workflows/electron-linux-ubuntu22.yml, .github/workflows/sync-releaes-to-r2.yml · Builds on: Runtime topology, Auth and multi-user, Docker build and deployment · Time: ~45 min The desktop app is the same two servers you met in the Docker image (FastAPI and the Next.js standalone server), but with no nginx, no start.js, and no account system. Electron's main process takes over every job those pieces did: it picks loopback ports, writes the environment, spawns a PyInstaller-frozen FastAPI binary and the Next.js server.js, mints a per-launch secret that both servers check on every request, and runs the PPTX/PDF export runner as a child process. This chapter follows the code from npm run build:all through first launch to shutdown, then covers signing, notarization, the Linux CI build, and how release files reach Cloudflare R2.

docs.x: All scripts live in electron/scripts/. Every one writes into electron/resources/, which build.js later packs.

docs.x: It deletes resources/nextjs and servers/nextjs/.next-build, then runs npm run build in servers/nextjs with two extra variables: PRESENTON_ELECTRON_BUILD=true and NEXT_PUBLIC_PRESENTON_ELECTRON_PLATFORM=<process.platform> (electron/scripts/build-nextjs-resources.cjs:26 to :36). Those two flags change the Next.js build: next.config.mjs:5 and :37 set images.unoptimized when PRESENTON_ELECTRON_BUILD is true, because a packaged app lives in a read-only directory such as /opt/Presenton and Next's image optimizer writes into <distDir>/cache. app/(presentation-generator)/components/SmartHtmlSlide.tsx:22 switches to an in-page renderer when the platform constant is linux. The script then copies .next-build/standalone/* into resources/nextjs/, and copies .next-build/static and public/ to both the bundle root and the nested servers/nextjs/ directory (electron/scripts/build-nextjs-resources.cjs:51 to :86), because Next.js 16 standalone output traces the app under servers/nextjs/ and runs server.js from there.

docs.x: ensure-spacy-model.cjs creates servers/fastapi/.venv if missing, checks spacy.load("en_core_web_sm") through uv run python -c, and otherwise installs the pinned wheel en_core_web_sm-3.8.0-py3-none-any.whl from the explosion/spacy-models GitHub release (electron/scripts/ensure-spacy-model.cjs:8 to :14). With MEM0_SPACY_STRICT=true (set by build:fastapi) a failure aborts the build; without it the script only warns that "Mem0 will self-disable at runtime" (:92 to :98). PyInstaller then freezes server.py using servers/fastapi/server.spec. The spec matters because much of FastAPI's dependency tree is loaded dynamically: collect_all for fastembed, fastembed_vectorstore, onnxruntime, pptx, docx2everything, greenlet, llmai, spacy, en_core_web_sm, wrapped in safe_collect_all so a missing optional package yields empty lists (servers/fastapi/server.spec:13 to :40). datas ships assets, templates/assets/fonts.json, static, alembic, and a pre-warmed fastembed_cache only if that directory exists (:42 to :44, :66 to :71). Hidden imports for mem0's string-loaded vector stores and embedders: mem0.configs.vector_stores.*, mem0.embeddings.fastembed, mem0.llms.openai, mem0.vector_stores.qdrant (:48 to :52). EXE(name="fastapi", console=True, upx=False, exclude_binaries=True) plus COLLECT(name="fastapi") produce a one-folder build (:111 to :136), so the output is electron/resources/fastapi/fastapi with _internal/ next to it. server.py is the entry point. It accepts --port (required), --reload ("true" or anything else), and --log-level (default info), and always binds host = "127.0.0.1" (servers/fastapi/server.py:7 to :21). Finally copy-fastapi-assets.cjs copies servers/fastapi/static and servers/fastapi/assets beside the binary (electron/scripts/copy-fastapi-assets.cjs:8 to :11), because FastAPI resolves read-only resources relative to its working directory (see servers/fastapi/utils/path_helpers.py:15). Gotcha: dynamic imports break the frozen binary silently If you add a dependency that imports modules by string (plugins, provider registries), PyInstaller will not trace it. The symptom is an ImportError only in the packaged app, never in npm run dev (which runs uv run python server.py). Add it to hiddenimports or a safe_collect_all call in server.spec.

docs.t: Step 9: The desktop transport guard on the servers
docs.b: Part VI: Auth, infra and ops
docs.x: Both servers enforce the secret from Step 6.4 before anything else. FastAPI's version (servers/fastapi/api/v1/auth/desktop.py:25 to :48) is the first statement of SessionAuthMiddleware.dispatch (servers/fastapi/api/middlewares.py:55 to :58): servers/fastapi/api/v1/auth/desktop.py (excerpt) The Next.js twin (servers/nextjs/lib/desktop-auth.ts:14 to :44) runs first in proxy() (servers/nextjs/proxy.ts:97 to :99) and therefore covers pages, API routes, /_next/image and the asset rewrites. It uses crypto.timingSafeEqual after a length check. Decision table, identical on both servers: Condition Response PRESENTON_ELECTRON is not true Guard is a no-op (Docker, local dev without Electron) Token shorter than 32 chars or no origins configured 503 {"detail":"Desktop session unavailable"} Host header not one of the two 127.0.0.1:<port> values, or an Origin header that is not exactly one of the two origins 403 {"detail":"Forbidden desktop origin"} CORS preflight from an allowed origin (FastAPI only) Passed to the CORS middleware Header or cookie token does not match 401 {"detail":"Unauthorized"} Otherwise Request proceeds A request from a malicious web page to http://127.0.0.1:40000/api/... therefore fails three ways: its Origin is wrong, it cannot read the httpOnly cookie, and the onBeforeSendHeaders hook will not attach the header to a foreign-origin request. A DNS-rebinding page fails the Host check, which deliberately ignores X-Forwarded-Host. Server-to-server calls carry the token too. The Electron export task gets cookieHeader: desktopCookieHeader() (electron/app/ipc/export_handlers.ts:89), and both servers expose a desktop_cookie_header() helper that returns presenton_desktop_session=<token> only when PRESENTON_ELECTRON=true (servers/fastapi/api/v1/auth/desktop.py:18 to :22, servers/nextjs/lib/desktop-auth.ts:7 to :12). Gotcha: anonymous desktop calls do not inherit admin DISABLE_AUTH=true makes the desktop single-user, but the guard still runs first. servers/fastapi/tests/unit/test_desktop_security.py:76 to :79 asserts that /api/v1/auth/status, /api/v1/auth/verify, /api/v1/admin/provider-settings, /docs, /openapi.json and /app_data/userConfig.json all return 401 without the token. If you add a new route that should be reachable from a non-Electron client in desktop mode, it will not be.

It unregisters global shortcuts, stops the update checker, kills active export children, stops both servers, and calls app.exit. window-all-closed, before-quit and will-quit all route to it (:532 to :546), cancelling the default quit so cleanup finishes first. Each server's stop() calls terminateChildProcess (electron/app/utils/lifecycle.ts:110 to :146): tree-kill with SIGTERM, wait up to 5 s for close, then SIGKILL and wait 2 s, then destroy the stdio streams. tree-kill matters because uv run and npm run dev spawn grandchildren. When newer, it injects a fixed banner into the page with executeJavaScript, HTML-escaping the release message (:175 to :182), whose "Download update" link points to https://presenton.ai/download and opens in the system browser through setWindowOpenHandler. The banner is re-injected after each full navigation. electron/version.json is the file that feeds it, and generate-version.cjs rewrites it on every build:electron. At the snapshot (the long multi-line message string between version and downloads is omitted here): electron/version.json (excerpt) Gotcha: pre-release labels are ignored in version comparison 0.9.12-beta and 0.9.12 both become [0, 9, 12], so moving from a beta to the final release of the same number shows no banner. Also note that the downloads URLs are not used by the banner; it always links to the website. Gotcha: test_server.py does not match the updater's schema The root test_server.py is described as a stub for the version endpoint, but it serves GET /versions with keys latest, versions, download_url, release_notes (test_server.py:19 to :29), while the updater reads data.version and data.message from the URL it is given. Pointing UPDATE_SERVER_URL at the stub makes isNewerVersion throw on undefined.replace, which is caught and logged as "Update check failed". Serve a copy of electron/version.json instead.

docs.x: npm run build:all:mac:signed sets PRESENTON_REQUIRE_MAC_SIGNING=1, and assertDirectMacReleaseReadiness (electron/build.js:516 to :530) then requires: macOS as the build host. A Developer ID Application identity, either PRESENTON_MAC_SIGN_IDENTITY/CSC_NAME (which must exist in the keychain and must not be a development, Apple Distribution or MAS certificate) or the first one found by security find-identity -v (:532 to :583). Notarization credentials: one complete group of APPLE_ID + APPLE_APP_SPECIFIC_PASSWORD + APPLE_TEAM_ID, or APPLE_API_KEY + APPLE_API_KEY_ID + APPLE_API_ISSUER, or APPLE_KEYCHAIN_PROFILE. PRESENTON_SKIP_NOTARIZATION=1 is rejected in this mode (:593 to :623). A preflight codesign --force --sign <identity> --options runtime on a temp file with a 30 s timeout, which catches a locked keychain before electron-builder starts (:625 to :650). Signing uses signDirectMacApp (:216 to :238), which wraps @electron/osx-sign in two ways: nested data files with extensions such as .pak, .onnx, .pyc, .ttf, .wasm, .json are signed with timestamp: "none" (Apple requires secure timestamps for Mach-O code only; :61 to :95), and codesign calls that fail with a timestamp error are retried with exponential backoff capped at 30 s, PRESENTON_CODESIGN_TIMESTAMP_RETRIES times (default 4; :240 to :287). The direct entitlements (electron/build/entitlements.mac.plist) are allow-jit, allow-unsigned-executable-memory and disable-library-validation. The last one lets a hardened-runtime app load libraries that are not signed by the same team; that this is needed for the PyInstaller and ImageMagick libraries is an inference, the plist carries no comment. docs/macos/dev/direct-distribution.md documents the one-time setup (install a Developer ID Application certificate, xcrun notarytool store-credentials "presenton-notary", then export APPLE_KEYCHAIN_PROFILE="presenton-notary") and the verification commands: codesign --verify --deep --strict, xcrun stapler validate, and spctl --assess expecting source=Notarized Developer ID. docs/macos/dev/signed-dmg-build-steps.md records the full manual flow including post-build steps: sign the DMG container with codesign --timestamp, xcrun notarytool submit --wait, xcrun stapler staple, regenerate the .blockmap with app-builder blockmap, and update sha512/size in latest-mac.yml. docs.t: Part VII: Data-Bound Documents for Apache Superset
docs.p: Part VII: Data-Bound Documents for Apache Superset
docs.x: Reads: superset/core/api/core_api_injection.py, superset/commands/chart/data/get_data_command.py, superset/tasks/scheduler.py, superset/utils/pdf.py · Builds on: Part I landing · Time: ~8 min Part VII is the design half of the book. It takes what Parts I to VI showed about Presenton (prompt plus template in, finished deck out) and specifies how to build the same workflow inside Apache Superset, with one hard difference: every number in every output comes from a live Superset query, and nothing is ever a screenshot. This page states the problem, gives the answer in one paragraph, shows the whole architecture on one diagram, maps the Presenton mechanisms we reuse to the chapters that explain them, and lists every Part VII chapter in reading order.

docs.p: Part VII: Data-Bound Documents for Apache Superset
docs.x: Presenton generates a deck from a prompt and a template. Its language model writes the chart numbers itself: the chart content schema asks the model for categories and series[].values (presenton: servers/fastapi/templates/v2/schema.py:1490-1534) and the hydrator copies them into the slide (presenton: servers/fastapi/api/v1/ppt/endpoints/presentation.py:1367-1432). That is acceptable for a pitch deck written from a paragraph of notes. It is not acceptable for a quarterly business review built from a governed BI tool, where the numbers must match the dashboard to the cent and must differ correctly between two users with different row-level security. Superset, on the other hand, has the governed numbers but no way to produce a native document from them. Its Alerts and Reports feature delivers dashboards as PNG screenshots or as a PDF made of those screenshots (apache/superset: superset/utils/pdf.py:30-41), because chart rendering lives only in the browser. A slide built that way is a picture: it cannot be edited, searched, refreshed or checked. The request behind Part VII asks for both at once: a common framework that brings Presenton's automated flow to Superset for decks, documents, text and pages, triggered on demand or by events, with dynamic data and no screenshots.

docs.p: Part VII: Data-Bound Documents for Apache Superset
docs.x: Superset Data-Bound Documents (Data-Bound Documents in prose, dbd and databound in identifiers) is one output-agnostic generation framework, shipped as a preinstalled Python wheel (superset-databound-docs) plus a thin Superset extension (databound-docgen-<version>.supx, extension id databound.docgen). A user, a schedule, an alert or an agent submits a prompt, a template and a Superset data context (a filtered dashboard, charts, datasets or a SQL Lab query). A Global Task Framework task runs inside Superset as that user, builds a token-budgeted Data Digest, lets the language model plan sections and choose among validated data bindings, resolves every binding through ChartDataCommand with the user's permissions and RLS, computes facts deterministically, has the model write prose that cites those facts only through tokens such as {{f:f_rev}}, verifies that prose, and renders the resulting Document Spec into native PPTX charts with embedded workbooks, DOCX, vector PDF, Markdown, email and Slack text, or a live HTML page. The language model never writes a number, and every artifact can be refreshed in place when the data changes.

docs.p: Part VII: Data-Bound Documents for Apache Superset
docs.x: Three properties of this picture matter more than any box in it: Superset is the data plane. All data access runs in-process under override_user, through the same ChartDataCommand the dashboard uses (apache/superset: superset/commands/chart/data/get_data_command.py:36), so raise_for_access and RLS apply without any credential handling. The agent proposes, the engine disposes. The language model outputs structure, ids chosen from enums and prose with tokens. Deterministic code produces every value, label and series. One spec, many renderers. The same DocumentSpec becomes a deck, a document, a page or a text brief, and it can be re-resolved later to refresh any of them.

docs.p: Part VII: Data-Bound Documents for Apache Superset
docs.x: Read the chapters in order the first time. Each one builds on the vocabulary of the previous one. Vision and requirements: the request, the interpretation adopted, personas, twelve use cases with prompts, functional and non-functional requirements, and the exact meaning of "dynamic data" and "no screenshots". Superset landscape (6.1): every Superset API and extension point the design builds on, with a 6.1.0 versus master availability table and the reasons Alerts and Reports cannot be reused for rendering. Target architecture: components, processes, deployment topology, configuration and the decisions that shaped them. Data-bound slide model: the Document Spec, bindings, facts, the token grammar, template data slots and provenance. Generation flow: the ten steps from Context Capture to export, with prompts, schemas, the Narrative Verifier and the event protocol. Native rendering, no screenshots: the PPTX, DOCX, HTML, PDF and Text Renderers, the viz_type mapping and the no-screenshot guarantee. Building the Superset extension: the .supx bundle, REST API, GTF tasks, MCP tools, frontend contributions and the Superset Adapter. Building the generation service: the databound_docs wheel, storage tables, the LLM provider layer, caching and Celery routing. Security, RLS, auth: identity propagation, permissions, RLS-safe narratives, sharing, prompt injection and webhook hardening. Scheduling and live refresh: live pages, refresh in place, narrative policies, triggers and provenance stamps. Roadmap: MVP, v1 and v2 scope, testing, prototype gates, risks and the upstream SIP outline.

Reads: superset/commands/chart/data/get_data_command.py, superset/charts/data/api.py, superset/reports/notifications/webhook.py, superset/utils/pdf.py, servers/fastapi/templates/v2/schema.py · Builds on: Part VII landing · Time: ~30 min This chapter turns a one-paragraph request into a specification you can build and test. You will read the request, the interpretation this design adopts and why, the people who use the system, twelve concrete use cases with the exact prompts and triggers they involve, the functional and non-functional requirements with numeric targets, and precise definitions of "dynamic data" and "no screenshots" that later chapters implement. It ends with the explicit non-goals, which matter as much as the goals because they keep the design small enough to ship on Superset 6.1.

The request that drives Part VII, in substance: I want to create a common framework and integrate it with Apache Superset, the way Presenton provides an automated workflow. You can generate a PPT out of it just by giving some prompts and, let's say, choosing some templates. Similarly, I want the same flow to be present for Apache Superset's documents, text, or pages for different event features, so that the user can automatically generate these things on the fly. It should also support dynamic data, and the prepared PPT should use dynamic data. It shouldn't use screenshots. Think from that perspective, and design a step-by-step technical-level explanation with respect to how it should be implemented for the Apache Superset project. Six phrases in it carry the requirements: Phrase What it demands Where it is met "a common framework" One engine and one data model shared by every output type, not four separate generators Data-bound slide model "the way Presenton provides an automated workflow" Prompt plus template in, finished artifact out, with Presenton's staged pipeline Generation flow "documents, text, or pages" Decks are only one of four output families Native rendering, no screenshots "for different event features ... on the fly" Interactive generation in seconds, plus generation started by events Scheduling and live refresh "dynamic data ... the prepared PPT should use dynamic data" Numbers come from live queries and can be refreshed in an already prepared file Scheduling and live refresh "It shouldn't use screenshots" No pixel capture of Superset UI anywhere, including the PDF path Native rendering, no screenshots

The design reads the request as follows, and every later chapter is bound by this reading. Build one common, output-agnostic generation framework, Superset Data-Bound Documents. It turns three inputs into an artifact: a prompt in natural language ("Q3 review for EMEA leadership, focus on growth drivers"); a chosen template from the Template Registry (a deck layout set, a document master, a page template or a text brief template); a Superset data context: a dashboard with its live native-filter state, saved charts, datasets with their saved metrics, a semantic view [M], or a SQL Lab query. It produces four kinds of output: (a) PowerPoint decks (PPTX) with native, editable charts, tables, KPI groups and speaker notes. (b) Documents: DOCX, PDF (printed from vector HTML) and Markdown. (c) Text: narratives, executive summaries, emails, Slack posts and alert briefs. (d) Web pages: interactive HTML reports that re-query as each viewer opens them, and in v2, generated Superset dashboards. Generation starts in one of two ways: On demand: a button or chat message in Superset, a REST call, or an MCP tool call from an agent. By events: cron schedules (cron), Superset Alerts firing a webhook when a data condition holds (alert_webhook), data freshness changes (freshness), chart or dashboard definition changes (definition_change) and signed external webhooks from tools such as dbt or Airflow (external_webhook). The data rules are strict and non-negotiable: Every chart, table, KPI and number comes from a live Superset query run with the requesting user's permissions and row-level security (RLS). For scheduled and event runs, the explicitly recorded run-as user is used instead. Data elements are rendered natively: editable PPTX and DOCX charts with an embedded workbook, real tables, real text, vector SVG on the web. No Superset UI page is ever captured as pixels. Every artifact is re-runnable. A refresh re-executes the queries and replaces data in place. The language model is involved in a refresh only when the narrative policy requires it. "The Presenton flow" means Presenton's stage shape (outline, layout structure, schema-constrained content, hydration, export; see Standard generation pipeline) with one essential change. Presenton asks the model for chart categories and series[].values (presenton: servers/fastapi/templates/v2/schema.py:1490-1534). Here, the language

Persona Superset role (typical) What they do with Data-Bound Documents Permissions on DataBoundDocs Analyst (author) Alpha or Gamma with dataset access Generates decks and reports from dashboards, refines them in chat, exports, shares can_read, can_generate, can_write, can_refresh Executive (consumer) Gamma, often read-only Receives emails and decks, opens live pages, asks for a quick brief can_read, sometimes can_generate for text briefs Regional manager (RLS viewer) Gamma with RLS restricting rows to a region Opens a shared live page and sees only their region's numbers and prose consistent with them can_read BI engineer (template admin) Alpha or Admin Imports branded PPTX and DOCX masters with named slots, publishes templates to roles, sets data exposure policies can_manage_templates, can_admin for policies Platform operator Superset Admin Installs the wheel and .supx, configures DATABOUND_DOCS, Celery routing, storage and the LLM endpoint, runs superset dbd doctor can_admin Scheduler owner Alpha Creates cron, alert and freshness triggers with an explicit run-as user, chooses delivery targets can_schedule Agent developer API or MCP client Drives generation from an external agent through dbd_* MCP tools or REST Same permissions as the user the agent resolves to On-call engineer Gamma Receives an alert brief in Slack within a minute of an alert firing, follows links to the live dashboard can_read The persona that shapes the design most is the regional manager. Because a shared live page re-resolves every binding as the viewer, two managers looking at the same page must see different numbers, and neither may see prose that was written from the other's data. That single requirement is why prose carries tokens instead of literal values or category names (see Security, RLS, auth).
